docs.title: ECEG-4192 — Data Structures
docs.text:
BSc Electrical Engineering (Computer) · Semester VII · Module: Data Storage and Analysis

This course builds the toolkit every computer engineer needs: how to store, organize, and manipulate data efficiently. You will learn the classic data structures — arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, and graphs — along with their operations, their complexity, and the trade-offs between them. You will also learn how to analyse an algorithm formally, using Big-O notation.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Analyse algorithms rigorously

    Write Big-O bounds for iterative and recursive code. Reason about best, average, and worst cases. Distinguish complexity from actual runtime.

  • Implement classic data structures

    Build arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, BSTs, AVL trees, heaps, hash tables, and graph representations from scratch — in Java and Python.

  • Choose the right structure

    Given an application, pick the structure that gives the best time/space trade-off. Justify the choice with complexity analysis.

  • Apply graph algorithms

    Traverse graphs with DFS and BFS. Solve shortest-path and minimum-spanning-tree problems. Recognise when each applies.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• Introduction & Analysis of Algorithms

    What a data structure is, why abstraction matters, and how to express runtime with Big-O notation.

    Chapter 1

  • Arrays

    Contiguous memory, indexing arithmetic, insertion and deletion costs, and when arrays beat everything else.

    Chapter 2

  • Linked Lists

    Nodes, pointers, singly vs. doubly-linked, circular lists — and the operation costs that differ from arrays.

    Chapter 3

  • Stacks and Queues

    LIFO and FIFO, array vs. linked implementations, and the algorithmic problems they solve.

    Chapter 4

  • Trees

    Binary trees, binary search trees, AVL balance, B+-trees, heaps, and tree traversals.

    Chapter 5

  • Hash Tables

    Hashing, hash functions, collisions, open addressing, and separate chaining — the fastest lookup structure.

    Chapter 6

  • Graphs

    Adjacency matrix vs. adjacency list, DFS, BFS, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees.

    Chapter 7

  • Sorting Algorithms

    Bubble, insertion, selection, merge, quicksort, heapsort — with complexity and stability trade-offs.

    Chapter 8

Test Covers Learning outcomes Test 1 (week 6) Ch 1–3 LO1, LO2, LO3 Test 2 (week 11) Ch 4–5 LO4, LO5

docs.text:
3 hours, closed book, one handwritten A4 formula sheet. Covers all chapters, roughly proportional to teaching hours:

Chapter Weight in final 1 — Introduction & Big-O 10% 2 — Arrays 8% 3 — Linked Lists 10% 4 — Stacks & Queues 12% 5 — Trees 20% 6 — Hash Tables 10% 7 — Graphs 20% 8 — Sorting 10%

Structure. 5–7 multi-part questions: - 2–3 structural problems (build a tree, trace a hash table, run a graph algorithm) - 1–2 complexity analyses (prove Big-O of code) - 1–2 comparison / design questions (which structure fits X, justify)

Permitted on formula sheet: Big-O table, tree rotation rules, hash probing formulas, sorting comparison table.

docs.title: Exam Bank — ECEG-4192 Data Structures
docs.text: 40 questions spanning all chapters. 3 hours. Closed book; one A4 handwritten formula sheet. 100 marks. Answer key and grading rubric at the end.

docs.title: Section A — Introduction & Big-O (10 marks)
docs.text:
A1. Multiple choice [2]. Which of these is a valid Big-O simplification?

(a) \(n^2 + n = O(n)\) (b) \(5n + 3 = O(n)\) (c) \(n \log n = O(n)\) (d) \(n^2 = O(n)\)

A2. Multiple choice [2]. The recurrence \(T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)\) solves to:

(a) \(O(n)\) (b) \(O(n \log n)\) (c) \(O(n^2)\) (d) \(O(2^n)\)

A3. Short answer [3]. State the formal definition of Big-O. Use it to prove that \(4n^2 + 3n = O(n^2)\) with explicit witnesses \((c, n_0)\).

A4. Derivation [3]. A loop has structure: for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 3) { for (j = 0; j < i; j++) { ... } }. Derive the total operation count as a function of \(n\) and state its Big-O.

docs.title: Section B — Arrays (10 marks)
docs.text:
B1. Multiple choice [2]. Inserting an element at position 0 of an n-element array costs:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

B2. Multiple choice [2]. Adding \(n\) elements to a dynamic array with doubling has total cost:

(a) O(n) (b) O(n log n) (c) O(n²) (d) O(2ⁿ)

B3. Short answer [3]. Prove that a[i] on an array takes O(1) time. Write the address arithmetic and count the primitive operations.

B4. Derivation [3]. An array of size \(n\) is rotated by \(k\) positions in place using the reverse-three-times trick. Show the three reversals restore the array, and give the time and space complexity.

docs.title: Section C — Linked Lists (10 marks)
docs.text:
C1. Multiple choice [2]. Deleting a given node in a doubly-linked list (given a pointer to it) costs:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

C2. Multiple choice [2]. Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm uses:

(a) hash set (b) stack (c) two pointers at different speeds (d) recursion

C3. Short answer [3]. Draw the state after each step of inserting 10, 20, 30 at the head of a singly-linked list. Final list order?

C4. Derivation [3]. Write the recurrence for the reverse of a singly-linked list (iterative version) and justify that it runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

docs.title: Section D — Stacks & Queues (12 marks)
docs.text:
D1. Multiple choice [2]. The circular queue wrap-around exists to avoid:

(a) overflow (b) O(n) shifts on dequeue (c) null pointers (d) recursion

D2. Multiple choice [2]. Postfix expression "5 3 2 * +" evaluates to:

(a) 16 (b) 11 (c) 10 (d) 25

D3. Short answer [4]. Evaluate "4 5 + 6 2 - * 3 +" using a stack. Show the stack after each token.

D4. Derivation [4]. Implement a FIFO queue using two LIFO stacks. State the amortised cost of enqueue and dequeue, with proof.

docs.title: Section E — Trees (20 marks)
docs.text:
E1. Multiple choice [2]. In-order traversal of a BST gives:

(a) pre-order (b) post-order (c) sorted order (d) reverse-sorted order

E2. Multiple choice [2]. AVL trees guarantee what height bound?

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

E3. Short answer [3]. Insert 10, 20, 30 into an empty BST. Draw the result. What is its height? Compare with the height of an AVL tree built from the same keys.

E4. Short answer [3]. Delete node 50 (root) from the tree below. Which case does this fall into? Show the tree after deletion.

      50
     /  \
    30   70
   / \   / \
  20 40 60 80

E5. Derivation [5]. Build a min-heap from [7, 3, 9, 1, 8, 2, 6] using bottom-up heapify. Show the array after each siftDown call. Then extract the minimum twice, showing the array after each.

E6. Derivation [5]. Trace the AVL insertion of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order. After each insertion, state whether a rotation was needed, and if so which type (LL / RR / LR / RL) and show the tree before and after.

docs.title: Section F — Hash Tables (10 marks)
docs.text:
F1. Multiple choice [2]. Separate chaining achieves average-case lookup:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

F2. Multiple choice [2]. Which clustering problem does linear probing suffer from?

(a) primary clustering (b) secondary clustering (c) tombstone accumulation (d) integer overflow

F3. Short answer [3]. Insert {10, 20, 30, 40} into a hash table of size m = 7 using linear probing. Use h(k) = k mod 7. Show the table after each insertion. What is the maximum probe count?

F4. Derivation [3]. Explain the tombstone problem in open addressing. Give a concrete example (small table) where setting deleted slots to EMPTY breaks lookups.

docs.title: Section G — Graphs (18 marks)
docs.text:
G1. Multiple choice [2]. Adjacency list memory is:

(a) O(n) (b) O(n + m) (c) O(n²) (d) O(2ⁿ)

G2. Multiple choice [2]. Dijkstra's algorithm requires:

(a) non-negative weights (b) at least one negative edge (c) symmetric graph (d) directed graph

G3. Short answer [3]. Run BFS on the following undirected graph from vertex 0. Give the visit order and the distance to each vertex.

0 — 1 — 3
|   |   |
2 — 4 — 5

G4. Short answer [3]. For the weighted graph below, run Dijkstra's algorithm from vertex 0. Show the distance array after each extraction. Edges: 0→1 (4), 0→2 (1), 1→3 (1), 2→1 (3), 2→3 (5), 3→4 (2), 2→4 (6).

G5. Derivation [4]. Construct a graph with negative weights where Dijkstra's algorithm returns the wrong answer but Bellman–Ford returns the correct one. Show both algorithms' traces on the graph.

G6. Derivation [4]. Run Kruskal's algorithm on the following 6-vertex graph. Sort edges, process in order, and show the MST.

Edge Weight (0,1) 6 (0,2) 5 (1,2) 1 (1,3) 5 (2,3) 5 (2,4) 6 (3,4) 2 (3,5) 4 (4,5) 6

docs.title: Section H — Sorting (10 marks)
docs.text:
H1. Multiple choice [2]. Which sort is stable and in-place?

(a) Merge sort (b) Quicksort (c) Insertion sort (d) Heapsort

H2. Multiple choice [2]. Quicksort's worst-case complexity is:

(a) O(n log n) (b) O(n) (c) O(n²) (d) O(2ⁿ)

H3. Short answer [3]. Trace insertion sort on [4, 1, 3, 2]. Show the array after each outer iteration. Count the total shifts.

H4. Derivation [3]. Explain why merge sort uses O(n) auxiliary space. Give one scenario where heapsort is preferred over merge sort despite both being O(n log n).

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Section A

A1. (b) — \(5n + 3 = O(n)\). All others fail.

A2. (b) — \(O(n \log n)\) (merge-sort recurrence). Recursion tree: depth \(\log n\), work per level \(O(n)\).

A3. Definition: \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if \(\exists c, n_0 > 0\) with \(f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\). Proof: need \(4n^2 + 3n \le c n^2\). Try \(c = 7\): \(4n^2 + 3n \le 7n^2\) ⟺ \(3n \le 3n^2\) ⟺ \(n \ge 1\). Witness: \(c = 7\), \(n_0 = 1\).

A4. Outer loop iterations: \(i = 1, 3, 9, 27, \ldots\) — stop when \(i \ge n\), i.e., \(\log_3 n\) iterations. Inner loop iteration count per outer iteration equals \(i\). Total operations: \(\sum_{i \in \{1, 3, 9, \ldots\}} i = 1 + 3 + 9 + \ldots + 3^{\log_3 n} = \frac{3^{\log_3 n + 1} - 1}{2} = \Theta(n)\). Big-O: \(O(n)\).

Section B

B1. (c) — O(n) shifting all elements right.

B2. (a) — O(n) total (geometric series sum: \(1 + 2 + 4 + \ldots + 2^{k} < 2n\)).

B3. Address of a[i] = base + i × width. Computation: one multiplication, one addition, one memory load = 3 primitive instructions, independent of i and n. O(1).

B4. Correctness: Let array = \(A[0..n-1]\). Rotation by \(k\) = permute to \(A[n-k..n-1]\) followed by \(A[0..n-k-1]\). Let \(U = A[0..n-k-1]\), \(V = A[n-k..n-1]\); result = \(VU\). Reverse 1: \(A \to (UV)^R = V^R U^R\). Reverse 2: reverse first \(k\) elements (which is \(V^R\)) \(\to V\). Now \(V U^R\). Reverse 3: reverse \(U^R\) portion \(\to U\). Result \(VU\). ✓ Cost: three O(n) reversals = O(n) time, O(1) space.

Section C

C1. (a) — O(1) using the prev pointer.

C2. (c) — two pointers at different speeds (slow 1 step, fast 2 steps per iteration).

C3. Insert 10: 10 → null. Insert 20: 20 → 10 → null. Insert 30: 30 → 20 → 10 → null. Final: 30 → 20 → 10 — reversed relative to insertion.

C4. Recurrence: one pass, each node visited once → T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1), solving to O(n). Space: only prev, cur, next variables — constant per iteration → O(1) auxiliary.

Section D

D1. (b) — O(n) shifts on dequeue (or O(n²) total).

D2. (b) — 11. Trace: 5, 3, 2 → push. * → pop 2, 3, push 6. + → pop 6, 5, push 11.

D3. Trace:

Token Action Stack 4 push [4] 5 push [4, 5] + pop 5,4; push 9 [9] 6 push [9, 6] 2 push [9, 6, 2] − pop 2,6; push 4 [9, 4] * pop 4,9; push 36 [36] 3 push [36, 3] + pop 3,36; push 39 [39]

Result: 39.

D4. Two stacks: in_stack (enqueue), out_stack (dequeue). Enqueue: push to in_stack. Dequeue: if out_stack empty, pop all from in_stack onto out_stack; pop top of out_stack. Amortised: each element pushed once to in_stack, moved once to out_stack, popped once — 3 operations total → O(1) amortised. Worst case single dequeue is O(n) if out_stack empty.

Section E

E1. (c) — sorted order.

E2. (b) — O(log n) (balance factor invariant guarantees height ≤ 1.44 log₂ n).

E3. BST: 10 \ 20 \ 30 (right-skewed). Height = 2 (edge count) or 3 (node count). AVL: after 30, RR rotation at 10 → 20 / 10 \ 30. Height = 1 (edge count) or 2. Both trees have the same 3 keys — different shapes.

E4. Case 3 (two children). In-order successor of 50 is 60 (smallest in right subtree = leftmost of 70's subtree = 60). Replace 50 with 60, delete 60 from its leaf.

      60
     /  \
    30   70
   / \    \
  20 40   80

E5. Starting array: [7, 3, 9, 1, 8, 2, 6]. n = 7, last internal = 7/2 − 1 = 2.

  • i=2 (value 9): children 8 (idx 5), 6 (idx 6). Min = 6. 9>6 → swap. [7, 3, 6, 1, 8, 2, 9].
  • i=1 (value 3): children 1, 8. Min = 1. 3>1 → swap. [7, 1, 6, 3, 8, 2, 9]. At idx 3 (value 3): no children.
  • i=0 (value 7): children 1, 6. Min = 1. 7>1 → swap. [1, 7, 6, 3, 8, 2, 9]. At idx 1 (value 7): children 3, 8. Min = 3. 7>3 → swap. [1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 2, 9]. At idx 3 (value 7): no children.

Heap: [1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 2, 9].

Extract 1 (min): save 1, move last (9) to root: [9, 3, 6, 7, 8, 2]. Sift-down: children 3, 6. Min 3 (idx 1). 9>3 swap → [3, 9, 6, 7, 8, 2]. At idx 1 (9): children 7, 8. Min 7 (idx 3). 9>7 swap → [3, 7, 6, 9, 8, 2]. At idx 3 (9): no children. Extracted: 1. Heap: [3, 7, 6, 9, 8, 2].

Extract 3 (min): save 3, move last (2) to root: [2, 7, 6, 9, 8]. Sift-down: children 7, 6. Min 6 (idx 2). 2<6 no swap. Extracted: 3. Heap: [2, 7, 6, 9, 8].

E6. AVL insertion trace for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5:

Insert Tree Rotation? 1 1 No 2 1 \ 2 No 3 1 \ 2 \ 3 RR at 1 → 2 / 1 \ 3 4 2 / 1 \ 3 \ 4 No 5 2 / 1 \ 3 \ 4 \ 5 RR at 3 → 2 / 1 \ 4 / 3 \ 5

All trees balanced after rotations. ✓

Section F

F1. (a) — O(1) average (O(1 + α) where α is load factor).

F2. (a) — primary clustering (long consecutive runs of occupied slots grow faster).

F3. Hash values: 10 mod 7 = 3, 20 mod 7 = 6, 30 mod 7 = 2, 40 mod 7 = 5. All distinct — no collisions. Table: [_, _, 30, 10, _, 40, 20] (indices 0..6). Max probes: 1.

(If asked "insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50" with 50 mod 7 = 1 — still distinct. With 40 mod 7 = 5, and 45 mod 7 = 3 → collides with 10 at 3 → probe 4. Max probes: 2.)

F4. Tombstone problem: suppose keys 10, 20, 30 all hash to slot 0 (linear probing). Table: [10, 20, 30, _, _]. Delete 20: setting slot 1 to EMPTY. Now lookup 30: hash to 0 → slot 0 (10, no match) → slot 1 (EMPTY → stop, not found). But 30 is at slot 2 — the search terminated too early. Fix: mark deleted slots as DELETED (tombstone), not EMPTY. Lookup continues past DELETED; only stops on EMPTY.

Section G

G1. (b) — O(n + m).

G2. (a) — non-negative weights required.

G3. BFS from 0:

Step Queue Visited 0 [0] {0} 1 [1, 2] {0,1,2} 2 [2, 3, 4] + 3 [3, 4] (2 has no new) 4 [4, 5] + 5 [5] — 6 [] done

Visit order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Distances: [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3].

G4. Dijkstra from 0:

Init: dist = [0, ∞, ∞, ∞, ∞].

Pop Relaxations dist (0, 0) 0→1: 4, 0→2: 1 [0, 4, 1, ∞, ∞] (2, 1) 2→1: 1+3=4 (no change), 2→3: 1+5=6, 2→4: 1+6=7 [0, 4, 1, 6, 7] (1, 4) 1→3: 4+1=5 < 6 → update [0, 4, 1, 5, 7] (3, 5) 3→4: 5+2=7 (no change) [0, 4, 1, 5, 7] (4, 7) none done

Final: [0, 4, 1, 5, 7].

G5. Graph: edges s→u (1), s→v (2), u→v (-5), u→w (10).

Dijkstra from s: - Pop s(0), relax: u←1, v←2. - Pop u(1), relax u→v: 1+(-5) = -4 < 2 → v←-4. u→w: 11. - Pop v(-4), no outgoing better. - Pop w(10).

Actually, to make Dijkstra fail, we need it to settle a node before a shorter path is discovered. Classic example: s→u (1), s→v (2), u→v (-5). Dijkstra pops u at 1, then v at -4 (via u), still correct here.

Failure case: s→u (5), s→v (3), u→v (-10), u→w (1), v→w (1). - Pop s(0), relax: u←5, v←3. - Pop v(3), relax v→w: 3+1 = 4. w←4. - Pop w(4) — settled at 4. - Pop u(5), relax u→v: 5 + (-10) = -5 < 3 → v←-5. u→w: 5+1 = 6 > 4, no change. - Pop v(-5). - Dijkstra returns w = 4. - Bellman–Ford: correct answer is w = 5 + (-10) + 1 = -4 (path s→u→v→w). Bellman–Ford gets it right because it relaxes all edges V-1 times.

G6. Kruskal trace:

Sorted edges: (1,2,1), (3,4,2), (3,5,4), (0,2,5), (1,3,5), (2,3,5), (0,1,6), (2,4,6), (4,5,6).

Edge Add? MST (1,2,1) ✓ {(1,2)} (3,4,2) ✓ {(1,2), (3,4)} (3,5,4) ✓ {(1,2), (3,4), (3,5)} (0,2,5) ✓ {(1,2), (3,4), (3,5), (0,2)} (1,3,5) ✓ (merges two components) {(1,2), (3,4), (3,5), (0,2), (1,3)} (2,3,5) ✗ (cycle) — (0,1,6) ✗ (cycle) —

MST edges: {(1,2), (3,4), (3,5), (0,2), (1,3)}, total weight = 17. ✓

Section H

H1. (c) — insertion sort is stable and in-place.

H2. (c) — O(n²).

H3. Trace [4, 1, 3, 2]:

i key shifts Array 1 1 1 (4) [1, 4, 3, 2] 2 3 1 (4) [1, 3, 4, 2] 3 2 2 (4, 3) [1, 2, 3, 4]

Total shifts: 4.

H4. Merge sort space: the merge step needs a temporary array of size \(n\) to hold the merged result before copying back. Hence O(n) auxiliary. Heapsort preferred when: O(1) auxiliary space is required (embedded systems, memory-constrained environments) — heapsort is in-place, merge sort is not. Also: heapsort has O(n log n) worst case while quicksort can degrade.

docs.title: Grading rubric
docs.text:
Band Marks Criteria A 90–100 All correct or with trivial arithmetic slips; traces and derivations rigorous B 75–89 Most correct; occasional conceptual gaps C 60–74 Basic understanding; some errors F < 60 Major gaps

Common error checks (deductions):

  • Wrong Big-O (dropping leading term or keeping constant): −1 to −2.
  • Confusing BST / heap ordering: −2.
  • Missing balance factor check in AVL rotation: −1.
  • Wrong heap array index ((i-1)/2 vs. i/2): −1.
  • Omitting tombstone in open-addressing delete: −2.
  • Dijkstra with negative edge: −2 to −3.
  • Forgetting MST has V−1 edges: −1.
  • Claiming quicksort stable: −1.
  • Not showing trace steps: −2 to −5 (partial credit depends on correct final answer alone).

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Introduction, Data Abstraction, and Analysis of Algorithms
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): introduction · overview of data structures · data abstraction · introduction to the analysis of algorithms · Big-O notation.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Say what a data structure is, and why a course about them exists.
  2. Distinguish an abstract data type (ADT) from a data structure implementation.
  3. Write the Big-O bounds of simple loops and nested loops.
  4. Distinguish Big-O, Big-\(\Omega\), and Big-\(\Theta\) notation.
  5. Analyse the complexity of a recursive algorithm by writing its recurrence and solving it.
  6. Recognise the common complexity classes (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)) and give one example of each.
  7. Explain why Big-O ignores constants but why those constants still matter in practice.

docs.title: 1.1 Why a course on data structures?
1.1.1 The problem
docs.text:
Programs spend most of their time finding, storing, and retrieving data. How that data is laid out in memory decides whether a program finishes in milliseconds or hours.

Two implementations of the same idea can differ by a factor of millions in runtime. Not a small percentage — a factor of 10⁶.

Concrete example. Suppose you store \(n = 10{,}000\) student records and want to find one by name:

  • Unsorted array, scan every record: up to \(10{,}000\) comparisons.
  • Sorted array, binary search: about \(\log_2(10{,}000) \approx 14\) comparisons.
  • Hash table: 1–2 comparisons, on average.

Same data. Same computer. Same programmer. Different storage strategy — 700× faster.

docs.title: 1.1.2 What a data structure is
docs.text:
Definition — Data structure

A data structure is a way of organizing data in memory together with the set of operations that can be performed on that data efficiently.

Notice both halves of the definition:

  • The layout — where each item lives in memory, how items relate to each other.
  • The operations — insert, delete, search, iterate, findMinimum — each has a cost.

A data structure is not just "how the data is stored." It is how the data is stored plus what it lets you do cheaply.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Two roles of a data structure
docs.text:
In practice you do two things with data structures:

  1. Use existing ones — pick from the standard library, justify the choice with complexity analysis.
  2. Create new ones — when no standard structure fits, build a new one out of the existing building blocks.

The rest of this course develops both skills: the first through implementation of the classics, the second through the reasoning that makes each classic work.

docs.title: 1.1.4 The recurring theme — time versus space
docs.text:
Every data structure trades time against space. Almost always:

  • More space = faster access (arrays: contiguous, O(1) indexing, but wasteful if sparse).
  • Less space = slower access (linked lists: no wasted memory, but O(n) lookup).

There is no free lunch. The rest of the course is a study of specific trade-offs.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The idea of abstraction
docs.text:
Abstraction means hiding the details behind a simple interface. You already know this from OOP:

  • You use List<String> without knowing whether it's an ArrayList or a LinkedList inside.
  • You call add(x) without thinking about resizing or pointer updates.

Data structures push this idea further. They separate what a structure does from how it does it.

docs.title: 1.2.2 ADT — Abstract Data Type
docs.text:
Definition — Abstract data type (ADT)

An abstract data type is a specification of a set of values and a set of operations, independent of any particular implementation.

An ADT says: "There is a collection of elements, and you can do these things with them." It does not say: "Elements are stored in an array" or "Elements are stored in nodes connected by pointers."

Examples of ADTs you'll meet in this course:

ADT Operations specified Possible implementations List insert, delete, get, size, iterate Array, linked list, dynamic array Stack push, pop, peek, isEmpty Array, linked list Queue enqueue, dequeue, peek Array, circular array, linked list Map / Dictionary put, get, remove, containsKey Hash table, balanced tree Set add, remove, contains Hash table, balanced tree Priority Queue insert, extractMin Binary heap, sorted array

Notice the pattern: one ADT, many implementations. The interface is the same; the cost of operations differs.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Why abstraction pays off
docs.text:
Three concrete reasons:

1. Choose the implementation that fits.

A program that only needs insert at the front and iterate is well-served by a linked list. A program that needs random access by index wants an array. The ADT tells you what the caller needs; the implementation is the engineer's decision.

2. Change it later without breaking callers.

If your code calls only stack.push(x) and stack.pop(), you can swap the underlying array for a linked list without touching the caller. The interface is the contract, and the implementation is free to change.

3. Reason at the interface level.

When reasoning about correctness or complexity, you can say "this algorithm makes \(n\) calls to insert" — that's true regardless of implementation. Cost analysis then multiplies by the per-operation cost of the chosen implementation.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — Same ADT, different costs
docs.text:
Consider a List ADT with three operations: insertAtEnd(x), get(i), and deleteAtEnd().

Two implementations:

Array-based list (contiguous memory):

Operation Cost Why insertAtEnd(x) O(1) amortised Append at index size; occasionally double the array (amortised) get(i) O(1) Direct indexing: array[i] deleteAtEnd() O(1) Decrement size

Linked-list (nodes with next pointers):

Operation Cost Why insertAtEnd(x) O(n) (or O(1) with tail pointer) Walk to the end get(i) O(n) Walk i steps deleteAtEnd() O(n) (or O(1) with doubly-linked + tail) Walk to the end

Interpretation. Same three operations, same names, same semantics. The array implementation is dramatically faster for these three operations. If you had chosen a linked list without thinking, you would have made the program hundreds of times slower for no reason.

The lesson. The ADT tells you what to expect. Complexity analysis tells you which implementation delivers.

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Choosing the right ADT for a problem
docs.text:
You are building a text editor that needs to:

  • Insert characters at the cursor position
  • Delete the character before the cursor
  • Move the cursor left or right
  • Undo the last operation

Which ADT fits?

Candidate 1: Array (dynamic). Insert at position p costs O(n) because everything after p shifts. For a 100,000-character document, editing near the start shifts 100,000 characters — perceptibly slow.

Candidate 2: Linked list (doubly-linked). Insert at cursor = O(1) (splice between two nodes). Cursor move = O(1). Undo = O(1) with a stack of operations. This fits.

Choice: a doubly-linked list plus a stack for undo.

Justification. The operations that must be fast (insert, delete, cursor move, undo) are all O(1) in this combination. The operations that would be slow (random access by index) are not needed — the editor never jumps to "position 72,391" directly.

This is the pattern: write down the operations, write down the cost of each in each candidate implementation, pick the one whose hot path is cheapest.

docs.title: 1.3 Analysing algorithms — the need for a formal measure
1.3.1 Why not just "run it and time it"?
docs.text:
Suppose you write a function sort and want to know how fast it is. You could:

import time
start = time.time()
sort(data)
elapsed = time.time() - start
print(f"{elapsed:.3f} s")

This gives you a number, but the number is useless for comparison across:

  • Machines. A laptop and a phone give different times.
  • Languages. The same algorithm in Python and C differ by 100×.
  • Data sizes. The result on 100 items tells you nothing about 10⁶ items.
  • Inputs. The same algorithm can be fast on sorted data and slow on random data.

What we want is a machine-independent, size-relative measure of how the algorithm's cost grows with input size.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Counting operations
docs.text:
Instead of wall-clock time, count primitive operations:

  • The number of comparisons
  • The number of assignments
  • The number of array accesses
  • The number of nodes visited

Different primitives have different physical times, but in asymptotic analysis they all count as one "step." The result is a step count \(T(n)\) as a function of input size \(n\).

Example. The array-sum function:

int sum(int[] a) {
    int total = 0;                 // 1 step
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {   // n+1 comparisons, n increments
        total += a[i];             // n additions
    }
    return total;                  // 1 step
}

Total steps: \(1 + (n+1) + n + n + 1 = 3n + 3\).

We say: \(T(n) = 3n + 3\), i.e., "the cost grows linearly in \(n\)."

docs.title: 1.3.3 Growth, not absolute value
docs.text:
The key question is not "how many steps at \(n = 100\)?" but "how many steps at \(n = 1000\), \(n = 10^6\)?"

\(n\) \(T(n) = 3n + 3\) \(T(n) = 0.001 n^2 + 5\) 10 33 5.1 100 303 15 1,000 3,003 1,005 10,000 30,003 100,005 1,000,000 3,000,003 1,000,000,005

For small \(n\), the quadratic (with a small leading constant) is faster. For large \(n\), the linear algorithm wins by a factor of ~300,000. Growth rate is what matters, and Big-O captures it.

docs.title: 1.4.1 The formal definition
docs.text:
Definition — Big-O

We write \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if there exist positive constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that

\[ f(n) \le c \cdot g(n) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0. \]

In words: \(f\) grows no faster than a constant times \(g\), eventually.

The intuition. \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) means "\(g\) is an upper bound on the growth of \(f\)." It ignores constants and small values of \(n\) — what's left is the shape of the growth curve.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Proving a Big-O claim
docs.text: To prove \(f(n) = O(g(n))\), you need to find constants \(c\) and \(n_0\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.3 — Prove \(3n + 3 = O(n)\)
docs.text:
We need \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that \(3n + 3 \le c \cdot n\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

Try \(c = 4\): \(3n + 3 \le 4n\) ⟺ \(3 \le n\). This holds for all \(n \ge 3\).

Try \(c = 6\): \(3n + 3 \le 6n\) ⟺ \(3 \le 3n\) ⟺ \(1 \le n\). Holds for \(n \ge 1\).

Conclusion. \(3n + 3 = O(n)\), with witness \(c = 6\), \(n_0 = 1\). ✓

Interpretation. For large \(n\), the linear term dominates; the constant term is negligible.

docs.title: Worked example 1.4 — Prove \(n^2 - 5n + 7 = O(n^2)\)
docs.text:
We need \(c, n_0\) such that \(n^2 - 5n + 7 \le c n^2\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

Try \(c = 2\): \(n^2 - 5n + 7 \le 2n^2\) ⟺ \(7 - 5n \le n^2\). Since \(n^2 \ge 0\) and \(7 - 5n \le 7\), we need \(7 \le n^2\) — holds for \(n \ge 3\).

Conclusion. \(n^2 - 5n + 7 = O(n^2)\), with witness \(c = 2\), \(n_0 = 3\). ✓

Interpretation. For large \(n\), the \(n^2\) term dominates both the linear and the constant terms.

docs.title: Worked example 1.5 — Prove a tighter bound
docs.text:
Prove \(5n^2 + 3n \ne O(n)\).

Proof by contradiction. Suppose \(5n^2 + 3n = O(n)\). Then there exist \(c, n_0\) such that \(5n^2 + 3n \le c \cdot n\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

Divide by \(n\) (positive): \(5n + 3 \le c\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

But \(5n + 3\) grows without bound as \(n\) grows. For any fixed \(c\), there exists \(n > (c - 3)/5\) where the inequality fails. Contradiction.

Conclusion. \(5n^2 + 3n \ne O(n)\) — the quadratic term makes the growth strictly faster than linear.

docs.title: 1.4.3 Rules of Big-O arithmetic
docs.text:
The following rules let you simplify expressions quickly:

Rule Statement Example Drop constants \(c \cdot f(n) = O(f(n))\) \(7n = O(n)\) Drop lower-order terms \(f(n) + g(n) = O(\max(f, g))\) \(n^2 + n = O(n^2)\) Transitivity \(f = O(g)\) and \(g = O(h)\) ⇒ \(f = O(h)\) — Sum rule \(f + g = O(\max(f, g))\) \(n \log n + n = O(n \log n)\) Product rule \(f \cdot g = O(f \cdot g)\) \(n \cdot \log n = O(n \log n)\)

The trick that catches students. In \(O(n^2 + n)\), the \(n\) term is not "small" — it's just dominated by \(n^2\) for large \(n\). The \(n^2 + n\) expression is exact; the \(O(n^2)\) is a simplification that captures the dominant growth.

docs.title: 1.5.1 Big-\(\Omega\) — a lower bound
docs.text:
Definition — Big-\(\Omega\)

We write \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) if there exist positive constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that

\[ f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0. \]

In words: \(f\) grows at least as fast as a constant times \(g\).

\(f = \Omega(g)\) means "\(g\) is a lower bound." For example, any sort that must examine every element has \(\Omega(n)\) runtime — no faster than linear is possible.

docs.title: 1.5.2 Big-\(\Theta\) — a tight bound
docs.text:
Definition — Big-\(\Theta\)

\(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\) if \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\).

In words: \(f\) and \(g\) grow at the same rate, up to constants.

\(\Theta\) is the strongest and most useful statement. "Sorting by comparison is \(\Theta(n \log n)\)" says: no comparison sort is faster than \(n \log n\), and algorithms exist that achieve it.

docs.title: 1.5.3 The hierarchy at a glance
docs.text: Notation Meaning Analogy \(f = O(g)\) \(f\) grows no faster than \(g\) \(f \le g\) (up to constant) \(f = \Omega(g)\) \(f\) grows no slower than \(g\) \(f \ge g\) (up to constant) \(f = \Theta(g)\) \(f\) grows at the same rate as \(g\) \(f = g\) (up to constant) \(f = o(g)\) \(f\) grows strictly slower than \(g\) \(f < g\) (strictly) \(f = \omega(g)\) \(f\) grows strictly faster than \(g\) \(f > g\) (strictly)

docs.title: Worked example 1.6 — Three statements about one function
docs.text:
Consider \(f(n) = 2n^2 + 5n\).

Claim True? Witness \(f(n) = O(n^2)\) ✓ \(c = 3\), \(n_0 = 5\) (verify: \(2n^2 + 5n \le 3n^2\) ⟺ \(5n \le n^2\) ⟺ \(n \ge 5\)) \(f(n) = \Omega(n^2)\) ✓ \(c = 1\), \(n_0 = 1\) (verify: \(2n^2 + 5n \ge n^2\) ✓) \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) ✓ Follows from both \(f(n) = O(n)\) ✗ See Worked example 1.5 method \(f(n) = \Theta(n)\) ✗ Would require the false \(O(n)\) bound

Conclusion. \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) — the tightest statement.

docs.title: 1.6 Analysing loops
docs.text: The single most important skill in complexity analysis is reading a loop and writing its Big-O. Here is the procedure.

docs.title: 1.6.1 Single loop
docs.text:
Rule. If a loop runs a constant number of operations per iteration and executes \(k\) iterations, its cost is \(O(k)\).

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    sum += a[i];
}

Iterations: \(n\). Per iteration: constant. Total: \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.7 — Loop with doubling index
docs.text:
for (int i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2) {
    sum += i;
}

How many iterations? Each step doubles i. Starting at 1, after \(k\) iterations we have \(i = 2^k\). Stop when \(2^k \ge n\), i.e., \(k = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\).

Total: \(O(\log n)\).

This pattern appears constantly — binary search, balanced-tree walks, exponentiation by squaring. Doubling or halving the index means \(\log n\) iterations.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Nested loops
docs.text: Rule. Multiply the iteration counts.

docs.title: Worked example 1.8 — Two independent nested loops
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        sum += a[i][j];
    }
}

Outer: \(n\) iterations. Inner: \(n\) iterations for each outer iteration. Total: \(n \times n = n^2\).

\(O(n^2)\).

docs.title: Worked example 1.9 — Nested with an "upper triangle" inner loop
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
        sum += a[i][j];
    }
}

Inner loop runs \(n - i\) times, for outer index \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\).

Total iterations: \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (n - i) = n + (n-1) + \ldots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\).

Total: \(O(n^2)\) (the \(n^2/2\) leading term dominates; the \(\frac12\) constant drops).

The lesson: halving the iteration count (from \(n^2\) to \(n^2/2\)) does not change the complexity class. Big-O ignores constants.

docs.title: Worked example 1.10 — Loop where the input drives the iterations
docs.text:
void print(int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {   // note: j < i, not j < n
            System.out.println(i + j);
        }
    }
}

Inner: \(i\) iterations per outer step \(i\). Total: \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i = \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = O(n^2)\).

Same class as Worked example 1.9 — a triangular pattern is \(O(n^2)\).

docs.title: 1.7 Analysing recursion
docs.text: For recursive algorithms, we don't count iterations. We write a recurrence relation — an equation for \(T(n)\) in terms of smaller inputs — and solve it.

docs.title: 1.7.1 The template
docs.text:
For a recursive function of input size \(n\) that:

  • Performs some constant work,
  • Makes \(a\) recursive calls on inputs of size \(n/b\),

the recurrence is:

\[ T(n) = a \cdot T(n/b) + O(1). \]

Its solution depends on whether \(a > b\), \(a = b\), or \(a < b\).

docs.title: 1.7.2 The three common cases
docs.text: Case Recurrence Solution Examples No branching (\(a = 1\)) \(T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(1)\) \(O(n)\) Factorial, linear search Halving (\(b = 2, a = 1\)) \(T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)\) \(O(\log n)\) Binary search Two halvings (\(b = 2, a = 2\)) \(T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) Merge sort Exponential (\(b=2, a>2\) or \(b=1\)) \(T(n) = 2^n\) \(O(2^n)\) Naive Fibonacci

docs.title: Worked example 1.11 — Linear recursion (factorial)
docs.text:
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

Recurrence: \(T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)\).

Unrolling: \(T(n) = T(n-1) + c = T(n-2) + 2c = \ldots = T(1) + (n-1)c = O(n)\).

Total: \(O(n)\). The recursion does not multiply — each call produces exactly one smaller call, so the work is linear.

docs.title: Worked example 1.12 — Binary search
docs.text:
int binarySearch(int[] a, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
    if (a[mid] < target) return binarySearch(a, target, mid + 1, hi);
    return binarySearch(a, target, lo, mid - 1);
}

The input is halved each call. Recurrence: \(T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)\).

Unrolling: \(T(n) = T(n/2) + c = T(n/4) + 2c = \ldots = T(1) + c \cdot \log_2 n = O(\log n)\).

Total: \(O(\log n)\).

Why? Because \(n / 2^k = 1\) when \(k = \log_2 n\). That's the depth of the recursion tree.

docs.title: Worked example 1.13 — Merge sort
docs.text:
The recursive call splits the array in half and processes both halves:

void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid);       // recurse on left half
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);   // recurse on right half
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi);       // O(n) merge
}

Recurrence: \(T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)\).

Recursion tree approach: at depth \(d\), there are \(2^d\) nodes, each of size \(n / 2^d\). Work at depth \(d\): \(2^d \times O(n / 2^d) = O(n)\). Depth: \(\log_2 n\). Total: \(O(n \log n)\).

Total: \(O(n \log n)\). Merge sort is fundamentally better than bubble/insertion/selection sort (\(O(n^2)\)) for large inputs — this is the payoff of the analysis we'll do in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Worked example 1.14 — Naive Fibonacci (why analysis matters)
docs.text:
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

Recurrence: \(T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)\).

This is exponential — \(T(n) = \Theta(\phi^n)\) with \(\phi \approx 1.618\). \(T(50) \approx 2 \times 10^{10}\) — hours on a laptop.

Contrast with an iterative version:

int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    int a = 0, b = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}

Total: \(O(n)\). For \(n = 50\), that's 50 additions — a microsecond.

Same math, same answer, 10⁶-times-faster implementation. The reason: the naive recursion repeats work — fib(n-2) is computed inside both fib(n-1) and fib(n). Complexity analysis reveals this — and tells you to write the iterative version.

docs.title: 1.8 The common complexity classes
docs.text: Every algorithm you meet in this course fits in one of these classes.

docs.title: 1.8.1 The table
docs.text: Class Name Grows Typical example O(1) constant does not grow array indexing, hash lookup (average) O(log n) logarithmic very slowly binary search, balanced-tree search O(n) linear linearly array scan, linked-list traversal O(n log n) linearithmic slightly super-linear merge sort, quicksort (average) O(n²) quadratic quadratically bubble/insertion/selection sort, nested loops O(n³) cubic cubically naive matrix multiplication O(2ⁿ) exponential explodes naive Fibonacci, exhaustive subset enumeration O(n!) factorial explodes faster brute-force TSP

docs.title: 1.8.2 How big is "big"?
docs.text:
For \(n = 1{,}000{,}000\) (1 million items) at \(10^9\) operations per second:

Class Operations Time \(O(1)\) 1 1 ns \(O(\log n)\) 20 20 ns \(O(n)\) 10⁶ 1 ms \(O(n \log n)\) 2 × 10⁷ 20 ms \(O(n²)\) 10¹² 11.6 days \(O(2ⁿ)\) astronomical billions of years

The practical message. Anything worse than \(O(n \log n)\) is unusable on million-item inputs. This is why the analysis matters — it tells you which algorithms are actually deployable.

docs.title: 1.9 Constants matter — but not the way you might think
1.9.1 Why Big-O ignores constants
docs.text:
Big-O is a statement about growth, not about performance. Two algorithms with the same Big-O may differ 100× in absolute speed:

  • Algorithm A: \(T_A(n) = 100\,n\)
  • Algorithm B: \(T_B(n) = 0.1\,n\)

Both are \(O(n)\). For \(n = 1000\), A takes \(100{,}000\) steps, B takes \(100\) steps. B is 1000× faster, but Big-O cannot see it.

docs.title: 1.9.2 Why constants matter anyway
docs.text:
For small \(n\), constants dominate. The crossover point:

  • Algorithm A: \(T_A(n) = 100\,n\) (fast per step)
  • Algorithm B: \(T_B(n) = 0.1\,n^2\) (slow per step, but quadratic)

At \(n = 10\): A takes \(1000\) steps, B takes \(10\) steps. B is 100× faster. At \(n = 1000\): A takes \(100{,}000\) steps, B takes \(100{,}000\) steps. Tie. At \(n = 10{,}000\): A takes \(10^6\) steps, B takes \(10^7\) steps. A is 10× faster.

The crossover at \(n = 1000\). For small datasets, use the "slower" algorithm. For large datasets, use the "faster" one. This is why quicksort (average \(O(n \log n)\), but with a small constant) is faster than merge sort in practice on small to medium inputs, even though both are \(O(n \log n)\) — and why insertion sort (\(O(n^2)\) but tiny constant) beats both on arrays of \(< 20\) elements.

Practical rule

Big-O tells you what scales. Constants tell you what fits in cache, what fits in a register, what dominates at your actual problem size. Always use both. Never pick an algorithm by Big-O alone when the actual data is small.

docs.title: 1.10 Space complexity
docs.text:
Time is only half the story. Space complexity measures how much extra memory an algorithm uses, as a function of input size \(n\).

Auxiliary space — memory in addition to the input. Total space — input + auxiliary.

Example. Array reversal:

// In-place reversal: O(1) auxiliary space
for (int i = 0; i < n/2; i++) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[n-1-i]; a[n-1-i] = t;
}

// Out-of-place reversal: O(n) auxiliary space
int[] b = new int[n];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) b[i] = a[n-1-i];

Both are \(O(n)\) time. But the first uses \(O(1)\) auxiliary space; the second uses \(O(n)\). On a memory-constrained embedded device, this matters.

Recursion uses space too

Every recursive call occupies a stack frame — typically tens to hundreds of bytes. So a recursion of depth \(d\) uses \(O(d)\) auxiliary space. Fibonacci's naive recursion uses \(O(n)\) stack space — the depth is \(n\).

docs.title: 1.11 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. A data structure is a way of organizing data and the operations on it. The layout and the operations are equally important.
  2. Abstraction — an ADT specifies what, an implementation specifies how. One ADT, many implementations.
  3. Big-O describes the growth of an algorithm's cost as input size increases. It drops constants and lower-order terms.
  4. Big-\(\Omega\) is a lower bound, Big-\(\Theta\) is a tight bound. \(\Theta\) is the strongest and most useful.
  5. Loops — count iterations; multiply for nested loops.
  6. Recursion — write the recurrence, solve it. No-branching → \(O(n)\); halving → \(O(\log n)\); two-halving → \(O(n \log n)\); exponential → \(O(2^n)\).
  7. The common complexity classes are \(O(1)\), \(O(\log n)\), \(O(n)\), \(O(n \log n)\), \(O(n^2)\), \(O(n^3)\), \(O(2^n)\), \(O(n!)\). Anything worse than \(O(n \log n)\) is un-deployable on large data.
  8. Constants matter. Big-O gives the growth shape; constants give the practical performance. Both matter, especially for small \(n\).
  9. Space complexity matters as much as time. Recursion costs stack space.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. What does it mean for \(f(n) = O(g(n))\)?

(a) \(f\) is always smaller than \(g\) (b) \(f\) grows no faster than \(g\), up to a constant (c) \(f\) and \(g\) have equal value at every \(n\) (d) \(f\) is an algorithm, \(g\) a program

  1. Which is not a valid Big-O simplification?

(a) \(5n + 3 = O(n)\) (b) \(n^2 + n = O(n^2)\) (c) \(n \log n + n = O(n \log n)\) (d) \(n^2 = O(n)\)

  1. A loop for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) has complexity:

(a) \(O(1)\) (b) \(O(\log n)\) (c) \(O(n)\) (d) \(O(n^2)\)

  1. A loop for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) has complexity:

(a) \(O(1)\) (b) \(O(\log n)\) (c) \(O(n)\) (d) \(O(n^2)\)

  1. Two nested loops, each iterating \(n\) times, give:

(a) \(O(n)\) (b) \(O(n \log n)\) (c) \(O(n^2)\) (d) \(O(2^n)\)

  1. The recurrence \(T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)\) solves to:

(a) \(O(n)\) (b) \(O(n \log n)\) (c) \(O(n^2)\) (d) \(O(2^n)\)

  1. The recurrence \(T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)\) solves to:

(a) \(O(1)\) (b) \(O(\log n)\) (c) \(O(n)\) (d) \(O(n \log n)\)

  1. Big-\(\Theta\) notation means:

(a) an upper bound (b) a lower bound (c) a tight upper and lower bound (d) the average case

  1. Which of these is the slowest-growing function?

(a) \(O(n)\) (b) \(O(\log n)\) (c) \(O(n \log n)\) (d) \(O(n^2)\)

  1. The naive recursive Fibonacci is which complexity class?

    (a) \(O(n)\) (b) \(O(n \log n)\) (c) \(O(n^2)\) (d) \(O(2^n)\)

  2. An array reversal done in place uses what auxiliary space?

    (a) \(O(1)\) (b) \(O(\log n)\) (c) \(O(n)\) (d) \(O(n^2)\)

  3. If Algorithm A is \(O(n)\) with constant 100, and B is \(O(n^2)\) with constant 0.1, which is faster for small \(n\)?

    (a) A always (b) B for small \(n\), A for large \(n\) (c) A always for \(n \ge 1\) (d) they are equal for all \(n\)

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A ______ data type (ADT) specifies a set of values and operations, independent of any implementation.

  2. The Big-O definition requires finding two constants: \(c\) and ______.

  3. The recurrence for binary search is \(T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)\), which solves to \(T(n) = O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

  4. Two nested loops, one counting to \(n\) and one counting to \(\log n\), give \(O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

  5. In Big-O notation, \(5n^2 + 100n + 7 = O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

  6. Big-\(\Theta\) means both Big-O and Big-______ hold.

  7. The naive recursive Fibonacci algorithm is exponential because each call ______ the same subproblems.

  8. The auxiliary space used by a recursion of depth \(d\) is \(O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

  9. An algorithm that halves the input on each recursive call runs in \(O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

  10. An algorithm that doubles a counter each iteration runs in \(O(\underline{\ \ \ \ })\).

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define a data structure. Why must the definition include operations, not just layout?
  2. Distinguish an ADT from an implementation. Give one ADT and two different implementations, and explain when each is preferred.
  3. State the formal definition of Big-O. Use it to prove that \(4n^2 + 3n + 1 = O(n^2)\).
  4. Distinguish Big-O, Big-\(\Omega\), and Big-\(\Theta\). Give one example function for which \(f = O(g)\), \(f = \Omega(g)\), and \(f = \Theta(g)\) all hold.
  5. Analyse this code and give its Big-O:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
        for (int k = 0; k < 10; k++) {
            sum += a[i] * a[j];
        }
    }
}
  1. Write the recurrence for the following function and solve it:
int f(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return f(n/2) + f(n/2) + n;
}
  1. Explain why Big-O ignores constants, and why constants still matter in practice. Give one concrete example where the "slower" algorithm is actually faster.
  2. Compare the time and auxiliary space complexity of computing the \(n\)-th Fibonacci number via recursion versus iteration.

docs.title: 1.13 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — \(f\) grows no faster than \(g\), up to a constant.
  2. (d) — \(n^2 = O(n)\) is false; the quadratic term dominates.
  3. (c) — \(O(n)\).
  4. (b) — \(O(\log n)\).
  5. (c) — \(O(n^2)\).
  6. (b) — \(O(n \log n)\).
  7. (c) — \(O(n)\).
  8. (c) — a tight bound (upper and lower).
  9. (b) — \(\log n\) is the slowest-growing.
  10. (d) — \(O(2^n)\).
  11. (a) — \(O(1)\).
  12. (b) — B for small \(n\), A for large \(n\) (crossover around \(n = 1000\)).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. abstract
  2. \(n_0\)
  3. \(\log n\)
  4. \(n \log n\)
  5. \(n^2\)
  6. \(\Omega\)
  7. recomputes (repeats)
  8. \(d\)
  9. \(\log n\)
  10. \(\log n\)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Data structure: a way of organizing data in memory together with the operations on that data. Why include operations: layout alone does not determine what you can do cheaply. Two layouts with the same data may have wildly different costs for insert, search, delete. A data structure is defined by what it enables, not just where the bits go.
  2. ADT vs. implementation: ADT = the interface, specification of operations independent of representation. Implementation = the concrete realization, with specific memory layout and operation costs. Example: the List ADT (insert, delete, get, size). Implementation 1: array-backed — O(1) get(i), O(n) insert(0, x). Implementation 2: linked list — O(n) get(i), O(1) insert(0, x). Preferred: array when reads dominate and index access is frequent (e.g., storing a matrix); linked list when insertions/deletions at arbitrary positions dominate (e.g., a text editor's cursor).
  3. Definition: \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if \(\exists c, n_0 > 0\) such that \(f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\). Proof of \(4n^2 + 3n + 1 = O(n^2)\): Need \(c, n_0\) with \(4n^2 + 3n + 1 \le c n^2\) for all \(n \ge n_0\). Take \(c = 8\): \(4n^2 + 3n + 1 \le 8n^2\) ⟺ \(3n + 1 \le 4n^2\) ⟺ \(4n^2 - 3n - 1 \ge 0\) ⟺ \((4n+1)(n-1) \ge 0\), which holds for \(n \ge 1\). Witness: \(c = 8\), \(n_0 = 1\).
  4. Definitions: \(O\) = upper bound, \(\Omega\) = lower bound, \(\Theta\) = both. Example: \(f(n) = 3n\) and \(g(n) = n\). Then: \(3n = O(n)\) (take \(c=3\), \(n_0=1\)); \(3n = \Omega(n)\) (take \(c=3\), \(n_0=1\)); \(3n = \Theta(n)\) (both hold).
  5. Analysis: The outermost loop runs \(n\) times. For each outer iteration, the inner runs \(n - i\) times, giving the triangular sum \(\sum_i (n-i) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = O(n^2)\). The innermost loop runs a constant 10 times — a constant factor does not change the class. Total: \(O(n^2)\). (Precisely \(10 \cdot n(n+1)/2\) — still \(O(n^2)\).)
  6. Recurrence: \(T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)\). This is the merge-sort recurrence. Recursion-tree solution: at depth \(d\), there are \(2^d\) nodes each with size \(n/2^d\), work per level \(O(n)\), depth \(\log_2 n\). Total: \(O(n \log n)\).
  7. Why Big-O ignores constants: it is a statement about growth, not absolute time. For comparing algorithms on large inputs, constants are dominated by the growth rate. Why constants still matter: (i) for small inputs, the constant dominates — insertion sort with tiny constant beats merge sort up to \(n \approx 20\); (ii) cache behavior — a cache-friendly O(n²) can beat a cache-thrashing O(n log n); (iii) memory constraints — an O(n) algorithm using \(O(n)\) extra space may be unusable on an embedded device, whereas an O(n²) algorithm with \(O(1)\) space may be preferred. Concrete example: Python's sorted() uses Timsort (\(O(n \log n)\), small constant) but switches to insertion sort (\(O(n^2)\)) inside sorted blocks of ≤ 64 elements — because the smaller constant wins for small arrays.
  8. Time and space comparison — Fibonacci:
  9. Recursive: Time \(O(2^n)\) (recomputes subproblems exponentially); auxiliary space \(O(n)\) (depth of recursion). For \(n = 50\): time ≈ hours, stack depth 50.
  10. Iterative: Time \(O(n)\) (single loop); auxiliary space \(O(1)\) (two variables). For \(n = 50\): time ≈ microseconds, memory ≈ 8 bytes. Iterative wins overwhelmingly on both time and space.

docs.title: 1.14 Further reading
docs.text:
• Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Chapters 1–2 — the standard reference for Big-O in a data-structures context.
  • Lafore, Data Structures & Algorithms in Java, Chapters 1–2 — gentler introduction with working code.
  • CLRS, Chapter 3 (growth of functions) — the formal definition of \(O\), \(\Omega\), \(\Theta\), and the Master Theorem.
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms, Section 1.4 (analysis of algorithms) — clear explanation of the doubling method.
  • Open Data Structures (free online) Chapter 1 — complexity primer with code in multiple languages.
  • VisuAlgo — visualgo.net — animate any algorithm from this chapter to build intuition.
  • MIT 6.006 lecture 1 (Big-O) — OCW — first 50 minutes are the classic introduction.
  • Python Tutor — pythontutor.com — step through the recursion examples above and watch the stack grow.

docs.title: 1.15 Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Prove Big-O statements. Prove each:
  2. \(7n^2 + 4n + 2 = O(n^2)\)
  3. \(3n + \log n = O(n)\)

  4. \(100\log n + 5 = O(\log n)\)

  5. Disprove Big-O statements. Show that:

  6. \(n^2 \ne O(n)\)
  7. \(n \log n \ne O(n)\)

  8. \(2^n \ne O(n^{100})\)

  9. Analyse these loops — give the Big-O of each:

  10. for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) { ... }
  11. for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 3) { ... }
  12. for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) for (k = 0; k < n; k++) { ... }

  13. for (i = 0; i < 100; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) { ... }

  14. Write a recurrence for each function and solve it:

int f(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return f(n - 1) + 1;
}

int g(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return g(n - 1) + g(n - 1);
}

int h(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return h(n/2) + h(n/2);
}

  1. Prove or disprove: if \(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\) and \(g(n) = \Theta(h(n))\), then \(f(n) = \Theta(h(n))\).

  2. Non-obvious case. Give an example of two functions \(f\) and \(g\) for which \(f = O(g)\) but \(f \ne \Theta(g)\).

  3. Same function, three bounds. For \(f(n) = 10n^3 + 100n^2 + 1000n + 10000\), give witnesses \((c, n_0)\) for all three: \(f = O(n^3)\), \(f = \Omega(n^3)\), \(f = \Theta(n^3)\).

  4. Space matters. An algorithm runs in \(O(n)\) time but uses \(O(n)\) auxiliary space. Can you always replace it with an \(O(1)\)-space version? Give an example where you can, and one where you can't.

  5. The crossover. Algorithm A is \(5n + 10\) (per step cost \(1\) ns); B is \(0.001n^2\) (per step cost \(0.001\) ns). Find the \(n\) at which B becomes slower than A.

  6. Practical comparison. On your laptop, time the naive recursive Fibonacci vs. the iterative version for \(n = 20, 25, 30, 35\). Plot the ratio of times. What do you see? What does Big-O predict?

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Arrays
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): memory allocation · operations in arrays.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the contiguous memory model that underlies arrays.
  2. Derive the indexing arithmetic that makes array[i] O(1).
  3. Write and analyse the cost of insert, delete, search, and traverse operations on static arrays.
  4. Explain dynamic arrays and the amortised analysis of doubling expansion.
  5. Compare linear search to binary search with Big-O proof.
  6. Handle 2D arrays and understand row-major versus column-major traversal costs.
  7. Recognise problems where arrays are the right data structure and where they are not.

docs.title: 2.1 The memory model — why arrays are fast
2.1.1 Contiguous memory
docs.text:
An array stores its elements in consecutive memory cells:

Memory address:   1000    1004    1008    1012    1016    1020
Element:         [ a0 ]  [ a1 ]  [ a2 ]  [ a3 ]  [ a4 ]  [ a5 ]
Index:             0       1       2       3       4       5

If the array starts at address B and each element takes w bytes (w = 4 for int on most systems, w = 8 for long / double), then the element at index i lives at:

\[ \boxed{\;\text{address}(a_i) = B + i \cdot w\;} \]

This is the entire reason arrays are fast. Given i, the CPU computes one multiplication and one addition — a couple of CPU cycles — and gets the address. No scanning, no pointer chasing.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Cache locality — the hidden superpower
docs.text:
Modern CPUs read memory in cache lines (typically 64 bytes). When you access a[i], the CPU fetches the entire line containing it — which contains 16 consecutive ints (64 / 4).

So when you access a[i], a[i+1], a[i+2], … in a loop, 15 of the next 15 accesses hit cache and cost almost nothing.

Access a[0]: misses cache, fetches 16 ints → cache hit for a[1]..a[15]
Access a[16]: misses cache, fetches next 16 ints → cache hit for a[17]..a[31]

Consequence: a linear scan of an array is often 10–100× faster in wall-clock terms than iterating a linked list of the same length — even though both are O(n) — because the linked list's nodes are scattered in memory.

We'll come back to this when we compare arrays to linked lists (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.1.3 Bounds checking (and why it costs almost nothing)
docs.text:
When you write a[i] in Java or Python, the runtime checks 0 ≤ i < a.length. If not, it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Java) or IndexError (Python).

This check takes one extra branch — almost free on modern CPUs (branch prediction handles it). But it's worth knowing: in C or C++, a[i] performs no check. If i is out of bounds, the program reads (or writes) whatever memory happens to be at B + i*w — undefined behaviour.

docs.title: 2.2 Static arrays — operations and costs
docs.text: A static array has a fixed size, declared at creation.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Traverse
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    sum += a[i];
}

\(n\) iterations, each O(1). Total: O(n).

docs.title: 2.2.2 Search — linear scan
docs.text:
int linearSearch(int[] a, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (a[i] == target) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}

Worst case: O(n) (target is at the end or absent). Best case: O(1) (target is first). Average: O(n) (uniform distribution).

docs.title: 2.2.3 Search — binary search (on sorted arrays)
docs.text:
int binarySearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;   // avoids overflow of (lo+hi)/2
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else                 hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

The search space halves each iteration:

  • After 1 iteration: size \(n/2\)
  • After 2: \(n/4\)
  • After \(k\): \(n / 2^k\)

Stop when \(n / 2^k < 1\), i.e., \(k = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\). Total: O(log n).

The catch: binary search requires the array to be sorted. Sorting is O(n log n) — you'd pay that cost once if you need many searches.

docs.title: 2.2.4 The full cost table
docs.text:
Operation Best Average Worst Access a[i] O(1) O(1) O(1) Traverse O(n) O(n) O(n) Linear search O(1) O(n) O(n) Binary search (sorted) O(1) O(log n) O(log n) Insert at end (static) — — not supported (array is full) Insert at position p O(1) (if p = n) O(n) O(n) Delete at position p O(1) (if p = n-1) O(n) O(n)

The "insert at end" that isn't supported for static arrays is a real limitation. That's what dynamic arrays fix (§2.3).

docs.title: 2.3 Dynamic arrays — resizing and amortised analysis
2.3.1 The idea
docs.text:
A dynamic array (Java ArrayList, Python list, C++ std::vector) hides a static array inside, with two extra fields:

class DynamicArray {
    private int[] data;
    private int size;     // how many elements actually in use

    public DynamicArray() {
        data = new int[1];   // start small
        size = 0;
    }

    public void add(int x) {
        if (size == data.length) {
            resize(data.length * 2);   // double the capacity
        }
        data[size++] = x;
    }

    private void resize(int newCap) {
        int[] newData = new int[newCap];
        System.arraycopy(data, 0, newData, 0, size);   // O(n) copy
        data = newData;
    }
}

The add operation is O(1) most of the time — but occasionally O(n) when the internal array is full and needs doubling.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Amortised analysis — why doubling wins
docs.text:
The key question: is add really O(1)?

Naively: no. Some calls take O(n) — those that resize. The worst case per call is O(n).

But amortised over a sequence of many calls, the average cost per add is O(1). Here's the proof.

Amortised cost of add (doubling strategy)

Suppose we do \(n\) additions starting from an empty dynamic array of capacity 1. Resizes happen at sizes \(1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots\) — i.e., at sizes \(1, 2, 4, \ldots, 2^k\) where \(2^k \le n\).

Total cost of all resizes: $$ 1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1 < 2n. $$

Total cost of all \(n\) insertions (each O(1)): \(n\).

Total cost: less than \(n + 2n = 3n = O(n)\).

Amortised cost per add: \(3n / n = O(1)\). ✓

The geometric series \(\sum 2^i = 2^{k+1} - 1\) is the key insight — the sum of all doubles is less than twice the last one. Doubling is what makes this work; if you grew by +1 each time (incrementing capacity), the cost would be \(1 + 2 + 3 + \ldots + n = O(n^2)\) → O(n) amortised — no better than a linked list without tail pointer.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Why not grow by 3× or 10×?
docs.text:
You can — but doubling is the sweet spot:

Growth factor Amortised add Space wasted Worst-case add +1 (increment) O(n) minimal O(n) ×1.5 O(1) ≤ 33% O(n) ×2 O(1) ≤ 50% O(n) ×3 O(1) ≤ 67% O(n) ×10 O(1) ≤ 90% O(n)

Growth factor 2 has a clean trade-off: amortised O(1), at most 50% wasted capacity. Anything ≥ 2 gives O(1); smaller gives more space efficiency at the cost of more frequent resizes.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Shrinking
docs.text:
If you add a million elements, then remove most of them, the internal array stays at a million — wasting 4 MB of memory for an empty array.

The shrinking strategy: when size drops below capacity / 4, halve the capacity.

Why capacity / 4 and not capacity / 2? If you shrink at exactly half, then adding one more element triggers an immediate resize back up. Alternating add/remove would cause thrashing — every operation resizes. Using capacity / 4 gives a buffer: shrink only when the array is comfortably empty.

docs.title: 2.4 Insert and delete — the shifting cost
docs.text: For a static array (or the internal array of a dynamic array), insert/delete at a position p requires shifting.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Insert at position p
docs.text:
// Assumes size < data.length
void insertAt(int[] data, int size, int p, int x) {
    for (int i = size; i > p; i--) {
        data[i] = data[i - 1];   // shift right
    }
    data[p] = x;
}

Shifts: elements at positions p, p+1, …, size-1 move right — that's size - p shifts.

p Shifts Cost 0 (front) size O(n) size/2 (middle) size/2 O(n) size (end) 0 O(1)

Worst case: O(n) (insert at front). Best case: O(1) (insert at end — append).

docs.title: 2.4.2 Delete at position p
docs.text:
void deleteAt(int[] data, int size, int p) {
    for (int i = p; i < size - 1; i++) {
        data[i] = data[i + 1];   // shift left
    }
}

Shifts: elements at p+1, …, size-1 move left — that's size - 1 - p shifts.

Same cost structure as insert: O(n) worst case, O(1) when deleting the last element.

Common mistake

Deleting the first element is the most expensive (all n-1 shift). Deleting the last is free. If your algorithm repeatedly deletes from the front, use a queue or linked list instead — not an array.

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — Proving a[i] is O(1)
docs.text:
Claim. Accessing a[i] on an array takes O(1) time.

Proof. The address of a[i] is \(B + i \cdot w\), where \(B\) is the base address and \(w\) is the element width. Computing this address requires:

  1. One multiplication: \(i \cdot w\) — a single CPU instruction.
  2. One addition: \(B + i \cdot w\) — a single CPU instruction.
  3. One memory load from that address — a single CPU instruction.

Total: 3 primitive operations, independent of \(i\) and of the array length. Therefore, O(1). ∎

Contrast with linked list. Accessing the \(i\)-th element of a linked list requires following \(i\) next pointers — O(i) time, O(n) worst case. This is the entire reason arrays are preferred when access by index is frequent.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — Insert at position p in a dynamic array
docs.text:
Setup. An array of size 8 with capacity 8 (full). Insert the value x at position p = 3.

Step-by-step trace.

Before:
Index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
Value: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
Size = 8, Capacity = 8   → full, must resize first.

Step 1 — Resize (double to capacity 16, copy 8 elements — O(n)). Now capacity = 16.

Step 2 — Shift right from size-1 = 7 down to p = 3:

After shift:
Index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Value: [10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
                     ↑
                     positions 3..7 shifted right

Wait — that's not right. Let me re-trace.

Correct shift (from i = 8 down to i = 4): - data[8] = data[7] → 80 at index 8 - data[7] = data[6] → 70 at index 7 - data[6] = data[5] → 60 at index 6 - data[5] = data[4] → 50 at index 5 - data[4] = data[3] → 40 at index 4

After shift:
Index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Value: [10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
                     ↑
                     index 3 is now overwritable

Step 3 — Insert x = 35 at index 3:

After insert:
Index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Value: [10, 20, 30, 35, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
Size = 9, Capacity = 16

Cost. Resize = O(n) copy (8 elements); shift = 5 = size - p operations; insert = 1 write. Total: O(n).

docs.title: Worked example 2.3 — Amortised cost of add with doubling
docs.text:
Setup. Start with capacity 1, empty. Insert 17 elements one at a time. Track the total number of element copies.

Insert # Size before Capacity Action Copies this step Total copies 1 0 1 append (no resize) 0 0 2 1 1 resize to 2 1 1 3 2 2 resize to 4 2 3 4 3 4 append 0 3 5 4 4 resize to 8 4 7 6–9 5–8 8 append 0 7 10 8 8 resize to 16 8 15 11–17 9–16 16 append 0 15

Total copies for 17 insertions: 15.

Amortised copies per insertion: \(15 / 17 < 1\) — constant, less than 1 per insertion.

The general pattern: inserting \(n\) elements into a doubling dynamic array copies at most \(2n - 1\) elements total. Per insertion: \(< 2\). O(1) amortised. ✓

docs.title: Worked example 2.4 — Why growing by +1 is O(n²)
docs.text:
Setup. Start with capacity 1, empty. Insert \(n\) elements, but each resize grows capacity by 1 (worst-case strategy).

Insert # Size before Capacity Copies 1 0 1 0 2 1 1 1 3 2 2 2 4 3 3 3 ... ... ... ... \(n\) \(n-1\) \(n-1\) \(n-1\)

Total copies: \(0 + 1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)\).

Amortised cost per insert: \(\Theta(n^2) / n = \Theta(n)\) — per insert, quadratic in the worst case.

Contrast with doubling: doubling gave total copies \(< 2n\) (linear); +1 gives \(n^2/2\) (quadratic). The growth factor is the difference between linear and quadratic overall cost.

docs.title: Worked example 2.5 — Binary search trace
docs.text:
Search for 42 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 42, 56, 72, 91] (sorted, n = 11).

Iteration lo hi mid a[mid] Compare 1 0 10 5 23 42 > 23 → lo = 6 2 6 10 8 56 42 < 56 → hi = 7 3 6 7 6 38 42 > 38 → lo = 7 4 7 7 7 42 found at index 7 ✓

Iterations: 4. Theory: \(\lceil \log_2 11 \rceil = 4\). ✓

Comparison with linear search. Linear search for 42 would take 8 iterations (indices 0 through 7). Binary search took 4. At \(n = 10^6\), binary search takes ~20 iterations; linear search takes up to a million. The gap is astronomical.

docs.title: Worked example 2.6 — Reverse an array in place
docs.text:
Goal. Reverse [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] → [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] using O(1) auxiliary space.

Algorithm — two-pointer swap.

void reverse(int[] a) {
    int left = 0, right = a.length - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int t = a[left];
        a[left] = a[right];
        a[right] = t;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

Trace on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:

Step left right Array 0 0 4 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 1 1 3 [5, 2, 3, 4, 1] 2 2 2 [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] — left == right, stop

Cost. \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor\) swaps, each O(1). Time: O(n). Auxiliary space: O(1).

Contrast — out-of-place reversal using a new array would also be O(n) time but O(n) space. In-place is strictly better if you can modify the input.

Python version (same idea, more concise):

def reverse(a):
    left, right = 0, len(a) - 1
    while left < right:
        a[left], a[right] = a[right], a[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1

docs.title: Worked example 2.7 — Rotate an array by k positions
docs.text:
Goal. Rotate [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] right by k = 3 → [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4].

Approach 1 (naive). Shift each element by k positions, one element at a time. \(\Theta(n \cdot k)\) — quadratic if k is large.

Approach 2 (using auxiliary array). Copy elements to their new positions in a new array, then copy back. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Approach 3 (in-place, O(1) space). The "reverse three times" trick:

  1. Reverse the whole array: [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
  2. Reverse the first k elements: [5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1]
  3. Reverse the remaining n-k elements: [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]

Wait — step 2 reverses the first k (indices 0..k-1 = 0..2), giving [5, 6, 7, ...]. ✓

Step 3 reverses the rest (indices k..n-1 = 3..6), giving [..., 1, 2, 3, 4]. ✓

Combined: [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4] — correct! ✓

void rotate(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length;
    k = k % n;              // handle k > n
    if (k == 0) return;
    reverse(a, 0, n - 1);
    reverse(a, 0, k - 1);
    reverse(a, k, n - 1);
}

void reverse(int[] a, int from, int to) {
    while (from < to) {
        int t = a[from]; a[from] = a[to]; a[to] = t;
        from++; to--;
    }
}

Cost. Three reversals, each O(n). Total: O(n) time, O(1) space. This is the optimal solution — beats the auxiliary-array approach on space.

docs.title: Worked example 2.8 — Two-pointer sum in a sorted array
docs.text:
Problem. Given a sorted array and a target T, find two elements that sum to T.

Brute force. Two nested loops: O(n²).

Two-pointer (sorted array).

boolean hasTwoSum(int[] a, int T) {
    int left = 0, right = a.length - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int sum = a[left] + a[right];
        if (sum == T) return true;
        if (sum < T) left++;
        else         right--;
    }
    return false;
}

Why it works. Because the array is sorted:

  • If sum < T: the current pair is too small. Increase left (larger element).
  • If sum > T: the current pair is too large. Decrease right (smaller element).

Correctness argument. Suppose the true pair is (a[i], a[j]) with i < j. At any iteration, either:

  • left < i or right > j: the algorithm hasn't reached the pair yet, but the sum tells it which direction to go — and the pair will eventually be reached.
  • If the algorithm ever sets left > i (i.e., passed i), then the previous step must have had a[left] + a[right] < T, meaning even with the largest possible right, left was too small — so left = i would have been a solution candidate. Contradiction.

So the algorithm never skips the pair.

Cost. left and right move toward each other at most \(n\) total steps. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Contrast. Brute force is O(n²). Two-pointer is O(n). The sorted precondition enables the linear algorithm.

docs.title: Worked example 2.9 — Traversing a 2D array: row-major vs. column-major
docs.text:
Setup. An array int[][] matrix of size \(n \times n\). Two traversals:

Row-major (outer loop over rows): 

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
        sum += matrix[i][j];

Column-major (outer loop over columns): 

for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        sum += matrix[i][j];

Big-O: both are O(n²). Same iteration count.

Wall-clock: row-major is often 2–5× faster.

Why? Java (like C, C++, Python's NumPy) stores 2D arrays in row-major order — element matrix[i][j] is at address \(B + (i \cdot n + j) \cdot w\).

Row-major traversal visits consecutive addresses → excellent cache behaviour. Column-major traversal jumps by n * w between accesses → poor cache behaviour (each access misses).

The Big-O is the same, but the constant is different — exactly the "constants matter" lesson from Chapter 1.

Python (NumPy) is the same: NumPy is row-major by default, so iterating over rows is faster than iterating over columns.

docs.title: 2.5 When arrays are the right choice
docs.text:
Arrays excel at:

  • Random access by index — O(1) per access; no other structure does better.
  • Dense iteration — visiting every element is cache-friendly and fast.
  • Fixed-size collections — if you know the size, arrays are the simplest and most efficient.
  • Storing data that needs sorting — arrays are the natural home for sort algorithms.

Arrays are the wrong choice when:

  • Frequent insertions or deletions in the middle or front — O(n) each shift.
  • Size unknown and highly variable — dynamic arrays amortise well but still resize occasionally.
  • Very sparse data — a dense array would waste memory.

The next chapters show the alternatives — linked lists for flexible size and cheap insertion at the front, hash tables for fast lookup, trees for ordered data.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Arrays store elements contiguously; the address of a[i] is B + i*w, computable in O(1).
  2. Cache locality makes arrays ~10–100× faster than pointers in wall-clock terms for linear scans.
  3. Static arrays support O(1) access and O(n) insert/delete at interior positions (shifting cost).
  4. Binary search on a sorted array is O(log n) — but requires the array to be sorted.
  5. Dynamic arrays grow by doubling; amortised add cost is O(1) because the sum of resize copies is < 2n.
  6. Growing by +1 instead of doubling gives O(n) amortised — a factor-of-n penalty.
  7. Shrinking should happen at capacity/4, not capacity/2, to avoid thrashing.
  8. In-place operations (reverse, rotate) can achieve O(1) auxiliary space.
  9. Two-pointer techniques exploit sortedness for O(n) algorithms where brute force is O(n²).
  10. Row-major traversal of a 2D array is faster than column-major in row-major languages — same Big-O, better constants.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. a[i] is O(1) because:

(a) arrays are immutable (b) the address is computable with a fixed number of operations (c) arrays are always sorted (d) Python caches results

  1. Inserting at the front of an n-element array takes:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. Binary search requires:

(a) the array to be unsorted (b) the array to be sorted (c) the array to contain only integers (d) the array to have an even length

  1. Adding n elements to a dynamic array with doubling has total cost:

(a) O(n) (b) O(n log n) (c) O(n²) (d) O(2ⁿ)

  1. Adding n elements to a dynamic array growing by +1 has total cost:

(a) O(n) (b) O(n log n) (c) O(n²) (d) O(2ⁿ)

  1. Amortised cost of one add with doubling is:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. Rotating an array by k positions in place (reverse-three-times trick) has cost:

(a) O(n) time, O(1) space (b) O(n log n) time, O(n) space (c) O(n²) time, O(1) space (d) O(n) time, O(n) space

  1. Row-major traversal of a 2D array in Java is faster than column-major because:

(a) row-major uses less memory (b) rows have fewer elements (c) cache locality is better (d) row-major uses a different algorithm

  1. Auxiliary space of an in-place array reversal is:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. Shrinking a dynamic array should trigger at:

    (a) size == capacity / 2 (b) size == capacity / 4 (c) size == 0 (d) never

  2. Two-pointer sum in a sorted array is:

    (a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  3. A static array of size 100 is full. Trying to add a 101st element:

    (a) silently drops it (b) throws an error or corrupts memory (c) grows automatically (d) queues it internally

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. An element at index i in an array with base B and width w is at address _____.

  2. Binary search on a sorted array of size n runs in O(_____).

  3. Inserting at the end of a static array (if not full) costs O(_____).

  4. Dynamic arrays grown by doubling have total copies $< $____ for n insertions.

  5. The amortised cost of add with doubling is O(_____).

  6. An in-place reversal of an array uses O(_____) auxiliary space.

  7. Rotating an array in place uses the _____ three-times trick.

  8. Row-major traversal of matrix[i][j] in Java accesses consecutive _____.

  9. The two-pointer sum trick requires the array to be _____.

  10. Shrinking a dynamic array at capacity/4 avoids _____ (repeated resize).

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Explain why a[i] is O(1) using the address arithmetic formula. Contrast with a linked list's get(i).

  2. Describe the cache locality advantage of arrays over linked lists. Why is it not visible in Big-O analysis?

  3. Derive the amortised cost of add with doubling, showing that n insertions copy < 2n elements total.

  4. Explain why growing by +1 gives O(n) amortised instead of O(1). Show the total-copies calculation.

  5. Compare the cost of insert at position p for p = 0, p = n/2, and p = n in a static array. Which is cheapest and why?

  6. State the binary search algorithm. Prove that it runs in O(log n).

  7. Describe the reverse-three-times algorithm for array rotation. Prove correctness using the rotation equation.

  8. Explain the two-pointer sum algorithm. Why does it work only on sorted arrays?

  9. Explain the difference between time complexity and wall-clock performance for 2D array traversal. Give an example where Big-O is the same but wall-clock is 5× different.

  10. Give three situations where arrays are the wrong choice and suggest what data structure would be better.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — fixed number of operations to compute the address.
  2. (c) — O(n) shifting.
  3. (b) — sorted array required.
  4. (a) — O(n) total with doubling.
  5. (c) — O(n²) with +1 growth.
  6. (a) — O(1) amortised.
  7. (a) — O(n) time, O(1) space.
  8. (c) — cache locality.
  9. (a) — O(1).
  10. (b) — capacity/4 avoids thrashing.
  11. (c) — O(n).
  12. (b) — error or corruption (undefined behaviour in C, exception in Java).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(B + i \cdot w\)
  2. \(\log n\)
  3. \(O(1)\)
  4. \(2n\)
  5. \(O(1)\)
  6. \(O(1)\)
  7. reverse
  8. addresses (or memory locations)
  9. sorted
  10. thrashing
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Address arithmetic: a[i] lives at B + i*w. Computing this takes one multiplication, one addition, one memory load — a constant number of CPU instructions, independent of i and n. Therefore O(1). Contrast with linked list: the \(i\)-th element requires following \(i\) next pointers, so get(i) is O(i) and worst case O(n). This is why arrays win on random-access workloads.
  2. Cache locality: the CPU fetches 64-byte cache lines containing 16 consecutive ints. Row-major traversal of an array touches each line once, reusing it 15 times. Linked list: nodes are scattered in memory — each access likely misses cache. Why Big-O misses this: Big-O counts operations, not memory accesses. Both traversals count \(n\) operations, but the array traversal only has \(n/16\) cache misses; the linked list traversal has \(n\). Wall-clock reflects the cache; Big-O does not.
  3. Amortised analysis with doubling: resizes happen at sizes \(1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots, 2^k\) where \(2^k \le n\). Total copies: \(1 + 2 + 4 + \ldots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1 < 2n\). Per-insertion amortised: \(< 2 = O(1)\). The key is the geometric series — the sum of all doubles is less than 2× the largest.
  4. +1 growth: resizes happen at every size \(1, 2, \ldots, n-1\), copying \(1, 2, \ldots, n-1\) elements respectively. Total: \(1 + 2 + \ldots + n-1 = n(n-1)/2 = O(n^2)\). Per-insertion amortised: \(O(n)\). The sum is arithmetic, not geometric — hence quadratic, not linear.
  5. Insert at position p: shifts elements at p, p+1, ..., n-1 right, which is n - p shifts. At p = 0: n shifts → O(n) worst case. At p = n/2: n/2 shifts → O(n). At p = n: 0 shifts → O(1) best case. The end is cheapest because no elements need to shift right — it's just an append. This is why the add operation (append) is the fastest insertion.
  6. Binary search: maintain a search interval [lo, hi]. Compute mid = (lo + hi) / 2. If a[mid] == target, return. If a[mid] < target, the target must be in [mid+1, hi].
