If a[mid] > target, in [lo, mid-1]. Proof of O(log n): each iteration halves the interval. Starting from size \(n\), after \(k\) iterations the interval has size \(n / 2^k\). Stop when size < 1, i.e., \(k = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\). Therefore \(T(n) = O(\log n)\).
  7. Reverse-three-times: Let \(A = UV\) where \(U\) is the first \(n-k\) elements and \(V\) is the last \(k\). Rotation is \((UV)^R\) = \(VU\). The trick: reverse all → \(V^R U^R\); reverse first \(k\) → \(V U^R\); reverse rest → \(VU\). ✓ Correct.
  8. Two-pointer sum: maintain left = 0, right = n-1. Compute sum = a[left] + a[right]. If sum == target, found. If sum < target, left++ (need larger element). If sum > target, right-- (need smaller). Why sorted required: the direction choice depends on whether a[left] and a[right] are the smallest and largest remaining candidates — true only in a sorted array. If unsorted, a[left] could be anything, so the pointer direction is meaningless. O(n) time, O(1) space.
  9. Time vs. wall-clock: Big-O counts operations, independent of memory hierarchy. Example: row-major vs. column-major traversal of a 1000×1000 matrix both take 10⁶ iterations. But row-major accesses consecutive addresses → good cache → ~5 ms. Column-major accesses strided addresses → cache misses every iteration → ~25 ms. Same operations, different memory access patterns, 5× wall-clock difference.
  10. Wrong choice of array: (i) Frequent insertions/deletions in the middle — every insert/delete is O(n); use a linked list or balanced tree. (ii) Size highly variable — resizing is amortised O(1) but still costly; use a linked list for truly unbounded/frequent-variable. (iii) Sparse data with large gaps — a dense array wastes memory; use a hash table or sparse representation. (iv) Frequent lookup by key (not index) — arrays require O(n) or O(log n) search; use a hash table for O(1) lookup.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Chapter 3 (Lists, Stacks, Queues) — includes an excellent section on the array vs. linked list trade-off.
  • Lafore, Chapter 2 (Arrays) — basic array operations.
  • CLRS, Section 17.4 (Dynamic tables) — amortised analysis of doubling in rigorous form.
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms, Section 1.3 (Bags, Queues, Stacks) — the dynamic-array analysis.
  • Joel Spolsky, "Back to Basics" — joelonsoftware.com/2001/12/11/back-to-basics/ — classic essay on the cache advantage of arrays.
  • Ulrich Drepper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory" — people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf — the definitive reference on why cache locality matters.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Prove a[i] is O(1). Write down the address computation and count the primitive operations.

  2. Insertion cost table. For an array of size 100, compute the number of shifts for insertions at positions 0, 25, 50, 75, 100. Which position is cheapest?

  3. Amortised cost, traced. Start with capacity 1, empty dynamic array with doubling. Insert 32 elements, tracking the total copies. Verify the total is < 2n.

  4. +1 growth. Repeat problem 3 but with +1 growth. Compute the total copies for n = 32. What is the ratio to doubling?

  5. Binary search tree of decisions. For an array of size 1024, how many binary-search iterations are needed to find the first element? The last? A missing element?

  6. Reverse a subarray. Write reverse(a, i, j) that reverses the segment a[i..j] in place. What is its cost?

  7. Rotate by k. Implement the three-reversal rotation. Verify by hand on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with k = 2.

  8. Two-pointer sum, missing pair. In the sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], find two elements summing to 15. Trace each step of the two-pointer algorithm.

  9. 2D array traversal. Allocate int[1000][1000]. Time a row-major scan vs. column-major scan. Report the ratio. Explain the difference in cache terms.

  10. Dynamic array shrink policy. Suppose the shrink trigger is size < capacity / 2. Show an adversarial sequence of insert/delete operations that alternates between growing and shrinking, causing O(n) work per operation. Then show that capacity / 4 avoids this.

  11. Array vs. linked list — quantitative. For n = 100,000 random lookups on a sorted array (binary search) vs. a sorted linked list (linear search), estimate the wall-clock ratio. Which wins by how much?

  12. Two-pointer sum on unsorted arrays. Can you adapt the two-pointer algorithm to work on an unsorted array by pre-sorting it first? What is the total cost, and how does it compare to brute force?

  13. Sliding-window average. Given an array and an integer k, find the maximum average of any k consecutive elements. Design an O(n) algorithm using a sliding window. Why is the naive algorithm O(n·k)?

  14. Duplicate detection. Given an unsorted array of n integers, find whether any value appears twice. Give O(n²), O(n log n), and O(n) solutions. What are their respective space costs?

  15. Missing number. An array contains n-1 distinct integers from {1, 2, …, n} (one is missing). Find the missing number in O(n) time and O(1) space. (Hint: use arithmetic or XOR.)

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Linked Lists
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): memory allocation · operations in linked lists · variations of linked lists: circular, doubly-linked.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the node-and-pointer memory model that underlies linked lists.
  2. Implement a singly-linked list with insert, delete, search, and traverse.
  3. Implement a doubly-linked list and explain when the extra pointer pays off.
  4. Implement a circular linked list and identify its applications.
  5. Reverse, merge, and sort a linked list.
  6. Detect cycles and find the middle of a linked list using Floyd's algorithm.
  7. Compare linked lists to arrays with a full operation-by-operation cost table.
  8. Justify choosing linked list over array (or vice versa) for a given problem.

docs.title: 3.1.1 The node
docs.text:
A node holds one value and (at least) one pointer to the next node:

class Node {
    int  value;
    Node next;   // reference to the next node, or null

    Node(int v) { this.value = v; this.next = null; }
}

In memory, a linked list is not contiguous. Each node is a separate heap allocation:

Heap:
  [Node{value:10, next:→}]  at address 0x1000
  [Node{value:20, next:→}]  at address 0x2050
  [Node{value:30, next:→}]  at address 0x3f00
  ...

The next pointer stores the address of the following node. The list is formed by following these pointers from the head:

head → 10 → 20 → 30 → null

docs.title: 3.1.2 The null terminator
docs.text:
The last node's next is null — the standard signal for "end of list." Every traversal loop must check for null before dereferencing:

Node cur = head;
while (cur != null) {
    System.out.println(cur.value);
    cur = cur.next;
}

Null pointer bugs are the dominant bug class in linked-list code. Forget the null check, and you'll get NullPointerException at runtime (Java) or a segfault (C).

docs.title: 3.1.3 Why not just use an array?
docs.text:
Different layout → different costs:

Operation Array Linked list Access by index a[i] O(1) O(n) Insert at front O(n) O(1) Insert at end O(1) O(1) with tail pointer Delete at front O(n) O(1) Cache locality Excellent Poor

The linked list trades random access for cheap insertion and deletion at known positions. Chapter 3 is about knowing when this trade is worth it.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Insert at head (front)
docs.text:
Node head = null;

void insertAtHead(int x) {
    Node n = new Node(x);
    n.next = head;      // new node points to old head
    head = n;            // update head pointer
}

Cost: O(1). Regardless of list length.

Trace. Insert 30, 20, 10 in that order:

Step List 0 null Insert 30 30 → null Insert 20 20 → 30 → null Insert 10 10 → 20 → 30 → null

The order of insertion is reversed in the final list — an important consequence of insert-at-head.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Insert at tail (end) — without tail pointer
docs.text:
void insertAtTail(int x) {
    Node n = new Node(x);
    if (head == null) {
        head = n;
        return;
    }
    Node cur = head;
    while (cur.next != null) cur = cur.next;   // walk to last
    cur.next = n;
}

Cost: O(n) — must traverse to the end every time.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Insert at tail — with tail pointer
docs.text:
Node head = null, tail = null;

void insertAtTail(int x) {
    Node n = new Node(x);
    if (head == null) { head = n; tail = n; return; }
    tail.next = n;
    tail = n;
}

Cost: O(1). The extra tail pointer costs one reference (8 bytes), saves O(n) per append.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Delete by value
docs.text:
void delete(int x) {
    if (head == null) return;
    if (head.value == x) { head = head.next; return; }
    Node cur = head;
    while (cur.next != null && cur.next.value != x) cur = cur.next;
    if (cur.next != null) cur.next = cur.next.next;   // skip over the match
}

Cost: O(n) — search for the value, then O(1) to unlink.

Careful trace. List 10 → 20 → 30 → null, delete 20:

  • cur = 10; cur.next.value = 20 == x → stop.
  • cur.next = cur.next.next → cur.next = 30.
  • Result: 10 → 30 → null ✓

docs.title: 3.2.5 Traverse — O(n)
docs.text:
void print() {
    for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) {
        System.out.println(cur.value);
    }
}

O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: 3.2.6 Search — O(n)
docs.text:
boolean contains(int x) {
    for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) {
        if (cur.value == x) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

O(n) worst case. Even with tail pointer, search requires walking.

docs.title: 3.2.7 Full cost table (singly-linked)
docs.text:
Operation Cost Insert at head O(1) Insert at tail (no tail) O(n) Insert at tail (with tail) O(1) Insert after given node O(1) Delete at head O(1) Delete by value O(n) Access by index O(n) Search O(n) Traverse O(n)

The pattern: anything involving the head is O(1); anything requiring reaching a specific position is O(n).

docs.title: 3.3.1 Node structure
docs.text:
A doubly-linked node adds a prev pointer:

class Node {
    int  value;
    Node prev;
    Node next;
    Node(int v) { this.value = v; }
}

The list can be traversed both directions:

null ← 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30 → null

docs.title: 3.3.2 Why the extra pointer pays off
docs.text:
With prev, you can:

  • Traverse backward — useful for reverse iteration.
  • Delete a node given a pointer to it in O(1) — no need to walk to find the predecessor.

The last is the big one. In a singly-linked list, deleting a node x requires finding its predecessor — O(n). In a doubly-linked list, x.prev gives it directly.

void deleteNode(Node x) {
    if (x.prev != null) x.prev.next = x.next;
    else                head = x.next;      // x was head
    if (x.next != null) x.next.prev = x.prev;
    // x is now unlinked; Java GC collects it
}

O(1). This is why a doubly-linked list is used for LRU caches — where nodes are constantly moved and removed by pointer.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Insert after a node
docs.text:
void insertAfter(Node x, int val) {
    Node n = new Node(val);
    n.next = x.next;
    n.prev = x;
    if (x.next != null) x.next.prev = n;
    x.next = n;
}

O(1). Four pointer updates.

docs.title: 3.3.4 Cost table (doubly-linked)
docs.text:
Operation Singly Doubly Insert at head O(1) O(1) Insert at tail O(1) with tail O(1) Insert after node O(1) O(1) Delete given node O(n) O(1) Traverse forward O(n) O(n) Traverse backward — O(n)

Extra cost: two pointers per node (16 bytes vs. 8 on 64-bit systems) — double the memory.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Structure
docs.text:
The last node's next points back to the head instead of null:

10 → 20 → 30 → 10 → 20 → 30 → ...
↑                              │
└──────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 3.4.2 When to use a circular list
docs.text:
• Round-robin scheduling — a scheduler cycles through processes; after the last, wraps to the first.
  • Circular buffers — streaming audio/video, where data wraps around.
  • Josephus problem — a group elimination game.
  • Anywhere "next after last" means "first" — the pointer structure naturally models this.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Careful — no null terminator
docs.text:
Circular lists have no null to signal the end. Traversal must stop when it returns to the head — otherwise it loops forever:

void printCircular(Node head) {
    if (head == null) return;
    Node cur = head;
    do {
        System.out.println(cur.value);
        cur = cur.next;
    } while (cur != head);
}

The do...while guarantees at least one iteration, and stops when cur returns to head.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — Insert at head, step by step
docs.text:
Goal. Build 10 → 20 → 30 by inserting at head.

Code:

void insertAtHead(int x) {
    Node n = new Node(x);
    n.next = head;
    head = n;
}

Trace.

Insert 10: n = Node(10), n.next = null, head = n. List: 10 → null.

Insert 20: n = Node(20), n.next = head (10), head = n (20). List: 20 → 10 → null.

Insert 30: n = Node(30), n.next = head (20), head = n (30). List: 30 → 20 → 10 → null.

Final list: 30 → 20 → 10 → null — reversed relative to insertion order.

Cost. Three insertions, each O(1). Total: O(1) regardless of list length.

Contrast with array. To build [30, 20, 10] by inserting at the front of an array: each insertion shifts all existing elements → O(n) per insert → O(n²) for n inserts. Linked list is n× faster here.

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — Insert at tail with tail pointer
docs.text:
Goal. Build 10 → 20 → 30 in original order.

Code:

Node head = null, tail = null;

void insertAtTail(int x) {
    Node n = new Node(x);
    if (head == null) { head = n; tail = n; return; }
    tail.next = n;
    tail = n;
}

Trace.

Insert 10: head = tail = Node(10). List: 10 → null.

Insert 20: tail.next = Node(20) (so 10.next = 20); tail = Node(20). List: 10 → 20 → null.

Insert 30: tail.next = Node(30) (so 20.next = 30); tail = Node(30). List: 10 → 20 → 30 → null.

Final list: 10 → 20 → 30 → null — original order preserved.

Cost. Three insertions, each O(1). Total: O(1) — but requires the extra tail pointer.

Trade-off. Without the tail pointer, insert-at-tail is O(n) per call; with it, O(1). The tail pointer is worth 8 bytes of memory in almost every scenario where you append.

docs.title: Worked example 3.3 — Delete by value — full trace
docs.text:
Goal. Delete 20 from 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → null.

void delete(int x) {
    if (head == null) return;
    if (head.value == x) { head = head.next; return; }
    Node cur = head;
    while (cur.next != null && cur.next.value != x) cur = cur.next;
    if (cur.next != null) cur.next = cur.next.next;
}

Trace.

  • head = 10. 10.value == 20? No.
  • cur = 10. cur.next.value = 20 == 20? No, we're checking cur.next.value. Wait — cur.next = Node(20), so cur.next.value = 20. Match! Exit loop.

Wait — that's the check cur.next.value != x — we exit when cur.next.value == x, i.e., when cur.next is the node to delete.

  • cur = 10. cur.next = Node(20), cur.next.value = 20. Match → exit loop.
  • cur.next = cur.next.next → cur.next = Node(30).
  • List: 10 → 30 → 40 → null.

Correct.

Cost. 1 comparison of head, 1 comparison of cur.next, 1 pointer update. Total: O(n) worst case — if the target is at the end, cur must walk the whole list.

Common bug. Forgetting to handle head as a special case. If x = 10 (head), the loop condition cur.next.value != x will never fire — cur starts at head, and head.value == x is not checked in the loop. The special case at the top is mandatory.

docs.title: Worked example 3.4 — Reverse a singly-linked list
docs.text:
Goal. Reverse 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → null in place → 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 → null.

Approach 1 — iterative three-pointer trick.

Node reverse(Node head) {
    Node prev = null, cur = head;
    while (cur != null) {
        Node next = cur.next;   // save next
        cur.next = prev;        // reverse current's pointer
        prev = cur;             // advance prev
        cur = next;             // advance cur
    }
    return prev;                 // new head
}

Trace on 1 → 2 → 3 → null:

Iteration prev cur cur.next (saved) After cur.next = prev After advance 0 null Node(1) Node(2) 1 → null prev=1, cur=2 1 Node(1) Node(2) Node(3) 2 → 1 prev=2, cur=3 2 Node(2) Node(3) null 3 → 2 prev=3, cur=null exit Node(3) null — — return prev (3)

Final list: 3 → 2 → 1 → null — reversed. Return prev as new head. ✓

Cost. One pass, each node visited once. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Approach 2 — recursive.

Node reverse(Node head) {
    if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;
    Node newHead = reverse(head.next);
    head.next.next = head;
    head.next = null;
    return newHead;
}

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) stack space (recursion depth = n). The iterative version is preferred for large lists.

Why reversal is easy on linked lists but O(n) on arrays. Reversing a linked list just flips pointers — no data movement. Reversing an array requires swapping n/2 pairs. Both are O(n) time, but the constant is much smaller for linked lists (3 pointer writes per node vs. 2 array writes + 2 reads per pair).

docs.title: Worked example 3.5 — Merge two sorted lists
docs.text:
Goal. Given two sorted lists 1 → 3 → 5 and 2 → 4 → 6, produce 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6.

Node merge(Node a, Node b) {
    Node dummy = new Node(0);
    Node tail = dummy;
    while (a != null && b != null) {
        if (a.value <= b.value) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }
        else                    { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;   // append remaining
    return dummy.next;
}

Trace on 1 → 3 → 5 and 2 → 4 → 6:

Step a b tail.next Output so far init 1 2 null dummy 1 3 2 1 dummy → 1 2 3 4 2 → 1 → 2 3 5 4 3 → 1 → 2 → 3 4 5 6 4 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 5 null 6 5 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 exit null 6 — append remainder: → 6

Final: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → null ✓

Cost. Each node visited once. O(m + n) time, O(1) space (reuses existing nodes).

The dummy node trick. Using Node dummy = new Node(0) avoids the "first iteration sets head" special case. The dummy is discarded (return dummy.next) — the actual data starts from dummy.next.

This is the most important linked-list idiom in competitive programming and production. Learn it, use it, teach it.

Why merge is easier on linked lists than arrays. Merging two arrays requires shifting to make room for the merged element — O(n²) if done naively. Merging two sorted arrays is O(m + n) with a new output array, but O(m + n) extra space. Merging two linked lists is O(m + n) time and O(1) space — just splice pointers.

docs.title: Worked example 3.6 — Detect a cycle (Floyd's tortoise and hare)
docs.text:
Problem. Given a linked list, determine whether it contains a cycle (a node whose next eventually points back to an earlier node).

Naive approach. Use a HashSet of visited nodes; detect duplicates. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Floyd's algorithm — O(1) space.

boolean hasCycle(Node head) {
    Node slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Why it works. If there's a cycle, the slow pointer (1 step/iter) and fast (2 steps/iter) eventually meet inside the cycle. If there's no cycle, fast reaches null and the loop terminates.

Trace with a cycle on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 2 → (3 → 4 → 2 → ...):

Step slow fast init 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 2 (wrapped) 3 4 4 4 2 3 5 3 2 6 4 4 — match! return true

Cost. O(n) time, O(1) space.

The tortoise and hare insight. In a cycle of length \(c\), once both pointers are in the cycle, the gap between them decreases by 1 per iteration (fast gains 1 on slow). After at most \(c\) iterations, they meet. Total time: O(n + c) = O(n).

Extension. Once they meet, to find the start of the cycle: reset slow to head; advance both slow and fast one step at a time. They meet at the cycle start. This follows from the fact that the distance from head to cycle-start equals the distance from meeting point to cycle-start.

docs.title: Worked example 3.7 — Find the middle of a linked list
docs.text:
Problem. Given a linked list, find the middle node in one pass.

Node middle(Node head) {
    Node slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    return slow;
}

Trace on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (odd length):

Step slow fast init 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 5 exit (fast.next = null) 3 5

Middle is node 3. ✓

Trace on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 (even length):

Step slow fast init 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 null exit 3 null

Middle is node 3 — the "upper middle" of 2 and 3. If you want the lower middle, initialize fast = head.next instead.

Cost. O(n) time, O(1) space.

This two-pointer pattern — slow + fast — is one of the most reusable tools for linked-list problems. Floyd's cycle detection (Example 3.6), middle-finding (this example), and palindrome-checking all use it.

docs.title: Worked example 3.8 — Doubly-linked list: LRU cache
docs.text:
LRU (Least Recently Used) cache is the classic application of a doubly-linked list. The cache keeps the k most recently used items. When full, it evicts the least recently used.

Design.

  • HashMap: key → node, for O(1) lookup.
  • Doubly-linked list: maintains recency order — head = most recent, tail = least recent.

Operations:

  • get(key): if key exists, move node to head (mark as recently used). O(1).
  • put(key, value): if key exists, update and move to head. If new and cache full, evict tail. Insert new node at head. O(1).
class LRUCache {
    class Node { int key, value; Node prev, next; }

    Map<Integer, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    Node head = new Node(), tail = new Node();   // sentinel nodes
    int capacity;

    LRUCache(int cap) {
        capacity = cap;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    int get(int key) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return -1;
        moveToHead(n);
        return n.value;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) {
            n.value = value;
            moveToHead(n);
        } else {
            if (map.size() == capacity) {
                Node lru = tail.prev;
                removeNode(lru);
                map.remove(lru.key);
            }
            Node nn = new Node();
            nn.key = key; nn.value = value;
            insertAtHead(nn);
            map.put(key, nn);
        }
    }

    void moveToHead(Node n) { removeNode(n); insertAtHead(n); }
    void removeNode(Node n)  { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    void insertAtHead(Node n) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
    }
}

Cost. Every operation is O(1). The doubly-linked list gives O(1) removal of any node; the hash map gives O(1) lookup.

Why not just a hash map alone? A hash map is unordered — it can't tell you which entry is "least recently used." The doubly-linked list maintains the ordering. Together, they provide O(1) LRU semantics.

Why not just a linked list alone? Finding a node by key would be O(n). The hash map provides O(1) access to the node.

This pattern — hash map + doubly-linked list — is used in every LRU cache in production, from Redis to Linux page caches to web browsers.

docs.title: Worked example 3.9 — Josephus problem with a circular list
docs.text:
Setup. \(n\) people numbered 1 to \(n\) sit in a circle. Starting from 1, we skip \(k-1\) people and eliminate the \(k\)-th. Then from the next person, skip \(k-1\) and eliminate the \(k\)-th. Repeat until one survives.

Example: \(n = 7\), \(k = 3\) → survivors eliminated in order: 3, 6, 2, 7, 5, 1. Survivor: 4.

With a circular linked list:

int josephus(int n, int k) {
    Node head = null, tail = null;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        Node nn = new Node(i);
        if (head == null) { head = nn; tail = nn; }
        else { tail.next = nn; tail = nn; }
    }
    tail.next = head;   // make it circular

    Node cur = head, prev = tail;
    while (cur.next != cur) {
        for (int i = 0; i < k - 1; i++) {
            prev = cur;
            cur = cur.next;
        }
        // eliminate cur
        prev.next = cur.next;
        cur = cur.next;
    }
    return cur.value;
}

Trace (n=3, k=2):

Initial circle: 1 → 2 → 3 → (back to 1).

  • Skip 1, eliminate 2: 1 → 3 → (back to 1).
  • Skip 3, eliminate 1: 3 → (back to 3).
  • Survivor: 3.

Closed form (for the record): the survivor is \(J(n, k) = (J(n-1, k) + k) \bmod n\) with \(J(1, k) = 0\), giving positions 0-indexed. The linked-list simulation is what most candidates write in interviews, then the recursion.

Cost. Each elimination is O(k) (skipping), total O(nk). The recursion is O(n) — but the linked-list version is easier to understand and to verify.

docs.title: 3.5 Comparison — arrays vs. linked lists
docs.text:
Operation Array Linked list Random access a[i] O(1) O(n) Search (unsorted) O(n) O(n) Search (sorted) O(log n) O(n) Insert at front O(n) O(1) Insert at end O(1) amortised O(1) with tail Insert in middle (position known) O(n) O(1) Insert in middle (must find) O(n) O(n) Delete at front O(n) O(1) Delete given node pointer — O(1) (doubly) Cache locality Excellent Poor Memory overhead None 8–16 bytes per node

How to choose:

  • Random access dominates? → Array.
  • Insert/delete at front dominates? → Linked list.
  • Insert/delete in middle dominates and you can find the node cheaply? → Doubly-linked list.
  • Sorted lookup dominates? → Array (binary search) or balanced tree (Chapter 5).
  • Cache friendliness matters? → Array — 10–100× faster in wall-clock for linear scans.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. A node holds a value and one or two pointers (next, prev). The list is formed by following pointers from the head.
  2. Singly-linked lists support O(1) insert at head, O(1) insert at tail with a tail pointer, O(n) search, and O(n) random access.
  3. Doubly-linked lists add a prev pointer, enabling O(1) delete of a given node — the basis of LRU caches.
  4. Circular lists have no null terminator; traversal stops when it returns to the head.
  5. Reversal, merge, cycle detection, and middle-finding are the classic patterns — all use the two-pointer trick.
  6. The dummy node trick eliminates special-casing the head — learn it and use it everywhere.
  7. Arrays win on random access and cache locality; linked lists win on insertion/deletion at known positions.
  8. Choose the right structure based on the operation mix, not on a generic preference.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. In a singly-linked list, insert at head costs:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. In a singly-linked list without a tail pointer, insert at tail costs:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. Adding a prev pointer to each node lets you delete a given node in:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm uses:

(a) a hash set (b) a stack (c) two pointers at different speeds (d) recursion

  1. Reversing a singly-linked list in place takes:

(a) O(1) time, O(1) space (b) O(n) time, O(1) space (c) O(n) time, O(n) space (d) O(n log n) time, O(1) space

  1. The dummy node trick is used to:

(a) save memory (b) eliminate the special case of the first insertion (c) avoid null checks (d) make the list circular

  1. Merging two sorted lists of sizes m and n takes:

(a) O(m + n) time, O(m + n) space (b) O(m + n) time, O(1) space (c) O(m · n) time (d) O(log m + log n) time

  1. In a circular linked list, traversal must stop when:

(a) next == null (b) the pointer returns to head (c) a counter reaches n (d) the value becomes negative

  1. In Floyd's algorithm, the two pointers advance at:

(a) the same speed (b) 1 and 2 steps per iteration (c) 1 and log n steps (d) 1 and n steps

    (a) array + hash map (b) doubly-linked list + hash map (c) stack + queue (d) two arrays

  3. Accessing the i-th element of a linked list costs:

    (a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(i) → O(n) worst case (d) O(n²)

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Explain the node-and-pointer model. Why is a linked list's memory scattered, not contiguous?

  2. Compare the cost of insert at head in an array vs. a singly-linked list. Why does the linked list win by a factor of n?

  3. Explain why insert at tail is O(n) without a tail pointer but O(1) with one. What is the trade-off?

  4. Describe the dummy node trick. Give one scenario where it eliminates nontrivial bugs.

  5. Explain the tortoise-and-hare algorithm (Floyd's cycle detection). Prove that if a cycle exists, the two pointers must meet.

  6. Compare singly-linked and doubly-linked lists on: insert at head, delete a given node, memory per node, and traversal in reverse.

  7. Describe the reverse-a-linked-list algorithm. Why does it need three pointers?

  8. Explain the LRU cache design. Why not just a hash map? Why not just a linked list?

  9. Compare the cost of accessing the i-th element in an array vs. a linked list. Give one application where this difference decides the choice.

  10. Explain why cache locality makes arrays faster than linked lists for linear scans, even though both are O(n). What is the wall-clock factor typically?

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (a) O(1).
  2. (c) O(n).
  3. (a) O(1).
  4. (c) two pointers at different speeds.
  5. (b) O(n) time, O(1) space.
  6. (b) eliminate first-insertion special case.
  7. (b) O(m + n) time, O(1) space (for linked lists).
  8. (b) returns to head.
  9. (b) 1 and 2.
  10. (b) doubly-linked + hash map.
  11. (a) O(1).
  12. (c) O(i), worst O(n).
B. Fill in the blank
  1. next
  2. \(O(1)\)
  3. null
  4. prev
  5. \(1\)
  6. dummy
  7. doubly-linked
  8. head
  9. three
  10. 2
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Node-and-pointer model: each node is a heap allocation containing a value and a pointer to the next node. The list is formed by following pointers. Why scattered: each node is a separate allocation — the allocator places them wherever there's free memory. Unlike arrays, there is no guarantee of adjacency — a node's "next" may be anywhere in the heap. This is why random access requires walking the list.
  2. Insert at head — array vs. linked list: array insertion at index 0 requires shifting all n existing elements right → O(n). Linked-list insertion creates one node, sets n.next = head, and updates head → O(1). The n× difference comes from the array's contiguous layout: to make room at the front, every element must move. The linked list just redirects a pointer.
  3. Insert at tail — without tail pointer: must walk from head to the last node, O(n). With tail pointer: tail.next = newNode; tail = newNode → O(1). Trade-off: the tail pointer is 8 bytes (one reference) per list; you save O(n) per append. Any application that appends more than a few times should use the tail pointer.
  4. Dummy node: create a throwaway Node(0) at the start, use it as the "previous" for building, and return dummy.next at the end. Scenario: merging two sorted lists (Example 3.5) — without the dummy, every iteration needs a conditional to check "is this the first element?" — with the dummy, the loop is uniform, no special cases, no bugs. Used everywhere in competitive programming.
  5. Tortoise and hare: both pointers start at head. Each iteration, slow = slow.next (1 step) and fast = fast.next.next (2 steps). Proof of cycle detection: if there's a cycle of length \(c\), once both pointers are inside the cycle, the gap between them decreases by 1 per iteration. After at most \(c\) iterations, they meet. If there's no cycle, fast (or fast.next) becomes null and the loop terminates. O(n) time, O(1) space.
  6. Singly vs. doubly:
  7. Insert at head: O(1) both.
  8. Delete given node: O(n) singly (need predecessor), O(1) doubly (prev pointer).
  9. Memory: 8 bytes singly, 16 bytes doubly (on 64-bit).
  10. Traversal in reverse: impossible singly, O(n) doubly.
  11. Reverse: three pointers — prev (last reversed node), cur (node being reversed), next (temporary save of cur.next). Loop: save next = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, advance prev = cur, cur = next. Return prev. Each node visited once, O(n) time, O(1) space.
  12. LRU cache design: a hash map gives O(1) key lookup, but has no order — it can't tell you "least recently used." A doubly-linked list maintains the recency order — head is most recent, tail is least recent. Together: O(1) get (via hash map), O(1) put (via hash map + O(1) unlink/relink on doubly-linked list). Neither structure alone suffices.
  13. i-th element access: array O(1) (address arithmetic); linked list O(i) (walk i steps). Application: a program that stores a 10-million-element temperature time-series and repeatedly accesses a[t] for random t must use an array — a linked list would be 10 million times slower per access. Conversely, a program that repeatedly inserts at the front of a growing list must use a linked list — an array would shift all elements each time.
  14. Cache locality: modern CPUs fetch 64-byte cache lines; an array stores 16 consecutive ints in one line → 1 miss, 15 hits per 16 accesses. A linked list stores each node in a separate heap allocation → every access misses cache. Wall-clock factor: typically 5–20× slower for linked-list traversal than array traversal on the same data, despite both being O(n). This is why Big-O is not the whole story — constants, especially cache misses, dominate for small-to-medium data.

  • Lafore, Chapters 5–6 — linked list and doubly-linked list.
  • CLRS, Section 10.2 (Linked lists).
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Section 1.3 — the "linked list vs. array" analysis.
  • Open Data Structures, Chapter 3 — rigorous linked list treatment with all operations.
  • Coding interview practice: LeetCode "Linked List" tag — 100+ problems, sorted by difficulty. Start with "Reverse Linked List," "Merge Two Sorted Lists," "Linked List Cycle."
  • "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory" (Ulrich Drepper) — Section 3.3 on array vs. linked list performance.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Insert at head trace. Build 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 by inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order using insertAtHead. Trace each step.

  2. Insert at tail trace. Same build, but using insertAtTail with a tail pointer.

  3. Delete all occurrences. Given a linked list and a value v, remove all occurrences of v. Edge cases: v is at the head; v is the only value.

  4. Reverse a linked list. Implement the iterative reverse. Then implement the recursive reverse. Compare memory usage.

  5. Merge two sorted lists. Implement Example 3.5. Verify with [1, 3, 5] and [2, 4, 6].

  6. Remove duplicates. Given a sorted linked list, remove all duplicate nodes. Given an unsorted linked list, do the same in O(n log n) using a sort first.

  7. Detect and remove a cycle. Use Floyd's algorithm to detect a cycle; then find and remove the entry point.

  8. Find the middle. Implement middle(head) using the two-pointer approach. Test on odd and even lengths.

  9. Merge sort a linked list. Implement merge sort — split by finding the middle, sort each half recursively, merge. What is the total cost, and how does it compare to sorting an array?

  10. Josephus. Implement the circular-list Josephus. Verify \(J(7, 3)\) returns 4.

  11. LRU cache. Implement LRUCache with get and put in O(1). Test with a sequence of operations.

  12. Palindrome check. Given a linked list, determine whether its values form a palindrome. Solve in O(n) time and O(1) space (hint: find middle, reverse second half, compare, then reverse back).

  13. Add two numbers. Given two linked lists representing digits of a number (reversed order), return a linked list representing their sum. E.g., 2 → 4 → 3 + 5 → 6 → 4 = 7 → 0 → 8 (342 + 465 = 807).

  14. Copy a list with random pointers. Each node has next and random pointers. Copy the list in O(n) time. (Hint: interleave clones with originals, then split.)

  15. Intersection of two lists. Given two linked lists, find the node where they intersect. Solve in O(m + n) time, O(1) space. (Hint: align tails.)

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Stacks and Queues
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): stacks (definition, implementation, application) · queues (definition, implementation, application).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the LIFO (stack) and FIFO (queue) principles and their ADT operations.
  2. Implement a stack using both an array and a linked list, with all O(1) operations.
  3. Evaluate a postfix expression with a stack — the classic stack algorithm.
  4. Detect balanced parentheses and matching brackets with a stack.
  5. Implement a circular queue on an array — avoiding the "wrap-around" bug.
  6. Implement a queue using a linked list with a tail pointer — O(1) enqueue and dequeue.
  7. Recognise the applications of deque and priority queue (deferred to Chapter 5).
  8. Choose between array and linked-list implementations based on the operation mix.

docs.title: 4.1.1 The principle
docs.text:
A stack is a collection with a single access point — the top. Items can only be added or removed at the top. This gives LIFO (Last In, First Out) behaviour.

Mental model: a stack of plates. You add at the top, you take from the top. The bottom plate is the last one you'll ever reach.

docs.title: 4.1.2 The ADT
docs.text:
The Stack ADT specifies these operations:

Operation Effect Returns push(x) Insert x at the top — pop() Remove and return the top element Top value peek() / top() Return the top without removing Top value isEmpty() Check whether the stack has elements true / false size() Number of elements int

All operations must be O(1) — anything else defeats the purpose.

docs.title: 4.1.3 The underlying idea — one end only
docs.text:
A stack is a special case of a list where you only operate at one end. That means:

  • No searching — you can't reach into the middle.
  • No random access — only the top is visible.
  • Both array and linked-list can implement it, and both give O(1) push/pop.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Array-based stack
docs.text:
class ArrayStack {
    private int[] data;
    private int top;   // index of the top element; -1 when empty

    ArrayStack(int capacity) {
        data = new int[capacity];
        top = -1;
    }

    void push(int x) {
        if (top == data.length - 1) throw new RuntimeException("Stack full");
        data[++top] = x;
    }

    int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("Stack empty");
        return data[top--];
    }

    int peek() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("Stack empty");
        return data[top];
    }

    boolean isEmpty() { return top == -1; }
    int size() { return top + 1; }
}

Cost: all operations O(1). Push might need to resize if the array is full — see the dynamic version below.

Drawback: fixed capacity. Push onto a full stack throws — unless you resize.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Dynamic array-based stack
docs.text:
Grow by doubling when full, shrink at capacity/4 (same policy as Chapter 2 dynamic arrays):

class DynamicArrayStack {
    private int[] data = new int[1];
    private int top = -1;

    void push(int x) {
        if (top == data.length - 1) resize(data.length * 2);
        data[++top] = x;
    }

    int pop() {
        int x = data[top--];
        if (top > 0 && top < data.length / 4) resize(data.length / 2);
        return x;
    }

    private void resize(int cap) {
        int[] nd = new int[cap];
        System.arraycopy(data, 0, nd, 0, top + 1);
        data = nd;
    }
    // peek, isEmpty, size as above
}

Amortised push/pop: O(1) — same analysis as Chapter 2 (geometric series bound).

Worst-case single push/pop: O(n) when a resize occurs.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Linked-list stack
docs.text:
Push at head, pop from head — both O(1):

class LinkedStack {
    private Node head;

    void push(int x) {
        Node n = new Node(x);
        n.next = head;
        head = n;
    }

    int pop() {
        if (head == null) throw new RuntimeException("Stack empty");
        int x = head.value;
        head = head.next;
        return x;
    }

    int peek() {
        if (head == null) throw new RuntimeException("Stack empty");
        return head.value;
    }

    boolean isEmpty() { return head == null; }
}

Cost: all operations O(1) worst case — no resize, no amortisation needed.

Trade-off vs. array:

Aspect Array stack Linked-list stack Push (amortised) O(1) O(1) Push (worst case) O(n) on resize O(1) Memory per element 4 bytes (int) 4 bytes + 8 for next = 16 bytes Cache locality Excellent Poor Total memory Allocated capacity (may waste up to 50%) Exact

Practical choice: dynamic array in almost every case — the cache advantage is worth the occasional resize. Linked-list stack only when you need strict O(1) worst case (real-time systems) or the number of elements varies wildly.

docs.title: 4.2.4 Python — same idea
docs.text:
Python's built-in list works as a stack with append and pop:

stack = []
stack.append(10)    # push
stack.append(20)
top = stack[-1]     # peek
value = stack.pop() # pop

append and pop() at the end are O(1) amortised (Python's list uses the same doubling policy). Perfect stack.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Balanced parentheses
docs.text:
Problem. Given a string of (), [], {}, determine if every opening bracket is closed by the correct closing bracket, in the right order.

boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') {
            stack.push(c);
        } else if (c == ')' || c == ']' || c == '}') {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) return false;
            char open = stack.pop();
            if (c == ')' && open != '(') return false;
            if (c == ']' && open != '[') return false;
            if (c == '}' && open != '{') return false;
        }
    }
    return stack.isEmpty();   // stack must be empty at end
}

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) space worst case (all opening brackets).

Why a stack? The most recently opened bracket must be the next one closed. That's LIFO. No other data structure handles this as cleanly.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Postfix (Reverse Polish) evaluation
docs.text:
Notation. Normal math is infix (3 + 4). Postfix writes operators after their operands: 3 4 +. This eliminates the need for parentheses and follows a simple left-to-right rule.

Examples: - 3 + 4 → 3 4 + = 7 - (3 + 4) × 5 → 3 4 + 5 × = 35 - 3 + 4 × 5 → 3 4 5 × + = 23

int evalPostfix(String expr) {
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (String tok : expr.trim().split("\\s+")) {
        if (isNumber(tok)) {
            stack.push(Integer.parseInt(tok));
        } else {
            int b = stack.pop();
            int a = stack.pop();
            int r = switch (tok) {
                case "+" -> a + b;
                case "-" -> a - b;
                case "*" -> a * b;
                case "/" -> a / b;
                default  -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(tok);
            };
            stack.push(r);
        }
    }
    return stack.pop();
}

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) space. Every token processed exactly once. No parsing complexity, no operator precedence, no parentheses.

Why postfix matters. All compilers lower expressions to postfix (or a similar stack-based representation) before generating code. The stack is what makes expression evaluation trivial.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Expression conversion (infix → postfix)
docs.text:
Given infix 3 + 4 × 5, use Dijkstra's shunting-yard to produce postfix.

Rules: - Number: emit directly. - Operator: pop and emit operators of higher or equal precedence from the stack, then push the new operator. - (: push. - ): pop and emit until (; discard the (.

String infixToPostfix(String expr) {
    StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
    Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : expr.toCharArray()) {
        if (Character.isDigit(c)) out.append(c).append(' ');
        else if (c == '(') ops.push(c);
        else if (c == ')') {
            while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '(') out.append(ops.pop()).append(' ');
            ops.pop();   // discard '('
        } else if ("+-*/".indexOf(c) >= 0) {
            while (!ops.isEmpty() && prec(ops.peek()) >= prec(c))
                out.append(ops.pop()).append(' ');
            ops.push(c);
        }
    }
    while (!ops.isEmpty()) out.append(ops.pop()).append(' ');
    return out.toString().trim();
}

int prec(char op) {
    return (op == '*' || op == '/') ? 2 : (op == '+' || op == '-') ? 1 : 0;
}

Trace on 3 + 4 * 5:

Token Output Operator stack 3 3 — + 3 + 4 3 4 + * 3 4 + * 5 3 4 5 + * end 3 4 5 * + —

Correct: 3 4 5 * + evaluates to 3 + (4 * 5) = 23. ✓

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: 4.3.4 Undo/redo
docs.text:
A simple text editor's undo feature is a stack of editor states. Each edit pushes the previous state; undo pops and restores.

Redo requires a second stack — every undo pushes onto the redo stack; a new edit clears the redo stack.

This is not just a toy — it's the same pattern used in browsers (back/forward buttons), IDEs (Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y), and version-control tools.

docs.title: 4.3.5 Function calls — the call stack
docs.text:
Every function call in every programming language uses a stack — the call stack:

  • Calling a function: push a stack frame (arguments, local variables, return address).
  • Returning: pop the frame.
  • Recursion: each recursive call is a new frame — depth of recursion = stack depth.

This is why deep recursion overflows the stack — the OS allocates a fixed-size call stack (typically 1–8 MB) and the program crashes when exceeded. Anything that grows the stack unboundedly (naive Fibonacci on \(n = 10^6\)) will crash — not run slowly, crash.

docs.title: 4.3.6 Other stack applications
docs.text:
• Depth-first search (DFS) — iterative DFS uses an explicit stack (Chapter 7).
  • Backtracking algorithms — maze solving, N-queens, sudoku — push/pop choices.
  • Tower of Hanoi — recursion is literally a stack.
  • Syntax parsing — compilers use a stack to parse nested constructs.

docs.title: 4.4.1 The principle
docs.text:
A queue is a collection where items are added at one end (rear) and removed at the other (front). This gives FIFO (First In, First Out).

Mental model: a checkout line. The first customer in is the first out.

docs.title: 4.4.2 The ADT
docs.text:
Operation Effect enqueue(x) Insert x at the rear dequeue() Remove and return the front element peek() / front() Return the front without removing isEmpty() Check whether empty size() Number of elements

All operations must be O(1).

docs.title: 4.4.3 The naive array implementation — and why it fails
docs.text:
Tempting first attempt:

class NaiveQueue {
    int[] data = new int[100];
    int front = 0, rear = 0;

    void enqueue(int x) { data[rear++] = x; }
    int dequeue() { return data[front++]; }
}

The bug: front and rear both move forward, never resetting. After 100 enqueues and 100 dequeues, the array is "empty" but front = 100, rear = 100 — the next enqueue overflows even though there's space.

Fix 1: shift every dequeue. Move all elements left by one — O(n) per dequeue → O(n²) for n operations. Unacceptable.

Fix 2: wrap around — the circular queue.

docs.title: 4.5.1 The idea
docs.text:
Treat the array as a circle: index (i + 1) % capacity wraps around. Front and rear both advance by 1 modulo capacity; when front catches up to rear, the queue is empty.

class CircularQueue {
    private int[] data;
    private int front, size;
    private final int capacity;

    CircularQueue(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        data = new int[capacity];
        front = 0;
        size = 0;
    }

    void enqueue(int x) {
        if (size == capacity) throw new RuntimeException("Queue full");
        data[(front + size) % capacity] = x;
        size++;
    }

    int dequeue() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("Queue empty");
        int x = data[front];
        front = (front + 1) % capacity;
        size--;
        return x;
    }

    int peek() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("Queue empty");
        return data[front];
    }

    boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    int size() { return size; }
}

Cost. All operations O(1) — constant time, no shifting, no waste.

Key design choice: use size not (rear - front). If you track rear and front both, you can't distinguish "empty" from "full" without an extra flag or a deliberate one-slot gap. Tracking size makes both checks trivial.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Why size matters
docs.text:
Consider the alternative:

int front = 0, rear = 0;
boolean isEmpty() { return front == rear; }
boolean isFull()  { return front == rear; }   // oops — same condition

Empty and full look identical without extra state. Options:

  • Sacrifice one slot: only capacity - 1 elements stored; full when (rear + 1) % capacity == front.
  • Track size: straightforward, no wasted slot. This is the cleaner approach.

docs.title: 4.5.3 Trace
docs.text:
Setup: capacity = 5, empty.

Operation data (index 0..4) front size enqueue(10) [10, _, _, _, _] 0 1 enqueue(20) [10, 20, _, _, _] 0 2 enqueue(30) [10, 20, 30, _, _] 0 3 dequeue() → 10 [_, 20, 30, _, _] 1 2 dequeue() → 20 [_, _, 30, _, _] 2 1 enqueue(40) [_, _, 30, 40, _] 2 2 enqueue(50) [_, _, 30, 40, 50] 2 3 enqueue(60) [60, _, 30, 40, 50] (wrapped!) 2 4 dequeue() → 30 [60, _, _, 40, 50] 3 3 dequeue() → 40 [60, _, _, _, 50] 4 2 dequeue() → 50 [60, _, _, _, _] 0 1 dequeue() → 60 [_, _, _, _, _] 1 0

The wrap-around keeps the queue O(1) per operation — no shifting, no waste. This is the standard queue implementation in every real system.

docs.title: 4.6 Linked-list queue
docs.text:
Alternative — no capacity limit:

class LinkedQueue {
    private Node head, tail;

    void enqueue(int x) {
        Node n = new Node(x);
        if (tail == null) { head = tail = n; }
        else { tail.next = n; tail = n; }
    }

    int dequeue() {
        if (head == null) throw new RuntimeException("Queue empty");
        int x = head.value;
        head = head.next;
        if (head == null) tail = null;   // queue became empty
        return x;
    }

    int peek() {
        if (head == null) throw new RuntimeException("Queue empty");
        return head.value;
    }

    boolean isEmpty() { return head == null; }
}

Cost. All operations O(1). Both enqueue and dequeue modify the ends.

Why both head and tail pointers matter. Enqueue at tail, dequeue from head — both O(1). With only head, enqueue would be O(n).

The empty-queue edge case. After the last dequeue, head = null but tail still points to the old node — a bug unless you explicitly reset tail = null. This is one of the two "classic" queue bugs (the other is the same for enqueue when starting from empty).

Trade-off vs. circular array:

Aspect Circular array Linked list Enqueue / dequeue O(1) O(1) Capacity Fixed (must resize) Unbounded Memory per element 4 bytes 4 + 8 = 16 bytes Cache locality Excellent Poor Bug risk Wrap-around index arithmetic Null-pointer bugs

Practical choice: circular array for fixed-size buffers (network packets, streaming); linked list when unbounded growth is needed.

docs.title: 4.7.1 Deque (double-ended queue)
docs.text:
A deque allows insert and remove at both ends — O(1) at each end.

Operations: addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, peekFirst, peekLast.

Implementation: doubly-linked list, or circular array (with two valid pointers).

Use cases:

  • Sliding window maximum — maintain a monotonic deque.
  • Palindrome check — remove from both ends, compare.
  • Undo/redo — push and pop at both ends.
  • Work-stealing schedulers — threads steal from the other end.

Java's ArrayDeque is the standard Deque implementation — fast, cache-friendly, O(1) amortised at both ends. Prefer ArrayDeque over Stack or LinkedList in Java unless you need linked semantics.

docs.title: 4.7.2 Priority queue
docs.text:
A priority queue — not FIFO or LIFO — returns the element with the highest (or lowest) priority first.

Standard implementation: binary heap (Chapter 5). All operations O(log n) except peek (O(1)).

Use cases: Dijkstra's algorithm (Chapter 7), Huffman coding, task scheduling by priority, event simulation.

We defer the full treatment to Chapter 5 — the heap is a tree.

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — Balanced parentheses trace
docs.text:
Input: "([{}])".

Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

Trace:

Char Action Stack (top on right) ( push ( [ push ( [ { push ( [ { } pop {, matches ( [ ] pop [, matches ( ) pop (, matches (empty)

Result: stack empty at end → balanced ✓

Input: "([)]":

Char Action Stack ( push ( [ push ( [ ) pop [ — mismatch —

Result: mismatch → not balanced ✓

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — Postfix evaluation trace
docs.text:
Input: "3 4 + 5 *" — that's (3 + 4) × 5 = 35.

Trace:

Token Action Stack 3 push [3] 4 push [3, 4] + pop 4, pop 3, push 7 [7] 5 push [7, 5] * pop 5, pop 7, push 35 [35]

Result: 35 ✓

Note the order of pops. For a b -, pop b first, then a, compute a - b. Order matters for non-commutative operators (-, /).

docs.title: Worked example 4.3 — Infix to postfix
docs.text:
Input: "a + b * c - d" (no parentheses — standard precedence).

Precedence: * and / = 2, + and - = 1.

Token Output Operator stack a a — + a + b a b + * a b + * c a b c + * - a b c * + (pop *, then +) - d a b c * + d - end a b c * + d - —

Result: a b c * + d -

Sanity check. Infix a + b*c - d = a + (b*c) - d. Postfix a b c * + d - = (a + b*c) - d. ✓

The - case. When the new operator - arrives, pop and emit all higher-or-equal precedence ops (*, +) first — then push -.

docs.title: Worked example 4.4 — Two-stack expression evaluator (infix with parentheses)
docs.text:
Input: "3 + 4 * (2 - 1)".

Two stacks: one for numbers, one for operators.

int evalInfix(String s) {
    Deque<Integer> nums = new ArrayDeque<>();
    Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (c == ' ') continue;
        if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
            int n = 0;
            while (i < s.length() && Character.isDigit(s.charAt(i))) {
                n = n * 10 + (s.charAt(i++) - '0');
            }
            i--;
            nums.push(n);
        } else if (c == '(') ops.push(c);
        else if (c == ')') {
            while (ops.peek() != '(') apply(nums, ops);
            ops.pop();
        } else {   // operator
            while (!ops.isEmpty() && prec(ops.peek()) >= prec(c)) apply(nums, ops);
            ops.push(c);
        }
    }
    while (!ops.isEmpty()) apply(nums, ops);
    return nums.pop();
}

void apply(Deque<Integer> nums, Deque<Character> ops) {
    char op = ops.pop();
    int b = nums.pop(), a = nums.pop();
    nums.push(op == '+' ? a + b : op == '-' ? a - b : op == '*' ? a * b : a / b);
}

Trace:

Char Action Num stack Op stack 3 push [3] — + push [3] + 4 push [3, 4] + * push (higher prec) [3, 4] + * ( push [3, 4] + * ( 2 push [3, 4, 2] + * ( - push [3, 4, 2] + * ( - 1 push [3, 4, 2, 1] + * ( - ) apply - [3, 4, 1] + * end apply * [3, 4] + end apply + [7] —

Result: 7 ✓ (3 + 4*(2-1) = 3 + 4 = 7)

Cost. O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Worked example 4.5 — Circular queue trace
docs.text:
Setup: capacity = 3.

Operation data (index 0..2) front size enqueue(1) [1, _, _] 0 1 enqueue(2) [1, 2, _] 0 2 enqueue(3) [1, 2, 3] 0 3 (full) dequeue() → 1 [_, 2, 3] 1 2 enqueue(4) [4, 2, 3] (wrapped: index (1+2) % 3 = 0) 1 3 enqueue(5) throw: size == capacity — — dequeue() → 2 [4, _, 3] 2 2 enqueue(5) [4, 5, 3] (index (2+2) % 3 = 1) 2 3

The wrap-around is what lets us reuse positions 0 and 1 without shifting. Without wrap, we'd hit the "array full" condition at position 3 even though only 2 elements exist.

docs.title: Worked example 4.6 — Queue used for BFS (preview)
docs.text:
Queue-based BFS on a tree/graph is the canonical queue application. Each node is enqueued when discovered; dequeued when processed.

void bfs(Node root) {
    if (root == null) return;
    Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.add(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        Node cur = q.remove();
        System.out.println(cur.value);
        if (cur.left  != null) q.add(cur.left);
        if (cur.right != null) q.add(cur.right);
    }
}

Why a queue? BFS visits nodes in level order — root, then all its children, then all grandchildren, etc. A queue is FIFO, so nodes are processed in the order discovered. A stack would give DFS instead (LIFO — dive deep first).

Cost. O(n) time per traversal, O(w) space where w = max width of tree. Chapter 7 covers graph BFS fully.

docs.title: 4.8 Comparison table
docs.text: Aspect Stack Queue Deque Priority queue Order LIFO FIFO Both ends Priority Push/enqueue O(1) O(1) O(1) at each end O(log n) Pop/dequeue O(1) O(1) O(1) at each end O(log n) Peek O(1) O(1) O(1) O(1) Implementation Array / list Circular array / list List or array Binary heap Example applications Undo, DFS, parsing BFS, scheduling, buffers Sliding window Dijkstra

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Stack is LIFO — push, pop, peek at one end. O(1) operations.
  2. Array stack (amortised O(1)) is faster than linked-list stack due to cache locality; linked-list stack is O(1) worst case (no resize).
  3. Balanced parentheses and postfix evaluation are the two canonical stack applications — O(n) time each.
  4. Infix to postfix via shunting-yard algorithm — O(n) time.
  5. The function call stack is a physical implementation of the stack ADT — recursion depth = stack depth.
  6. Queue is FIFO — enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. O(1) operations.
  7. Circular array queue wraps front and size modulo capacity — no shifting, no waste.
  8. Linked-list queue with head and tail — O(1) at both ends.
  9. Deque — O(1) at both ends; Java's ArrayDeque is the standard implementation.
  10. Priority queue returns the highest-priority element — implemented with a binary heap (Chapter 5).

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. A stack operates on which principle?

(a) FIFO (b) LIFO (c) Priority (d) Random

  1. Push and pop on an array-based stack are:

(a) O(1) each (b) O(log n) each (c) O(n) each (d) O(n²) each

  1. Postfix expression "5 3 2 * +" evaluates to:

(a) 16 (b) 11 (c) 10 (d) 25

  1. Balanced parentheses detection uses a stack because:

(a) brackets are LIFO-nested (b) it's the only option (c) it uses less memory (d) it's faster than a queue

  1. A circular queue avoids the "array full" bug by:

(a) shifting elements (b) wrapping indices modulo capacity (c) using a linked list (d) always keeping the array half empty

  1. Enqueue and dequeue on a circular array queue are:

(a) O(1) each (b) O(log n) each (c) O(n) each (d) O(n²) each

  1. In a linked-list queue, enqueue at tail requires:

(a) walking to the end (b) a tail pointer for O(1) (c) a head pointer only (d) a doubly-linked list

  1. ArrayDeque in Java is:

(a) array-based (b) linked-list based (c) hash-based (d) tree-based

  1. "a + b * c" in postfix is:

(a) a b c * + (b) a b + c * (c) + a * b c (d) a b * c +

  1. A queue is used for BFS because:

    (a) it dives deep (b) it processes nodes in discovery order (c) it's faster than a stack (d) it uses less memory

  2. In the two-stack infix evaluator, the two stacks hold:

    (a) operands and results (b) numbers and operators (c) values and pointers (d) inputs and outputs

  3. Priority queue is typically implemented with:

    (a) array (b) binary heap (c) hash table (d) stack

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A stack operates on _____ (Last In, First Out).

  2. A queue operates on _____ (First In, First Out).

  3. Push on a dynamic array stack is O(_____) amortised.

  4. The postfix expression "3 4 +" evaluates to _____.

  5. Balanced parentheses uses the stack's _____ property.

  6. A circular queue wraps indices with the modulo of _____ (the array's size).

  7. Dequeue from a linked-list queue with a tail pointer costs O(_____).

  8. "a b + c *" in infix is _____.

  9. The shunting-yard algorithm converts _____ to postfix.

  10. ArrayDeque in Java is preferred over Stack because it's _____ -friendly.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. State the stack ADT — its operations and their complexity.

  2. Explain why postfix evaluation is simpler than infix evaluation — what algorithm does infix require that postfix doesn't?

  3. Implement a balanced parentheses checker in pseudocode. Why is a stack the right choice?

  4. Describe the circular queue wrap-around logic. Draw a diagram of enqueue/dequeue wrapping.

  5. Explain why size is a better state variable than tracking front and rear independently for a circular queue.

  6. Compare array-based and linked-list stacks on: worst-case push, memory per element, cache locality.

  7. Describe the two-stack infix evaluator. What does each stack contain?

  8. Explain why BFS uses a queue and DFS uses a stack (or recursion). What property of the graph traversal does each data structure give?

  9. What is a deque? Give two applications.

  10. Explain the difference between a queue and a priority queue. When would you prefer a priority queue?

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) LIFO.
  2. (a) O(1).
  3. (b) 11 (5 + 3*2 = 11).
  4. (a) LIFO-nested.
  5. (b) wrap indices.
  6. (a) O(1).
  7. (b) tail pointer.
  8. (a) array-based.
  9. (a) a b c * +.
  10. (b) discovery order.
  11. (b) numbers and operators.
  12. (b) binary heap.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. LIFO
  2. FIFO
  3. \(1\)
  4. 7
  5. LIFO
  6. capacity
  7. \(1\)
  8. (a + b) * c
  9. infix
  10. cache
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Stack ADT: operations push(x), pop(), peek(), isEmpty(), size(). All must be O(1). LIFO ordering: last element pushed is first element popped. Implementation is either array-backed (amortised O(1)) or linked-list-backed (strict O(1)).
  2. Postfix vs. infix evaluation: postfix processes tokens left-to-right — push operands, pop for operators. No precedence rules, no parentheses. Infix requires either two passes (convert to postfix first) or two stacks (operators and operands, with precedence rules and parenthesised sub-expressions). The postfix representation embeds precedence and grouping structurally; infix forces the evaluator to reconstruct them.
  3. Balanced parentheses pseudocode: for each character: if opening bracket, push. If closing, pop and check it matches. At end, stack must be empty. Return true iff no mismatch and empty at end. Why a stack: the most recently opened bracket must be closed first — that's LIFO. Any other structure (queue, list, hash) would give wrong answers because they don't respect nesting order.
  4. Circular queue: maintain front (index of oldest element) and size (element count). enqueue(x) writes at (front + size) % capacity, then size++. dequeue() reads data[front], then front = (front + 1) % capacity and size--. Diagram: as front and size advance past the end, they wrap to index 0 — the array is treated as a ring. No element moves.
  5. Why size beats front+rear: if you track front and rear as two independent indices, the condition front == rear is ambiguous — it's both "empty" (initial state) and "full" (wrapped around). Resolving this requires either a waste-one-slot convention (store at most capacity-1 elements) or an extra size variable anyway. Tracking size directly makes both isEmpty and isFull trivial and unambiguous — no discarded slot, no extra flags.
  6. Array vs. linked-list stack: (i) worst-case push — array O(n) on resize, linked-list O(1); (ii) memory per element — array 4 bytes (int), linked-list 16 bytes (value + next pointer, 64-bit); (iii) cache locality — array has 10–100× better cache hit rate for sequential push/pop. Practical choice: array stack unless strict O(1) worst case is required (real-time systems).
  7. Two-stack infix evaluator: one stack holds operands (numbers), the other holds operators (and parentheses). When an operator arrives, pop and apply operators of higher-or-equal precedence; when ) is seen, pop and apply until (; at the end, apply all remaining operators. Result: one number on the operand stack.
  8. BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack (or recursion): BFS must process nodes in breadth-first order — nearest first, then next-nearest. A FIFO queue naturally produces this: enqueue all children of a dequeued node; they get processed after all currently queued nodes. DFS must go deep first — LIFO stack or recursion naturally pushes the "next child" onto the front of the processing order. Property: BFS gives shortest-path distance in unweighted graphs; DFS gives structural properties (cycles, topological order).
  9. Deque (double-ended queue): O(1) insert and remove at both ends. Operations: addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, peekFirst, peekLast. Applications: (i) sliding-window maximum — monotonic deque tracks candidates; (ii) palindrome check — compare from both ends inward.
  10. Queue vs. priority queue: a queue processes elements in FIFO order; a priority queue processes elements in priority order — highest (or lowest) priority first, regardless of insertion order. Prefer priority queue when: the ordering that matters is priority, not arrival time — e.g., Dijkstra's algorithm (process nearest unexplored node first), task scheduling by priority, event simulation (earliest event first), Huffman coding (merge two smallest first).
