B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(m\)
  2. collision
  3. \(m\)
  4. prime
  5. 31
  6. linked list
  7. array
  8. primary
  9. step (or interval)
  10. tombstone
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Hash table idea: a hash function h(k) maps each key to an array index; storing and retrieving is then a constant-time array access at that index. Why O(1) average: under uniform hashing, each lookup lands on a bucket with expected load α = n/m. If α is bounded (e.g., 0.75), the expected number of comparisons is ~1 + α/2 — a constant. So average case is O(1). Worst case is O(n) if all keys collide, but with good hash + bounded α this is astronomically unlikely.
  2. Properties: deterministic, uniform over [0, m-1], fast to compute (O(1) with small constant), avalanche (small input change → large output change). Why prime m: if m has nontrivial factors, keys that share those factors all hash to multiples of those factors, creating systematic collisions. Example: m = 10, keys {10, 20, 30} — all multiples of 10 — all land at index 0. Prime m has no nontrivial factors, so no such pattern arises.
  3. Separate chaining: each table slot is a linked list. On collision, append (or prepend) to the list. Cost: O(1 + α) where α = n/m is the load factor. Under uniform hashing, expected chain length = α; expected comparisons per lookup ≈ 1 + α/2. Keep α ≤ 0.75 → constant cost per operation. Resize (double) when α exceeds threshold.
  4. Open addressing: all keys stored directly in the array; on collision, probe a deterministic sequence of alternative indices. Memory/cache: no per-element pointers → half the memory of chaining. Excellent cache locality because the whole table is contiguous. Trade-off: deletion requires tombstones; performance degrades faster as α grows (linear probing at α = 0.9 is 50 probes per lookup).
  5. Linear probing: h(k, i) = (h(k) + i) mod m — simplest, but suffers primary clustering (runs of occupied slots grow). Quadratic probing: h(k, i) = (h(k) + c₁i + c₂i²) mod m — breaks primary clustering, but suffers secondary clustering (same initial hash → same probe sequence). Double hashing: h(k, i) = (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m — no clustering at all, since different keys with the same h₁ have different probe sequences (determined by h₂). Best performance, but requires two hash computations per probe.
  6. Tombstone problem: suppose keys {10, 27, 8} all hash to slot 3. Using linear probing: slot 3 = 10, slot 4 = 27, slot 5 = 8. Now delete slot 4 (27). If we set slot 4 = EMPTY, a lookup for 8 will probe slot 3 (10, no), then slot 4 (EMPTY → stop) → returns "not found", even though 8 is at slot 5. Solution: set slot 4 = DELETED (tombstone). Lookup continues past DELETED slots; insertion can reuse them. Consequence: long tombstone chains degrade performance — periodically rehash to sweep them.
  7. Universal hashing: a family H of hash functions such that for any two distinct keys k₁ ≠ k₂, the probability (over random choice of h ∈ H) that h(k₁) = h(k₂) is at most 1/m. Definition family: h_{a,b}(k) = ((a·k + b) mod p) mod m for p prime, a, b chosen uniformly at random (with a ≠ 0). Defends against adversarial input: the adversary doesn't know which hash function is active, so they cannot craft all-colliding inputs. Even if they send keys with a predicted pattern, the random choice of a, b means the expected number of collisions is bounded by α. This is the standard defence against HashDoS attacks.
  8. Hash vs. balanced BST: (i) Ordered operations (range, min/max, predecessor) → BST (hash tables can't answer these efficiently). (ii) Worst-case guarantee — BST gives O(log n) worst case, hash table O(n) worst case → BST for adversarial input (or hash with universal hashing). (iii) Insertion-order preservation (e.g., LRU tracking) → BST with a custom key, or a separate linked list. For pure unordered lookup on large datasets, hash table wins in average practice.
  9. Polynomial rolling hash: h(s) = (Σ s[i] · p^i) mod m. Each character is weighted by a power of p. Why p = 31: (i) small enough that arithmetic stays in machine integers; (ii) prime, so no divisor-related pattern in the output; (iii) for English text, gives good distribution — adjacent strings (differing in one character) produce very different hashes. p = 131 is also common (better for long strings). Java's String.hashCode() uses 31.
  10. Two-sum with a hash set: iterate through the array once. For each element x, check if (target − x) is already in the set (O(1)); if yes, return true; otherwise insert x into the set. Total: 2n hash operations = O(n) time. Space: O(n) for the set. Trade-off: beats the sorted-array approach's O(n log n) time but uses O(n) extra memory.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• CLRS, Chapter 11 (Hash Tables) — the definitive treatment; universal hashing in detail.
  • Weiss, Chapter 5 (Hashing).
  • Lafore, Chapter 11 (Hash Tables).
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Chapter 3.4 (Hash Tables).
  • Open Data Structures, Chapter 5 (Hash Tables) — with rigorous analysis of open addressing.
  • Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3 (Sorting and Searching) — Section 6.4 (Hashing) — the classic.
  • Joel Spolsky, "The Law of Leaky Abstractions" — joelonsoftware.com/2002/11/11/the-law-of-leaky-abstractions/ — relevant for understanding why hash tables fail in adversarial settings.
  • "HashDoS": cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2011-4461 — the class of attacks that motivated universal hashing in production.

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Division method, m choice. Insert {3, 6, 9, 12, 15} into tables of size 4, 5, and 7 with h(k) = k mod m. Count the number of collisions in each. Which m is best? Why?

  2. Multiplication method. Compute h(k) = ⌊m · (k · 0.618 mod 1)⌋ for m = 16 and keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Plot the distribution of 100 random keys.

  3. String hash. Compute polynomial hash of "dog" with p = 31 and m = 101. Then "god" — do they differ?

  4. Chaining trace. With m = 5, insert keys {12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37} using h(k) = k mod 5. Draw the chained table. What is the maximum chain length?

  5. Linear probing trace. Same keys, same hash, using linear probing with m = 7. Show the table after each insert. What is the maximum probe count?

  6. Quadratic probing trace. Same as problem 5 but with quadratic probing. Show the table.

  7. Double hashing. For m = 11, h₁(k) = k mod 11, h₂(k) = 1 + (k mod 10), insert keys {22, 33, 44, 55, 66}. Show each key's probe sequence.

  8. Tombstone trace. Insert keys {10, 20, 30} into m = 5 table with linear probing. Delete 20. Now look up 30 — how many probes? Now delete 10 and look up 30 — how many probes?

  9. Load factor. At α = 0.5 with linear probing, how many probes on average for successful and unsuccessful lookups?

  10. Amortised rehashing. Insert 1000 elements into a hash table starting with size 2, doubling whenever α > 0.75. Compute the total number of rehash steps and the amortised cost per insert.

  11. Universal hashing. Let p = 1009, m = 20. Choose a = 17, b = 43. Compute h(50), h(150), h(250). Are these keys likely to collide under this hash? What about under h(k) = k mod 20?

  12. Two-sum. Given [3, 5, 2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9, use a hash set to find a pair. Trace each step.

  13. Longest substring without repeating characters. Given a string, find the longest substring without repeating characters. Use a sliding window with a hash map (char → last index). O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet_size)) space.

  14. Group anagrams. Given a list of strings, group anagrams together. Use a hash map from sorted-string → list of anagrams.

  15. Subarray sum equals K. Given an array of integers and K, count the number of contiguous subarrays summing to K. Use a hash map of prefix sums.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Graphs
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): definition · implementation (adjacency matrix, adjacency list) · DFS and BFS · selected graph algorithms (shortest path, minimum spanning tree) · applications.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define the graph terminology: vertex, edge, directed vs. undirected, weighted, cycle, path.
  2. Represent a graph using adjacency matrix, adjacency list, and (for weighted graphs) edge list.
  3. Explain the time/memory trade-offs of each representation.
  4. Implement DFS and BFS — both recursively and iteratively.
  5. Use DFS and BFS to solve: connected components, cycle detection, topological sort, bipartite check.
  6. Implement Dijkstra's algorithm for single-source shortest paths (non-negative weights).
  7. Implement Bellman–Ford for graphs with negative edges; detect negative cycles.
  8. Implement Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms for minimum spanning trees.
  9. Recognise when to use Dijkstra vs. Bellman–Ford vs. BFS for shortest paths.
  10. Apply graph algorithms to real problems (networks, routing, dependency resolution, recommendation).

docs.title: 7.1.1 Definition
docs.text:
A graph \(G = (V, E)\) consists of:

  • \(V\) — a set of vertices (nodes).
  • \(E\) — a set of edges — pairs of vertices.
Term Meaning Directed Edges have direction: \((u, v) \ne (v, u)\) Undirected Edges are symmetric: \(\{u, v\} = \{v, u\}\) Weighted Each edge has a numeric weight (cost, distance, capacity) Adjacent Two vertices connected by an edge Degree Number of edges touching a vertex Path Sequence of vertices with edges between consecutive ones Cycle Path that starts and ends at the same vertex, with no repeated edges Connected Every vertex reachable from every other (undirected) Strongly connected Every vertex reachable from every other, following edges (directed) DAG Directed Acyclic Graph — directed, no cycles

docs.title: 7.1.2 Sparse vs. dense
docs.text:
A graph with \(n\) vertices can have up to \(\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) edges (undirected).

Density Edges m Memory implication Sparse \(m \approx O(n)\) Adjacency list is best Dense \(m \approx O(n²)\) Adjacency matrix is fine

Most real-world graphs are sparse. A road network with a million cities has maybe 2–3 million road segments — not \(10^{12}\).

docs.title: 7.2.1 Adjacency matrix
docs.text:
A 2D array matrix[i][j] = 1 if there's an edge from i to j; 0 otherwise. For weighted graphs, store the weight instead.

class AdjacencyMatrix {
    int[][] matrix;
    int n;

    AdjacencyMatrix(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        this.matrix = new int[n][n];   // 0 = no edge, weight = edge present
    }

    void addEdge(int u, int v, int w) {
        matrix[u][v] = w;
        matrix[v][u] = w;   // for undirected
    }

    boolean hasEdge(int u, int v) {
        return matrix[u][v] != 0;
    }

    List<Integer> neighbors(int u) {
        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
            if (matrix[u][v] != 0) result.add(v);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
Operation Cost Add edge O(1) Check edge O(1) List neighbors O(n) Memory O(n²)

Best for: dense graphs, or when you need O(1) edge lookup. Worst for: sparse graphs (wasted memory).

docs.title: 7.2.2 Adjacency list
docs.text:
An array of lists — adj[i] contains all neighbors of i.

class AdjacencyList {
    List<List<Integer>> adj;
    int n;

    AdjacencyList(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        this.adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    }

    void addEdge(int u, int v) {
        adj.get(u).add(v);
        adj.get(v).add(u);   // for undirected
    }

    boolean hasEdge(int u, int v) {
        return adj.get(u).contains(v);   // O(degree(u))
    }

    List<Integer> neighbors(int u) {
        return adj.get(u);
    }
}
Operation Cost Add edge O(1) Check edge O(degree(u)) — worst O(n) List neighbors O(degree(u)) — optimal Memory O(n + m) — optimal for sparse

Best for: sparse graphs (the common case). Worst for: edge lookup.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Weighted adjacency list
docs.text:
class Edge {
    int to, weight;
    Edge(int to, int w) { this.to = to; this.weight = w; }
}

class WeightedGraph {
    List<List<Edge>> adj;
    int n;

    WeightedGraph(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    }

    void addEdge(int u, int v, int w) {
        adj.get(u).add(new Edge(v, w));
        adj.get(v).add(new Edge(u, w));
    }
}

This is what Dijkstra, Prim, and Kruskal expect.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Comparison
docs.text:
Aspect Adjacency matrix Adjacency list Memory O(n²) O(n + m) Add edge O(1) O(1) Check edge O(1) O(degree) List neighbors O(n) O(degree) Dense graph fine O(n²) too — no savings Sparse graph wastes O(n²) best

Rule: adjacency list unless the graph is dense (> ~30% of possible edges) or the algorithm needs many edge lookups.

docs.title: 7.3.1 The algorithm
docs.text:
void bfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[adj.size()];
    Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.add(start);
    visited[start] = true;
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int u = queue.remove();
        System.out.println(u);
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (!visited[v]) {
                visited[v] = true;
                queue.add(v);
            }
        }
    }
}

Idea: expand outward from the start, visiting all distance-1 vertices first, then all distance-2, then all distance-3, etc.

Cost: O(V + E) — every vertex and edge visited at most once.

Space: O(V) for the queue and visited set.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Properties
docs.text:
• Shortest paths in unweighted graphs. BFS explores by edge count; the first time it reaches a vertex, that's the shortest path.
  • Level-order in trees (Chapter 5).
  • Undirected connectivity: BFS from a start vertex reaches all vertices in its connected component.

docs.title: 7.3.3 BFS computes shortest distances
docs.text:
int[] bfsDistances(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
    int[] dist = new int[adj.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
    dist[start] = 0;
    Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.add(start);
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int u = queue.remove();
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                queue.add(v);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Proof of correctness. BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance from start. When it reaches v from u, dist[v] is set to dist[u] + 1. If a shorter path existed, BFS would have found it earlier (contradiction with the FIFO order). ✓

Cost: O(V + E).

docs.title: 7.4.1 The algorithm — recursive
docs.text:
void dfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, boolean[] visited) {
    visited[u] = true;
    System.out.println(u);
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited);
    }
}

Idea: dive as deep as possible before backtracking. Follow one neighbor all the way to a dead end, then backtrack.

Cost: O(V + E).

Space: O(V) for visited + O(h) call stack, where h is the maximum depth.

docs.title: 7.4.2 The algorithm — iterative
docs.text:
void dfsIterative(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[adj.size()];
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(start);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        int u = stack.pop();
        if (visited[u]) continue;
        visited[u] = true;
        System.out.println(u);
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (!visited[v]) stack.push(v);
        }
    }
}

Same result as recursive DFS — but no recursion depth risk.

docs.title: 7.4.3 DFS properties
docs.text:
• Cycle detection — if we find a back edge to an ancestor, there's a cycle.
  • Topological sort — reverse postorder of a DFS on a DAG.
  • Connected components — count separate DFS starts.
  • Bipartite check — 2-coloring during DFS.
  • DFS tree depth = O(V) worst case — recursive DFS can stack-overflow on large graphs.

docs.title: Worked example 7.1 — BFS trace on a small graph
docs.text:
Graph (undirected): 

0 — 1 — 3
|   |   |
2 — 4 — 5

Edges: {(0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,4), (3,5), (4,5)}.

BFS from 0:

Step Queue Visited dist 0 [0] {0} 0:0 1 [1, 2] {0, 1, 2} 1:1, 2:1 2 [2, 3, 4] {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} 3:2, 4:2 3 [3, 4] (none new from 2) 4 [4, 5] {0–5} 5:3 5 [5] 6 [] done

Visit order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — level by level. Distances: [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3].

The BFS tree edges (parent of each vertex): 0 → {1, 2}, 1 → {3, 4}, 4 → 5.

Note: there are two shortest paths to vertex 5 (via 3 and via 4), both length 3. BFS finds one — the one reached first in BFS order.

docs.title: Worked example 7.2 — DFS trace on the same graph
docs.text:
DFS from 0 (recursive, neighbors in sorted order):

Trace:

Step Stack (call) Action Visited 1 dfs(0) visit 0 {0} 2 dfs(1) visit 1 {0, 1} 3 dfs(3) visit 3 (from 1) {0, 1, 3} 4 dfs(5) visit 5 (from 3) {0, 1, 3, 5} 5 neighbor 4 (from 5) 6 dfs(4) visit 4 {0, 1, 3, 4, 5} 7 neighbor 0 (visited), 1 (visited), 2 (unvisited) 8 dfs(2) visit 2 {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} 9 back up

Visit order: 0, 1, 3, 5, 4, 2 — not the same as BFS. DFS dives deep first.

The DFS tree edges: 0 → 1, 1 → 3, 3 → 5, 5 → 4, 4 → 2. A path-shaped tree — depth 5.

Contrast with BFS tree depth: 3.

docs.title: 7.5.1 The problem
docs.text:
Given a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, find the shortest path from a source vertex s to every other vertex.

"Shortest" means minimal sum of edge weights — not edge count. BFS solves this only when all weights are equal (unweighted = weight 1 each).

docs.title: 7.5.2 The algorithm
docs.text:
int[] dijkstra(List<List<Edge>> adj, int source) {
    int n = adj.size();
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[source] = 0;

    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);
    pq.add(new int[]{source, 0});

    boolean[] settled = new boolean[n];

    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int u = cur[0];
        if (settled[u]) continue;
        settled[u] = true;

        for (Edge e : adj.get(u)) {
            int v = e.to, w = e.weight;
            if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w;
                pq.add(new int[]{v, dist[v]});
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Idea:

  1. Start with dist[s] = 0, all others infinity.
  2. Repeatedly pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance.
  3. Relax its outgoing edges: if dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v], update dist[v].
  4. Repeat until all vertices settled.

The priority queue (Chapter 5 heap) makes picking the minimum vertex O(log V).

docs.title: 7.5.3 Correctness
docs.text:
Invariant: once a vertex u is settled (popped from PQ), its dist[u] is final.

Proof by contradiction. Suppose u is settled with tentative distance D, but there's a shorter path P of length L < D. Along P, at least one vertex is unsettled. Let x be the first unsettled vertex on P, with predecessor p (settled). By induction, dist[p] is final. When p was settled, dist[x] was updated to dist[p] + w(p,x) ≤ L < D. So x's tentative distance is < D. Since the PQ pops minimum, x (or some vertex with even smaller tentative distance) would have been popped before u — contradicting that u was popped now. Therefore D = L. ✓

Requires non-negative weights — the invariant breaks with negative edges (a path through a settled vertex might be improved later).

docs.title: 7.5.4 Complexity
docs.text:
Implementation Complexity Binary heap PQ O((V + E) log V) Fibonacci heap O(E + V log V) Array (for dense) O(V²)

For sparse graphs (E ≈ V), binary heap gives ~O(V log V). For dense graphs (E ≈ V²), the array version O(V²) wins.

docs.title: Worked example 7.3 — Dijkstra trace
docs.text:
Graph (directed weighted, 6 vertices): 

        0
       / \
      4   1
     /    \
    1 —— 2 —— 3
      3  1   2
        \  /
         5

More formally:

Edges: 0→1 (4), 0→2 (1), 1→3 (1), 2→1 (3), 2→3 (5), 3→4 (2), 2→4 (6).

Dijkstra from 0:

Init: dist = [0, ∞, ∞, ∞, ∞], PQ = {(0, 0)}.

Step Pop (u, d) Settled set dist (0..4) 1 (0, 0) {0} [0, 4, 1, ∞, ∞] 2 (2, 1) {0, 2} [0, 4, 1, 6, 7] — relax 2→1 (4), 2→3 (5), 2→4 (7) 3 (1, 4) {0, 1, 2} [0, 4, 1, 5, 7] — relax 1→3 (5 < 6) 4 (3, 5) {0, 1, 2, 3} [0, 4, 1, 5, 7] — 3→4 (7, no update) 5 (4, 7) {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} done

Final distances from 0: - dist[0] = 0 - dist[1] = 4 (direct edge 0→1, weight 4) - dist[2] = 1 (direct edge 0→2) - dist[3] = 5 (path 0→2→1→3, total 1+3+1=5) - dist[4] = 7 (path 0→2→4, total 1+6=7)

Verify by hand: shortest path to 3 is 0→2→1→3 (5), not 0→1→3 (5) — actually equal here. Shortest to 4 is 0→2→4 (7) or 0→2→1→3→4 (1+3+1+2=7) — again equal.

docs.title: 7.6.1 The problem
docs.text:
Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights. If the graph has negative edges, Dijkstra's invariant breaks — it may settle a vertex too early.

Example. Graph s → u (weight 1), s → v (weight 4), u → v (weight -3). Dijkstra settles u first (dist 1), then v at dist 4 (via direct edge) — but the path s → u → v has cost 1 + (-3) = -2, shorter. Dijkstra misses this because it settled u before considering the negative edge.

docs.title: 7.6.2 Bellman–Ford algorithm
docs.text:
int[] bellmanFord(int n, List<int[]> edges, int source) {
    // edges: [u, v, w]
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[source] = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            int u = e[0], v = e[1], w = e[2];
            if (dist[u] != Integer.MAX_VALUE && dist[u] + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w;
            }
        }
    }

    // Check for negative-weight cycles
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        int u = e[0], v = e[1], w = e[2];
        if (dist[u] != Integer.MAX_VALUE && dist[u] + w < dist[v]) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Negative cycle detected");
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Idea: relax every edge V - 1 times. Why V - 1?

The shortest path has at most V - 1 edges. (If it had V edges, it would visit V+1 vertices — contradiction, since a shortest path visits each vertex at most once.) After k full passes, dist[v] is the shortest path using at most k edges. After V-1 passes, all shortest paths are found.

Negative cycle detection: if a further pass improves any distance, there must be a negative cycle (a cycle whose total weight is negative) — no finite shortest path exists.

docs.title: 7.6.3 Complexity
docs.text:
O(V · E) — V passes × E edge relaxations.

Graph Cost Sparse (E ≈ V) O(V²) Dense (E ≈ V²) O(V³)

Much slower than Dijkstra — but handles negative edges and detects negative cycles.

docs.title: Worked example 7.4 — Bellman–Ford with a negative edge
docs.text:
Graph: s=0 → 1 (4), 0 → 2 (5), 1 → 2 (-3).

Bellman–Ford from 0:

Init: dist = [0, ∞, ∞].

Pass 1 (over all edges): - Edge (0, 1, 4): dist[1] = min(∞, 0 + 4) = 4. - Edge (0, 2, 5): dist[2] = min(∞, 0 + 5) = 5. - Edge (1, 2, -3): dist[2] = min(5, 4 + (-3)) = 1.

Pass 2 (over all edges): - Edge (0, 1, 4): dist[1] = 4 (no change). - Edge (0, 2, 5): dist[2] = min(1, 5) = 1 (no change). - Edge (1, 2, -3): dist[2] = min(1, 4 - 3) = 1 (no change).

Pass 3 (over all edges): no changes → converged.

Final: dist = [0, 4, 1].

Correct: dist[2] = 1 (via 0 → 1 → 2, cost 4 + (-3) = 1), not 5 (direct). Dijkstra would have returned 5 because it would settle node 2 at cost 5 before discovering the negative edge.

Verify — Dijkstra on this graph: settle 0 (dist 0), then 1 (dist 4, since direct edge weight 4 < ... nothing else), then 2. When we relax 0 → 2, dist[2] = 5. When we later relax 1 → 2 (weight -3), we'd update dist[2] to 1 — but only if 1 is popped from the PQ before 2. If PQ pops 2 first (dist 5 < ∞), then 2 is settled at 5, and the -3 edge updates never help. Dijkstra returns 5 — wrong. ✓ (This confirms Bellman–Ford is needed.)

docs.title: 7.7.1 The problem
docs.text:
Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph, find a subset of edges that connects all vertices with minimum total weight.

A spanning tree has exactly V - 1 edges, connects all vertices, contains no cycles.

MST applications:

  • Network design — laying cable / fiber to connect all homes with minimum total cost.
  • Road networks — building roads to connect all towns with minimum total length.
  • Clustering — MST edges connect similar items; cutting MST edges gives clusters.
  • Approximation algorithms — the MST gives a 2-approximation to the Traveling Salesman Problem.

docs.title: 7.7.2 The cut property — the underlying theorem
docs.text:
Cut. A partition of V into two non-empty sets S and V - S.

Cut property. For any cut (S, V - S), the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST.

Why this is the key. Both Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms are grounded in this property — they greedily select edges that are minimum-weight crossing some cut.

docs.title: 7.7.3 Kruskal's algorithm
docs.text:
Idea: sort all edges by weight; add them to the MST one at a time, skipping edges that would create a cycle. Uses Union-Find for fast cycle detection.

class UnionFind {
    int[] parent, rank;
    UnionFind(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        rank = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
    }
    int find(int x) {
        if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);   // path compression
        return parent[x];
    }
    boolean union(int x, int y) {
        int rx = find(x), ry = find(y);
        if (rx == ry) return false;   // already in same set
        if (rank[rx] < rank[ry]) parent[rx] = ry;
        else if (rank[rx] > rank[ry]) parent[ry] = rx;
        else { parent[ry] = rx; rank[rx]++; }
        return true;
    }
}

List<int[]> kruskal(int n, List<int[]> edges) {
    // edges: [u, v, w]
    edges.sort((a, b) -> a[2] - b[2]);
    UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(n);
    List<int[]> mst = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        if (uf.union(e[0], e[1])) {
            mst.add(e);
            if (mst.size() == n - 1) break;
        }
    }
    return mst;
}

Cost: O(E log E) for sorting + O(E α(V)) for Union-Find operations. O(E log E) total — dominated by sorting.

Sparse graphs: O(E log E) ≈ O(V log V) — competitive. Dense graphs: O(V² log V) — Prim's with an array is faster.

docs.title: 7.7.4 Prim's algorithm
docs.text:
Idea: grow the MST from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge connecting a vertex inside the current tree to one outside.

int prim(List<List<Edge>> adj, int start) {
    int n = adj.size();
    boolean[] inMST = new boolean[n];
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);
    pq.add(new int[]{start, 0});
    int totalWeight = 0;

    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int u = cur[0], w = cur[1];
        if (inMST[u]) continue;
        inMST[u] = true;
        totalWeight += w;

        for (Edge e : adj.get(u)) {
            if (!inMST[e.to]) pq.add(new int[]{e.to, e.weight});
        }
    }
    return totalWeight;
}

Cost: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap — same as Dijkstra.

For dense graphs: array-based version O(V²).

Advantage over Kruskal: grows the MST from a specific start — useful when edges are not known in advance (e.g., a physical network you're exploring).

docs.title: Worked example 7.6 — Prim's on the same graph
docs.text:
Start at vertex 0.

Step Tree vertices Min edge to outside Add 1 {0} (0,2, 5) 2 (weight 5) 2 {0,2} (1,2, 1) 1 (weight 1) 3 {0,1,2} (1,3, 5) 3 (weight 5) 4 {0,1,2,3} (3,4, 2) 4 (weight 2) 5 {0–4} (3,5, 4) 5 (weight 4) done all — —

Total: 5 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 17. Same as Kruskal. ✓

MST is not unique — when there are ties in edge weights, multiple MSTs may exist. But total weight is unique (all MSTs have the same total).

docs.title: 7.8 Which shortest-path algorithm?
docs.text:
Algorithm Handles negative weights? Detects negative cycles? Time complexity Best for BFS n/a (unweighted) n/a O(V + E) Unweighted graphs Dijkstra No No O((V+E) log V) Non-negative weights, single source Bellman–Ford Yes Yes O(VE) Negative edges, negative-cycle detection Floyd–Warshall Yes Yes O(V³) All-pairs shortest paths (small graphs)

Flowchart:

Weights negative? → No → Unweighted? → Yes → BFS
                  |     → No → Single source? → Yes → Dijkstra
                  |                            → No → Floyd-Warshall
                  → Yes → Single source? → Yes → Bellman-Ford
                                       → No → Floyd-Warshall (with negative cycle detection)

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Graph = vertices + edges. Directed vs. undirected; weighted vs. unweighted; sparse vs. dense.
  2. Adjacency matrix: O(n²) memory, O(1) edge lookup — best for dense graphs.
  3. Adjacency list: O(n + m) memory, O(degree) edge lookup — best for sparse graphs (most real graphs).
  4. BFS — level-by-level, uses a queue, O(V + E). Finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
  5. DFS — dives deep, uses a stack (or recursion), O(V + E). Basis for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.
  6. Dijkstra — single-source shortest paths on non-negative weights, uses a priority queue. O((V + E) log V).
  7. Bellman–Ford — handles negative weights, detects negative cycles. O(VE) — slower but more general.
  8. MST — minimum total weight to connect all vertices. Kruskal (edge-sort + union-find) and Prim (grow from vertex) both compute MST in O(E log E) or O((V+E) log V).
  9. Cut property — the minimum edge across any cut is in some MST. This theorem justifies the greedy strategies of both Kruskal and Prim.

docs.text:

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) number of edges touching it.
  2. (b) O(n + m).
  3. (b) queue.
  4. (a) stack (or recursion).
  5. (b) unweighted graphs.
  6. (a) / (b) non-negative weights (both answers equivalent; (b) is the same as (a)).
  7. (b) negative-weight cycles.
  8. (c) Union-Find.
  9. (a) priority queue.
  10. (b) minimum edge across cut is in some MST.
  11. (c) O((V + E) log V).
  12. (b) V - 1.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) (undirected, no self-loops) or \(n(n-1)\) (directed)
  2. \(n^2\)
  3. \(n + m\)
  4. level / breadth-first
  5. depth-first
  6. non-negative
  7. \(V \cdot E\)
  8. weight
  9. some
  10. \(V - 1\)
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Graph: \(G = (V, E)\) — a set of vertices and a set of edges (pairs of vertices). Directed vs. undirected: directed edges have orientation \((u, v) \ne (v, u)\); undirected edges are symmetric \(\{u, v\} = \{v, u\}\). Weighted vs. unweighted: weighted edges carry a numeric cost; unweighted edges all cost 1. Sparse vs. dense: sparse has \(E \approx O(V)\); dense has \(E \approx O(V^2)\). Most real graphs are sparse.
  2. Matrix vs. list: (a) memory — matrix O(n²), list O(n + m). (b) edge lookup — matrix O(1), list O(degree). (c) neighbor iteration — matrix O(n) (must scan row), list O(degree). Preferred: matrix for dense graphs or frequent edge lookups; list for sparse graphs (the common case) or when iterating neighbors frequently.
  3. BFS: use a FIFO queue, mark start visited, enqueue. Dequeue one vertex, visit its unvisited neighbors (mark visited, enqueue). Why shortest paths in unweighted graphs: BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing distance. When it first reaches vertex v from u, dist[v] = dist[u] + 1. If a shorter path existed, that path's intermediate vertex would have been reached earlier — contradicting FIFO order. So the first assignment is optimal.
  4. DFS: visit vertex, then recursively DFS each unvisited neighbor, backtracking when stuck. Problems: (i) cycle detection — if we visit an already-visited ancestor, cycle exists; (ii) topological sort — reverse postorder of DFS on a DAG gives topological order; (iii) connected components — a new DFS start reveals a new component.
  5. Dijkstra: start with dist[source] = 0, all ∞. Use a priority queue. Repeatedly pop the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance; relax its outgoing edges. Requires non-negative: the invariant "once popped, distance is final" relies on the fact that extending a path via a non-negative edge cannot make it shorter. With negative edges, a path through a settled vertex could later be improved — invalidating the invariant.
  6. Dijkstra vs. Bellman–Ford: Dijkstra is faster O((V+E) log V but requires non-negative weights. Bellman–Ford is slower O(VE) but handles negative edges and detects negative cycles. Example where Dijkstra fails: s→u (1), s→v (4), u→v (-3). Dijkstra settles v at 4 (via direct edge), missing the shorter path s→u→v (1-3=-2). Bellman–Ford correctly gives dist[v] = -2.
  7. Cut property: for any partition (S, V-S) of vertices, the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to at least one MST. Kruskal justification: at each step, we add the minimum-weight edge that doesn't create a cycle. Consider the moment the algorithm adds edge e = (u, v). Define S = the connected component containing u in the current MST (before adding e). e is the minimum edge crossing (S, V-S) in the remaining edges (because Kruskal processes in sorted order). By the cut property, e is in some MST of the graph. By induction over Kruskal's steps, the final tree is an MST.
  8. Kruskal vs. Prim: Kruskal — sort edges, then add if not creating cycle, using Union-Find. O(E log E). Best for sparse graphs (few edges). Prim — grow tree from a vertex using a priority queue. O((V+E) log V). Best for dense graphs (array-based Prim O(V²) beats Kruskal's O(E log E) = O(V² log V)). Also: Kruskal gives an edge-list MST — good when edges are known upfront. Prim grows from a vertex — good when the graph is explored dynamically.
  9. BFS from 3: neighbors of 3 = {1, 5}. Visit 3, then 1 and 5. From 1: {0, 3, 4}, so 0 and 4. From 5: {3, 4} — 4 already visited. From 0: {1, 2}, so 2. From 4: {1, 2, 5}, 2 already visited. Visit order: 3, 1, 5, 0, 4, 2. Distances: dist[3]=0, dist[1]=1, dist[5]=1, dist[0]=2, dist[4]=2, dist[2]=3.
  10. Dijkstra from 2: dist = [∞, ∞, 0, ∞, ∞]. Pop 2 (dist 0): relax 2→1 (3), 2→3 (5), 2→4 (6). PQ: (1, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6). Pop 1 (3): relax 1→3 (1+3=4 < 5, update to 4). PQ: (3, 4), (4, 6). Pop 3 (4): relax 3→4 (2+4=6, no change). PQ: (4, 6). Pop 4 (6): no outgoing edges. Final: dist = [∞, 3, 0, 4, 6]. Node 0 is unreachable from 2 (∞). ✓

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Adjacency matrix vs. list. Build both for the graph in Example 7.1. Compare memory (bytes) for n = 6, m = 7.

  2. BFS trace. Run BFS on the graph of Example 7.1 from vertex 4. Record visit order and distances.

  3. DFS trace. Run DFS on the same graph from vertex 2 (recursive, neighbors sorted ascending). Record visit order and DFS tree edges.

  4. Connected components. Given a graph with two disjoint components, modify BFS to count the number of connected components in O(V + E).

  5. Bipartite check. Modify BFS or DFS to check whether a graph is bipartite. What coloring invariant must hold?

  6. Cycle detection (undirected). Modify DFS to detect a cycle in an undirected graph. What's the key observation about "back edges"?

  7. Cycle detection (directed). Modify DFS to detect a cycle in a directed graph. Why does the undirected approach fail? (Hint: 3-color DFS.)

  8. Topological sort. Given a DAG, implement topological sort using (a) DFS postorder reversal; (b) Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees). Verify both give the same order (up to ties).

  9. Dijkstra trace. Run Dijkstra on the graph of Example 7.3 from vertex 2. Record all iterations.

  10. Dijkstra fails with negative edges. Construct a 3-vertex graph where Dijkstra gives the wrong answer but Bellman–Ford gives the right one.

  11. Bellman–Ford trace. Run Bellman–Ford on the graph of Worked example 7.4 with a 4th vertex and edge 2→3 (-1). Detect the resulting negative cycle.

  12. Kruskal trace. Run Kruskal on the graph of Example 7.5. Show the union-find state after each edge.

  13. Prim trace. Run Prim on the same graph from vertex 3. Compare the final MST total weight to Kruskal's (must be the same).

  14. MST uniqueness. When is the MST of a graph unique? Give a graph where two different MSTs exist and identify both.

  15. Road network. Design a graph representation for a road network (cities = vertices, roads = weighted edges). Which representation fits? Which algorithm finds the shortest route? Which finds the cheapest road-construction plan?

  16. Friend network. A social network has 100 million users. You want to find the shortest path from Alice to Bob. Estimate the memory for adjacency matrix vs. adjacency list. Which representation fits on a modern server?

docs.title: Chapter 8 — Sorting Algorithms
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 1 tutorial + 2 lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage (syllabus): introduction to sorting algorithms.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what a stable sort is, and why stability matters.
  2. Explain what an in-place sort is, and its memory implications.
  3. Implement and analyse: bubble, insertion, selection, merge, quicksort, heapsort.
  4. State the best, average, and worst-case complexities of each.
  5. Trace each algorithm on a small array.
  6. Choose the right sort based on data properties (size, distribution, existing order, stability requirements).
  7. Explain why comparison-based sorting has an Ω(n log n) lower bound.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Stability
docs.text:
A sort is stable if equal elements keep their original relative order.

Example. Sort [(3, "a"), (1, "x"), (3, "b")] by the first field:

  • Stable → [(1, "x"), (3, "a"), (3, "b")]
  • Unstable → [(1, "x"), (3, "b"), (3, "a")] (possible)

Why it matters. When you sort by one key, then by another, stability preserves the first sort as a tiebreaker. Example: sort by name, then by department — a stable sort gives alphabetically-ordered names within each department.

docs.title: 8.1.2 In-place
docs.text: A sort is in-place if it uses O(1) auxiliary memory (beyond a few variables). Merge sort is not (needs O(n)); heapsort and quicksort are (O(1) or O(log n) for recursion).

docs.title: 8.1.3 The comparison lower bound
docs.text:
Any comparison-based sort must do at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

Proof (information-theoretic). There are n! possible permutations of input. Each comparison is a binary decision (yes/no). A decision tree that distinguishes all n! permutations must have height ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log n − n (Stirling). Therefore ≥ Ω(n log n) comparisons. ∎

This means: no comparison-based sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case. Faster sorts exist only with additional assumptions (counting, radix).

docs.title: 8.1.4 The summary table
docs.text: Algorithm Best Average Worst Space Stable? Bubble O(n) (already sorted, with flag) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) Yes Insertion O(n) (nearly sorted) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) Yes Selection O(n²) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) No Merge O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) Yes Quicksort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) No Heapsort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) No

docs.title: 8.2 Bubble sort
docs.text:
Idea. Repeatedly compare adjacent pairs; if out of order, swap. After each pass, the largest remaining element "bubbles" to the end.

void bubbleSort(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        boolean swapped = false;
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) {
                int t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t;
                swapped = true;
            }
        }
        if (!swapped) break;   // already sorted
    }
}

Cost. Worst: O(n²) — n passes × n comparisons. Best (with swapped flag): O(n) — one pass, no swaps. Average: O(n²).

Stable: yes. In-place: yes.

Practical use: pedagogic only — never use for real data.

docs.title: Worked example 8.1 — Bubble sort trace
docs.text:
Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].

Pass 1: - Compare (5, 2) → swap → [2, 5, 8, 1, 9] - Compare (5, 8) → keep → [2, 5, 8, 1, 9] - Compare (8, 1) → swap → [2, 5, 1, 8, 9] - Compare (8, 9) → keep → [2, 5, 1, 8, 9] - After pass 1: [2, 5, 1, 8, 9] — largest (9) at end ✓

Pass 2 (n-1-i = 3 comparisons): - (2, 5) → keep - (5, 1) → swap → [2, 1, 5, 8, 9] - (5, 8) → keep - After pass 2: [2, 1, 5, 8, 9]

Pass 3: - (2, 1) → swap → [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] - (2, 5) → keep

Pass 4: - (1, 2) → keep → [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] — sorted, swapped = false → break.

Total: 4 passes, 10 comparisons. O(n²).

docs.title: 8.3 Insertion sort
docs.text:
Idea. Build the sorted array one element at a time — insert each new element into its correct position in the already-sorted prefix.

void insertionSort(int[] a) {
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        int key = a[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {
            a[j + 1] = a[j];
            j--;
        }
        a[j + 1] = key;
    }
}

Cost. Best (nearly sorted): O(n) — one comparison per element, no shifts. Average: O(n²) — n/2 shifts per element. Worst (reverse-sorted): O(n²).

Stable: yes. In-place: yes.

Practical use: excellent for small arrays and nearly-sorted data. Java's Arrays.sort for primitive ints uses dual-pivot quicksort with insertion sort for subarrays < 47 elements. Python's Timsort uses insertion sort on small runs.

docs.title: Worked example 8.2 — Insertion sort trace
docs.text:
Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].

i key j loop Array after 1 2 j=0: a[0]=5 > 2, shift 5 → j=-1 [2, 5, 8, 1, 9] 2 8 j=1: a[1]=5 ≤ 8 → stop [2, 5, 8, 1, 9] 3 1 j=2: 8>1 shift; j=1: 5>1 shift; j=0: 2>1 shift; j=-1 [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] 4 9 j=3: 8≤9 → stop [1, 2, 5, 8, 9]

Total: 4 insertions, 4 shifts total. Nearly sorted = fast.

Best case — array already sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] → 0 shifts, 4 comparisons. O(n).

docs.title: 8.4 Selection sort
docs.text:
Idea. Repeatedly find the minimum element in the unsorted suffix, swap it into position.

void selectionSort(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int minIdx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
            if (a[j] < a[minIdx]) minIdx = j;
        if (minIdx != i) {
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[minIdx]; a[minIdx] = t;
        }
    }
}

Cost. Always O(n²) — n passes, each scanning the remaining suffix. Best case is also O(n²) — no early exit.

Stable: No — the swap can move equal elements past each other. In-place: yes.

Practical use: rare — its only advantage is that it does at most n−1 swaps (useful when writes are expensive). Otherwise insertion sort or quicksort wins.

docs.title: Worked example 8.3 — Selection sort trace
docs.text:
Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].

i Min in a[i..n-1] Swap with a[i] Array after 0 1 (index 3) swap a[0] ↔ a[3] [1, 2, 8, 5, 9] 1 2 (index 1) no swap [1, 2, 8, 5, 9] 2 5 (index 3) swap a[2] ↔ a[3] [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] 3 8 (index 3) no swap [1, 2, 5, 8, 9]

Total: 2 swaps, 10 comparisons. O(n²) comparisons, O(n) swaps.

docs.title: 8.5 Merge sort
docs.text:
Idea. Divide the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves in O(n).

void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid);
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi);
}

void merge(int[] a, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
    int[] temp = new int[hi - lo + 1];
    int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = 0;
    while (i <= mid && j <= hi) {
        if (a[i] <= a[j]) temp[k++] = a[i++];
        else              temp[k++] = a[j++];
    }
    while (i <= mid) temp[k++] = a[i++];
    while (j <= hi)  temp[k++] = a[j++];
    System.arraycopy(temp, 0, a, lo, temp.length);
}

Cost. Recurrence: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n) all cases. No adversarial input.

Stable: yes (with <= in the merge comparison). In-place: No — needs O(n) auxiliary space.

Practical use: excellent general-purpose sort. Java's Arrays.sort for objects uses Timsort (a merge-sort variant). Python's sorted() uses Timsort. Use merge sort when you need guaranteed O(n log n) and stability.

docs.title: Worked example 8.4 — Merge sort trace
docs.text:
Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].

Divide recursively: 

           [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]
              /        \
        [5, 2, 8]    [1, 9]
        /      \        |
    [5, 2]   [8]     [1] [9]  (already size 1)
    /   \
  [5]   [2]

Merge back: - [5] + [2] → [2, 5] - [2, 5] + [8] → [2, 5, 8] - [1] + [9] → [1, 9] - [2, 5, 8] + [1, 9] → [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] ✓

Total: 5 elements, log₂ 5 ≈ 2.32, ~3 merge levels. O(n log n).

docs.title: 8.6 Quicksort
docs.text:
Idea. Pick a pivot. Partition the array so that everything < pivot is left, everything > pivot is right. Recursively sort both halves.

void quickSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    quickSort(a, lo, p - 1);
    quickSort(a, p + 1, hi);
}

int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    int pivot = a[hi];
    int i = lo - 1;
    for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
        if (a[j] <= pivot) {
            i++;
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
        }
    }
    int t = a[i + 1]; a[i + 1] = a[hi]; a[hi] = t;
    return i + 1;
}

Cost. Best/average: O(n log n) (balanced partitions). Worst: O(n²) (already-sorted input with last-element pivot — the classic trap).

Stable: No. In-place: yes (except recursion stack, O(log n) average / O(n) worst).

Practical use: the fastest general-purpose sort in practice — small constants. Java uses dual-pivot quicksort for primitives; C++ std::sort is introsort (quicksort + heapsort + insertion sort). Always randomise or median-of-three the pivot to avoid O(n²) on sorted input.

docs.title: Worked example 8.5 — Quicksort trace
docs.text:
Sort [3, 7, 8, 5, 2, 1, 9, 4] using last-element pivot.

Partition (pivot = 4, index 7):

j a[j] ≤ 4? Action Array 0 3 ✓ i=0, swap a[0]↔a[0] [3, 7, 8, 5, 2, 1, 9, 4] 1 7 ✗ — 2 8 ✗ — 3 5 ✗ — 4 2 ✓ i=1, swap a[1]↔a[4] [3, 2, 8, 5, 7, 1, 9, 4] 5 1 ✓ i=2, swap a[2]↔a[5] [3, 2, 1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 4] 6 9 ✗ —

Final swap: a[i+1] = a[3] ↔ a[7] → [3, 2, 1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 5]. Pivot at index 3.

Recurse left [3, 2, 1] (pivot = 1): → [1, 2, 3]. Recurse right [7, 8, 9, 5] (pivot = 5): → [5, 7, 8, 9].

Final: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9] ✓

docs.title: Worked example 8.6 — Quicksort worst case
docs.text:
Input: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] (already sorted).

Pivot rule: last element.

  • Pivot = 9. Partition: everything else is smaller → pivot at end (index 8). Recurse on [1..8].
  • Pivot = 8. Partition: pivot at end (index 7). Recurse on [1..7].
  • ...

Each partition does O(n) work but only splits off one element. Total: n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... = O(n²).

Fix: random pivot, median-of-three, or shuffle before sorting. Always do one of these — an already-sorted input is a common real-world case (e.g., re-sorting a previously-sorted list).

docs.title: 8.7 Heapsort (recap from Chapter 5)
docs.text:
Idea. Build a max-heap from the array (O(n)); repeatedly extract the max (swap root with last, sift-down).

void heapSort(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    for (int i = n/2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) siftDown(a, i, n);   // build max-heap
    for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) {
        int t = a[0]; a[0] = a[i]; a[i] = t;
        siftDown(a, 0, i);
    }
}

void siftDown(int[] a, int i, int n) {
    while (true) {
        int left = 2*i + 1, right = 2*i + 2, largest = i;
        if (left  < n && a[left]  > a[largest]) largest = left;
        if (right < n && a[right] > a[largest]) largest = right;
        if (largest == i) break;
        int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[largest]; a[largest] = t;
        i = largest;
    }
}

Cost. Always O(n log n) — no adversarial input.

Stable: No. In-place: yes (O(1) auxiliary).

Practical use: when you need guaranteed O(n log n) with O(1) space. C++'s introsort falls back to heapsort when quicksort recursion gets too deep. Also: the basis of priority queues.

docs.title: Worked example 8.7 — Heapsort on [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]
docs.text:
Phase 1 — Build max-heap:

Starting array: [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].

  • i = 1 (value 2): children 1 (value 1), 9 (value 9). Sift-down: 2 < 9, swap → [5, 9, 8, 1, 2].
  • i = 0 (value 5): children 9, 8. Max child 9. 5 < 9, swap → [9, 5, 8, 1, 2]. At index 1 (value 5): children 1, 2. Max child 2. 5 > 2, no swap.

Max-heap built: [9, 5, 8, 1, 2].

Phase 2 — Extract max repeatedly:

Step Array (before extract) Swap root with last Sift-down range Array after 1 [9, 5, 8, 1, 2] swap 9 ↔ 2 [2, 5, 8, 1] → sift [8, 5, 2, 1, 9] 2 [8, 5, 2, 1, 9] swap 8 ↔ 1 [1, 5, 2] → sift [5, 1, 2, 8, 9] 3 [5, 1, 2, 8, 9] swap 5 ↔ 2 [2, 1] → sift [2, 1, 5, 8, 9] 4 [2, 1, 5, 8, 9] swap 2 ↔ 1 [1] no sift [1, 2, 5, 8, 9]

Sorted: [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] ✓

Cost. Build: O(n). Extract n times: O(n log n). Total: O(n log n).

docs.title: 8.8 Choosing the right sort
docs.text:
Situation Best choice Why Small array (n < 20) Insertion sort Minimal constant Nearly sorted Insertion sort O(n) best case Large, generic, stability needed Merge sort O(n log n), stable Large, generic, speed critical Quicksort (randomised pivot) Fastest in practice Large, need O(1) space Heapsort O(n log n), O(1) space Integer keys in bounded range Counting/radix sort O(n) time External (data > RAM) External merge sort Streamable Partially sorted segments Timsort (Java/Python) Detects and merges runs

Java's Arrays.sort: - Primitives: dual-pivot quicksort (fast, non-stable). - Objects: Timsort (stable, merge-based).

Python's sorted(): Timsort.

C++ std::sort: introsort (quicksort + heapsort + insertion sort).

In practice, never implement your own sort for production — the language's built-in has 30 years of engineering.

docs.title: Worked example 8.8 — Stability matters
docs.text:
Input: [(3, "Alice"), (1, "Bob"), (3, "Carol"), (2, "Dave")].

Sort by the first field.

Stable sort output: [(1, "Bob"), (2, "Dave"), (3, "Alice"), (3, "Carol")] — Alice before Carol.

Unstable sort output: [(1, "Bob"), (2, "Dave"), (3, "Carol"), (3, "Alice")] — Carol before Alice. Both 3s have the same key but swapped relative order.

Impact. If you now sort by the second field (name), the stable sort preserves Alice-before-Carol for the tie in department 3. The unstable sort loses that information.

Rule: use stable sorts (merge, insertion, bubble) when doing multi-key sorts. Use quicksort only when you don't care about relative order of equal elements.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Comparison-based sorting has Ω(n log n) worst-case lower bound — information-theoretic.
  2. Bubble sort — O(n²) average, O(n) best (with early exit). Pedagogical only.
  3. Insertion sort — O(n²) average, O(n) best. Excellent for small and nearly-sorted arrays.
  4. Selection sort — always O(n²), O(n) swaps. Rarely preferred.
  5. Merge sort — O(n log n) all cases, stable, but O(n) space.
  6. Quicksort — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst on sorted input with last-element pivot. Randomise the pivot.
  7. Heapsort — O(n log n) all cases, O(1) space, not stable.
  8. Stability preserves relative order of equal elements — critical for multi-key sorting.
  9. In-place sorts use O(1) auxiliary memory; merge sort does not.
  10. Practical choice: primitives → quicksort; objects → Timsort (Java/Python); O(1) space required → heapsort; small/nearly-sorted → insertion sort.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. Which sort is stable?

(a) Selection (b) Quicksort (c) Merge (d) Heapsort

  1. Which sort has O(n²) worst-case but is fastest in practice on average?

(a) Merge (b) Quicksort (c) Insertion (d) Bubble

  1. Which sort uses O(n) auxiliary space?

(a) Quicksort (b) Heapsort (c) Merge (d) Insertion

  1. Insertion sort's best case is:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) O(n²)

  1. The comparison-sort lower bound is:

(a) O(1) (b) O(log n) (c) O(n) (d) Ω(n log n)

  1. Quicksort's worst case is triggered by:

(a) Random data (b) Already-sorted data with last-element pivot (c) Reverse data (d) All-distinct values

  1. Heapsort's space complexity is:

(a) O(1) (b) O(1) (c) O(log n) (d) O(n)

  1. Which algorithm is never used in production?

(a) Insertion (b) Bubble (c) Quicksort (d) Merge

  1. Which sort processes in-place with O(1) space?

(a) Merge (b) Heapsort (c) Timsort (d) Radix

  1. Java's Arrays.sort for objects uses:

    (a) Quicksort (b) Timsort (c) Heapsort (d) Bubble

  2. Which sort has an O(n) best case?

    (a) Selection (b) Insertion (c) Merge (d) Heapsort

  3. Stable sorting means:

    (a) The algorithm is deterministic (b) Equal elements keep original relative order (c) It always terminates (d) It uses O(1) space

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. A sort is _____ if it preserves the relative order of equal elements.

  2. A sort is _____ if it uses O(1) auxiliary memory.

  3. Any comparison sort requires at least Ω(_____) comparisons in the worst case.

  4. Merge sort's recurrence is T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(_____), giving O(n log n).

  5. Quicksort's worst case occurs when the pivot is always the _____ or _____ element.

  6. _____ sort builds a max-heap, then repeatedly extracts the max.

  7. _____ sort is used by Java's Arrays.sort for objects.

  8. _____ sort is best for already-sorted input.

  9. _____ sort always does at most n−1 swaps.

  10. _____ sort has O(n log n) worst case AND O(1) space.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. Define stability and in-place. Give one sort of each combination.

  2. Prove the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts.

  3. Explain why quicksort's worst case is O(n²). How do you prevent it?

  4. Compare merge sort and quicksort on: stability, space, worst case, practical speed.

  5. Trace bubble sort on [4, 1, 3, 2]. How many swaps?

  6. Trace insertion sort on [4, 1, 3, 2]. How many shifts?

  7. Trace merge sort on [4, 1, 3, 2]. Show all merge steps.

  8. Explain why stability matters for multi-key sorting. Give a concrete example.

  9. Why is insertion sort used inside quicksort for small subarrays?

  10. Which sort would you choose for each scenario: (a) sorting 10 million integers in memory; (b) sorting 1 million objects needing stable order; (c) nearly-sorted data; (d) sorting in O(1) space.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (c) Merge.
  2. (b) Quicksort.
  3. (c) Merge.
  4. (c) O(n).
  5. (d) Ω(n log n).
  6. (b) Already-sorted with last-element pivot.
  7. (a) O(1) (same as b).
  8. (b) Bubble.
  9. (b) Heapsort.
  10. (b) Timsort.
  11. (b) Insertion.
  12. (b) Equal elements keep original order.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. stable
  2. in-place
  3. \(n \log n\)
  4. \(n\)
  5. minimum; maximum (smallest; largest)
  6. Heapsort
  7. Timsort
  8. Insertion
  9. Selection
  10. Heapsort
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. Stable: preserves original relative order of equal elements (merge, insertion, bubble — stable; quicksort, heapsort, selection — unstable). In-place: uses O(1) auxiliary memory (bubble, insertion, selection, heapsort, quicksort — in-place; merge — not). Combinations: stable+in-place = insertion; stable+not-in-place = merge; unstable+in-place = quicksort or heapsort; unstable+not-in-place = selection with extra buffer (rarely used).
  2. Lower-bound proof: comparison sorts distinguish n! possible input orderings. Each comparison yields 1 bit. A binary decision tree distinguishing n! possibilities must have depth ≥ log₂(n!). Stirling: log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n − n log₂ e = Ω(n log n). So any comparison sort makes ≥ Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. ∎
  3. Quicksort worst case: with last-element pivot, sorted input causes each partition to split off one element (the pivot at the end). n partitions, each scanning ~n elements → n + (n-1) + ... = O(n²). Prevention: random pivot (expected O(n log n) with high probability), median-of-three, or shuffle before sort.
  4. Merge vs. quicksort: merge — stable, O(n) space, O(n log n) worst, slower constants. Quicksort — unstable, O(1) space, O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst, faster constants. When to choose: merge when stability or worst-case guarantee required; quicksort when speed matters and you control the pivot.
  5. Bubble sort trace on [4, 1, 3, 2]: Pass 1 — (4,1)→swap, (4,3)→swap, (4,2)→swap → [1, 3, 2, 4]. Pass 2 — (1,3) keep, (3,2)→swap → [1, 2, 3, 4]. Pass 3 — no swap → done. Total swaps: 4.
  6. Insertion sort trace on [4, 1, 3, 2]: i=1, key=1, shift 4 → [1, 4, 3, 2]. i=2, key=3, shift 4 → [1, 3, 4, 2]. i=3, key=2, shift 4, shift 3 → [1, 2, 3, 4]. Total shifts: 4.
  7. Merge sort trace on [4, 1, 3, 2]: divide → [4,1] and [3,2]. Sort each → [1,4] and [2,3]. Merge → [1,2,3,4]. Cost: O(n log n) = O(4 log 4) = O(8) comparisons.
  8. Why stability matters: for multi-key sorting, you sort by one key, then by another. Stability preserves the first sort as a tiebreaker. Example: sort employees by department, then by name — a stable sort yields alphabetically-ordered names within each department. An unstable sort scrambles the name order within each department.
  9. Insertion sort for small subarrays: its constant factor is tiny (~1 comparison per element when data is already nearly sorted from prior partitioning). The overhead of quicksort's partition and recursion dominates for < ~20 elements. So switch to insertion sort at the base case — faster than continuing to recurse.
  10. Sort choice:
    • (a) 10M ints in memory: dual-pivot quicksort (fastest in practice).
    • (b) 1M objects, stable: Timsort (Java/Python default).
    • (c) Nearly sorted: insertion sort (O(n) best case).
    • (d) O(1) space: heapsort (guaranteed O(n log n), O(1) space).
