docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. Bubble trace. Sort [5, 3, 1, 4, 2] with bubble sort. Count passes, comparisons, swaps.

  2. Insertion trace. Same array, insertion sort. Count comparisons, shifts.

  3. Selection trace. Same array, selection sort. Count swaps.

  4. Merge trace. Same array, merge sort. Show all merge steps and total comparisons.

  5. Quicksort trace. Same array, quicksort with last-element pivot. Show the partition steps.

  6. Quicksort worst case. Sort [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] with last-element pivot quicksort. Count comparisons. Compare with sorted input.

  7. Heapsort trace. Same array as problem 1, heapsort. Show build-heap and extract-max steps.

  8. Stability test. Given [(3,A),(1,B),(2,C),(3,D),(1,E)], sort by key with merge sort and with quicksort. Which preserves A before D and B before E?

  9. Nearly-sorted analysis. For an array that is 90% sorted (only a few elements out of place), which sort is fastest? Estimate comparisons.

  10. Comparison count. For n = 1000, estimate comparisons for each sort: best, average, worst.

  11. External sort. Design a sort for 10 GB of data on a machine with 1 GB of RAM. What's the strategy? (Hint: external merge sort.)

  12. Sorting integers. Given an array of 10 million integers in [0, 1000], which sort is fastest? Why? (Hint: counting sort.)

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Introduction, Data Abstraction, and Analysis of Algorithms
docs.text:
Semester VII · 2025/26

This chapter sets the foundation. Everything that follows — arrays, lists, trees, graphs — is judged by the analysis framework we build today.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Say what a **data structure** is, and why a course about them exists. 2. Distinguish an **abstract data type (ADT)** from a **data structure implementation**. 3. Write the **Big-O** bounds of simple loops and nested loops. 4. Distinguish **Big-O**, **Big-Ω**, and **Big-Θ**. 5. Analyse the complexity of a **recursive** algorithm by writing its recurrence and solving it. 6. Recognise the **common complexity classes** — O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ) — and give one example of each. 7. Explain why **Big-O ignores constants** but why constants still matter in practice.

docs.title: 1.1 — Why a course on data structures?
The problem
docs.text:
Programs spend most of their time finding, storing, and retrieving data.

How that data is laid out in memory decides whether a program finishes in milliseconds or hours.

Two implementations of the same idea can differ by a factor of **millions** in runtime. Not a small percentage — a factor of 10⁶. Ask the class: how many records does a typical university store? Tens of thousands. A bank? Millions. At those scales, the difference between an unsorted array and a hash table is the difference between a working app and a timeout.

docs.title: Concrete example
docs.text:
Store \(n = 10{,}000\) student records, find one by name:

???+ note "Three storage strategies" | Approach | Comparisons | |---|---| | Unsorted array, scan | up to $10{,}000$ | | Sorted array, binary search | $\log_2(10{,}000) \approx 14$ | | Hash table | 1–2 (average) | Same data. Same computer. Same programmer. **Different storage strategy → ~700× faster.** This is the motivating example for the entire course. Notice: the programmer did not write better code. They chose a better data structure. That's the skill we're building.

docs.title: Definition — Data structure
docs.text:
Definition

A data structure is a way of organizing data in memory together with the set of operations that can be performed on that data efficiently.

Notice **both** halves of the definition: - The **layout** — where each item lives in memory, how items relate to each other. - The **operations** — `insert`, `delete`, `search`, `iterate`, `findMinimum` — each has a cost. A data structure is **not just "how the data is stored."** It is **how the data is stored *plus* what it lets you do cheaply.**

docs.title: Two roles of a data structure
docs.text:
In practice you do two things with data structures:

???+ note "Role 1 — Use existing ones" Pick from the standard library. Justify the choice with **complexity analysis**. ???+ note "Role 2 — Create new ones" When no standard structure fits, build a new one out of **existing building blocks**. The rest of this course develops both skills: the first through **implementation** of the classics, the second through the **reasoning** that makes each classic work.

docs.title: The recurring theme — time vs space
docs.text:
Every data structure trades time against space. Almost always:

- **More space** = **faster access** (arrays: contiguous, O(1) indexing, but wasteful if sparse). - **Less space** = **slower access** (linked lists: no wasted memory, but O(n) lookup). !!! warning "There is no free lunch." The rest of the course is a study of **specific trade-offs**.

docs.title: The idea of abstraction
docs.text:
Abstraction means hiding the details behind a simple interface.

You already know this from OOP: - You use `List` without knowing whether it's an `ArrayList` or a `LinkedList` inside. - You call `add(x)` without thinking about resizing or pointer updates. Data structures push this idea further. They separate **what** a structure does from **how** it does it.

docs.title: ADT — Abstract Data Type
docs.text:
Definition — Abstract data type (ADT)

An abstract data type is a specification of a set of values and a set of operations, independent of any particular implementation.

An ADT says: *"There is a collection of elements, and you can do these things with them."* It does **not** say: *"Elements are stored in an array"* or *"Elements are stored in nodes connected by pointers."*

docs.title: ADTs you will meet in this course
docs.text: ADT Operations specified Possible implementations List insert, delete, get, size, iterate Array, linked list, dynamic array Stack push, pop, peek, isEmpty Array, linked list Queue enqueue, dequeue, peek Array, circular array, linked list Map / Dictionary put, get, remove, containsKey Hash table, balanced tree Set add, remove, contains Hash table, balanced tree Priority Queue insert, extractMin Binary heap, sorted array   **The pattern:** one ADT, **many implementations**. The **interface** is the same; the **cost of operations** differs.

docs.title: Why abstraction pays off
docs.text: Three concrete reasons   **1. Choose the implementation that fits.** A program that only needs `insert` at the front and `iterate` is well-served by a linked list. A program that needs random access by index wants an array.     **2. Change it later without breaking callers.** Swap the underlying array for a linked list without touching the caller. The **interface is the contract**.     **3. Reason at the interface level.** "This algorithm makes $n$ calls to `insert`" — true regardless of implementation.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — Same ADT, different costs
docs.text:
Consider a List ADT with insertAtEnd(x), get(i), deleteAtEnd().

???+ note "Array-based list" | Operation | Cost | Why | |---|:---:|---| | `insertAtEnd(x)` | **O(1)** amortised | Append at index `size`; occasionally double | | `get(i)` | **O(1)** | Direct indexing | | `deleteAtEnd()` | **O(1)** | Decrement `size` | ???+ note "Linked-list" | Operation | Cost | Why | |---|:---:|---| | `insertAtEnd(x)` | **O(n)** | Walk to the end | | `get(i)` | **O(n)** | Walk `i` steps | | `deleteAtEnd()` | **O(n)** | Walk to the end | **Same operations, same semantics.** The array implementation is **dramatically faster** for these three operations.

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Choosing an ADT for a text editor
docs.text:
You are building a text editor that needs to: insert characters at cursor, delete before cursor, move cursor, undo.

???+ note "Candidate 1 — Dynamic array" Insert at position `p` costs **O(n)** because everything after `p` shifts. For a 100,000-character document, editing near the start shifts 100,000 characters — **perceptibly slow**. ???+ note "Candidate 2 — Doubly-linked list" Insert at cursor = **O(1)** (splice between two nodes). Cursor move = **O(1)**. Undo = **O(1)** with a stack of operations. **This fits.** **Choice:** a **doubly-linked list** plus a **stack** for undo. Operations that must be fast are all O(1). Operations that would be slow (random access by index) are not needed.

docs.title: 1.3 — The need for a formal measure
Why not just "run it and time it"?
docs.text:
import time
start = time.time()
sort(data)
elapsed = time.time() - start
The number is **useless for comparison** across: - **Machines** — a laptop and a phone give different times. - **Languages** — Python vs C differ by 100×. - **Data sizes** — the result on 100 items tells you nothing about 10⁶. - **Inputs** — the same algorithm can be fast on sorted data and slow on random data. What we want is a **machine-independent, size-relative** measure of how the algorithm's cost **grows** with input size.

docs.title: Counting operations
docs.text:
Instead of wall-clock time, count primitive operations:

- The number of comparisons - The number of assignments - The number of array accesses - The number of nodes visited Different primitives have different physical times, but in asymptotic analysis **they all count as one "step."** The result is a **step count** $T(n)$ as a function of input size $n$.

docs.title: Example — counting steps
docs.text:
int sum(int[] a) {
    int total = 0;                        // 1 step
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {  // n+1 comparisons, n increments
        total += a[i];                    // n additions
    }
    return total;                         // 1 step
}
Total steps: $1 + (n+1) + n + n + 1 = 3n + 3$. We say: **$T(n) = 3n + 3$** — "the cost grows **linearly** in $n$."

docs.title: Growth, not absolute value
docs.text:
The key question is not "how many steps at \(n = 100\)?" but "how many steps at \(n = 10^6\)?"

\(n\) \(T(n) = 3n + 3\) \(T(n) = 0.001 n^2 + 5\) 10 33 5.1 100 303 15 1,000 3,003 1,005 10,000 30,003 100,005 1,000,000 3,000,003 1,000,000,005 For small $n$, the quadratic (with a small leading constant) is **faster**. For large $n$, the linear algorithm wins by a factor of ~300,000. **Growth rate is what matters, and Big-O captures it.**

docs.title: 1.4 — Big-O notation
docs.text:
Definition — Big-O

We write \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if there exist positive constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that

\[ f(n) \le c \cdot g(n) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0. \]

In words: \(f\) grows no faster than a constant times \(g\), eventually.

**Intuition.** $f(n) = O(g(n))$ means "$g$ is an **upper bound** on the growth of $f$." It ignores constants and small values of $n$ — what's left is the **shape of the growth curve**.

docs.title: Worked example 1.3 — Prove \(3n + 3 = O(n)\)
docs.text:
We need \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that \(3n + 3 \le c \cdot n\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

**Try $c = 4$:** $3n + 3 \le 4n$ ⟺ $3 \le n$. Holds for all $n \ge 3$. **Try $c = 6$:** $3n + 3 \le 6n$ ⟺ $3 \le 3n$ ⟺ $1 \le n$. Holds for $n \ge 1$. **Conclusion.** $3n + 3 = O(n)$, with witness $c = 6$, $n_0 = 1$. ✓ **Interpretation.** For large $n$, the linear term dominates; the constant is negligible.

docs.title: Worked example 1.4 — Prove \(n^2 - 5n + 7 = O(n^2)\)
docs.text:
We need \(c, n_0\) such that \(n^2 - 5n + 7 \le c n^2\) for all \(n \ge n_0\).

**Try $c = 2$:** $n^2 - 5n + 7 \le 2n^2$ ⟺ $7 - 5n \le n^2$. Since $n^2 \ge 0$ and $7 - 5n \le 7$, we need $7 \le n^2$ — holds for $n \ge 3$. **Conclusion.** $n^2 - 5n + 7 = O(n^2)$, with witness $c = 2$, $n_0 = 3$. ✓

docs.title: Worked example 1.5 — Prove a tighter bound does not hold
docs.text:
Prove \(5n^2 + 3n \ne O(n)\).

**Proof by contradiction.** Suppose $5n^2 + 3n = O(n)$. Then there exist $c, n_0$ such that $5n^2 + 3n \le c \cdot n$ for all $n \ge n_0$. Divide by $n$ (positive): $5n + 3 \le c$ for all $n \ge n_0$. But $5n + 3$ grows without bound as $n$ grows. For any fixed $c$, there exists $n > (c - 3)/5$ where the inequality **fails**. Contradiction. **Conclusion.** $5n^2 + 3n \ne O(n)$ — the quadratic term makes the growth strictly faster than linear.

docs.title: Rules of Big-O arithmetic
docs.text: Rule Statement Example Drop constants \(c \cdot f(n) = O(f(n))\) \(7n = O(n)\) Drop lower-order terms \(f(n) + g(n) = O(\max(f, g))\) \(n^2 + n = O(n^2)\) Transitivity \(f = O(g)\) and \(g = O(h)\) ⇒ \(f = O(h)\) — Sum rule \(f + g = O(\max(f, g))\) \(n \log n + n = O(n \log n)\) Product rule \(f \cdot g = O(f \cdot g)\) \(n \cdot \log n = O(n \log n)\)   !!! warning "The trick that catches students."     In $O(n^2 + n)$, the $n$ term is **not** "small" — it's just **dominated by** $n^2$ for large $n$. The $n^2 + n$ expression is *exact*; the $O(n^2)$ is a simplification that captures the dominant growth.

docs.title: 1.5 — Big-Ω and Big-Θ
docs.text:
Definition — Big-Ω

We write \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) if there exist positive constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) such that

\[ f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0. \]

In words: \(f\) grows at least as fast as a constant times \(g\).

$f = \Omega(g)$ means "$g$ is a **lower bound**." For example, any sort that must examine every element has $\Omega(n)$ runtime — no faster than linear is possible.

docs.title: Definition — Big-Θ
docs.text:
Definition — Big-Θ

\(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\) if \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\).

In words: \(f\) and \(g\) grow at the same rate, up to constants.

$\Theta$ is the **strongest and most useful** statement. "Sorting by comparison is $\Theta(n \log n)$" says: no comparison sort is faster than $n \log n$, and algorithms exist that achieve it.

docs.title: The hierarchy at a glance
docs.text: Notation Meaning Analogy \(f = O(g)\) \(f\) grows no faster than \(g\) \(f \le g\) (up to constant) \(f = \Omega(g)\) \(f\) grows no slower than \(g\) \(f \ge g\) (up to constant) \(f = \Theta(g)\) \(f\) grows at the same rate as \(g\) \(f = g\) (up to constant) \(f = o(g)\) \(f\) grows strictly slower than \(g\) \(f < g\) (strictly) \(f = \omega(g)\) \(f\) grows strictly faster than \(g\) \(f > g\) (strictly)

docs.title: Worked example 1.6 — Three statements about one function
docs.text:
Consider \(f(n) = 2n^2 + 5n\).

Claim True? Witness \(f(n) = O(n^2)\) ✓ \(c = 3\), \(n_0 = 5\) \(f(n) = \Omega(n^2)\) ✓ \(c = 1\), \(n_0 = 1\) \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) ✓ Follows from both \(f(n) = O(n)\) ✗ See Worked example 1.5 method \(f(n) = \Theta(n)\) ✗ Would require the false \(O(n)\) bound **Conclusion.** $f(n) = \Theta(n^2)$ — the tightest statement.

docs.title: 1.6 — Analysing loops
docs.text:
The single most important skill in complexity analysis is reading a loop and writing its Big-O.

Single loop rule

If a loop runs a constant number of operations per iteration and executes \(k\) iterations, its cost is \(O(k)\).

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    sum += a[i];
}
Iterations: $n$. Per iteration: constant. **Total: $O(n)$.**

docs.title: Worked example 1.7 — Loop with doubling index
docs.text:
for (int i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2) {
    sum += i;
}
How many iterations? Each step **doubles** `i`. Starting at 1, after $k$ iterations we have $i = 2^k$. Stop when $2^k \ge n$, i.e., $k = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$. **Total: $O(\log n)$.** This pattern appears constantly — binary search, balanced-tree walks, exponentiation by squaring. !!! tip "Rule of thumb" **Doubling or halving the index means $\log n$ iterations.**

docs.title: Worked example 1.8 — Two independent nested loops
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        sum += a[i][j];
    }
}
Outer: $n$ iterations. Inner: $n$ iterations **for each outer iteration**. $n \times n = n^2$. **$O(n^2)$.**

docs.title: Worked example 1.9 — Nested with an "upper triangle" inner loop
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
        sum += a[i][j];
    }
}
Inner loop runs $n - i$ times, for outer index $i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$. Total: $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (n - i) = n + (n-1) + \ldots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. **Total: $O(n^2)$** — the $n^2/2$ leading term dominates; the $\frac12$ constant drops. !!! tip "The lesson" Halving the iteration count (from $n^2$ to $n^2/2$) does **not** change the complexity class. **Big-O ignores constants.**

docs.title: Worked example 1.10 — Loop where the input drives the iterations
docs.text:
void print(int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {   // note: j < i, not j < n
            System.out.println(i + j);
        }
    }
}
Inner: $i$ iterations per outer step $i$. Total: $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i = \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = O(n^2)$. Same class as Worked example 1.9 — a triangular pattern is $O(n^2)$.

docs.title: 1.7 — Analysing recursion
docs.text:
For recursive algorithms, we don't count iterations. We write a recurrence relation — an equation for \(T(n)\) in terms of smaller inputs — and solve it.

The template

For a recursive function of input size \(n\) that:

  • Performs some constant work,
  • Makes \(a\) recursive calls on inputs of size \(n/b\),

the recurrence is: \(T(n) = a \cdot T(n/b) + O(1)\).

docs.title: The three common cases
docs.text: Case Recurrence Solution Examples No branching (\(a = 1\)) \(T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(1)\) \(O(n)\) Factorial, linear search Halving (\(b = 2, a = 1\)) \(T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)\) \(O(\log n)\) Binary search Two halvings (\(b = 2, a = 2\)) \(T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) Merge sort Exponential (\(b=2, a>2\)) \(T(n) = 2^n\) \(O(2^n)\) Naive Fibonacci

docs.title: Worked example 1.11 — Linear recursion (factorial)
docs.text:
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}
Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)$. Unrolling: $T(n) = T(n-1) + c = T(n-2) + 2c = \ldots = T(1) + (n-1)c = O(n)$. **Total: $O(n)$.** The recursion **does not multiply** — each call produces exactly one smaller call, so the work is linear.

docs.title: Worked example 1.12 — Binary search
docs.text:
int binarySearch(int[] a, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
    if (a[mid] < target) return binarySearch(a, target, mid + 1, hi);
    return binarySearch(a, target, lo, mid - 1);
}
The input is **halved** each call. Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$. Unrolling: $T(n) = T(1) + c \cdot \log_2 n = O(\log n)$. **Total: $O(\log n)$.** Why? Because $n / 2^k = 1$ when $k = \log_2 n$. That's the depth of the recursion tree.

docs.title: Worked example 1.13 — Merge sort
docs.text:
void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid);       // recurse on left half
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);   // recurse on right half
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi);       // O(n) merge
}
Recurrence: $T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n)$. **Recursion tree:** at depth $d$, there are $2^d$ nodes, each of size $n / 2^d$. Work at depth $d$: $2^d \times O(n / 2^d) = O(n)$. Depth: $\log_2 n$. Total: $O(n \log n)$. **Total: $O(n \log n)$.** Merge sort is fundamentally better than bubble/insertion/selection sort ($O(n^2)$) for large inputs.

docs.title: Worked example 1.14 — Naive Fibonacci
docs.text:
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}
Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)$. This is **exponential** — $T(n) = \Theta(\phi^n)$ with $\phi \approx 1.618$. $T(50) \approx 2 \times 10^{10}$ — **hours** on a laptop. ???+ tip "Contrast with an iterative version" 
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    int a = 0, b = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}
**Total: $O(n)$.** For $n = 50$, that's 50 additions — a microsecond. **Same math, same answer, 10⁶-times-faster implementation.** The reason: the naive recursion **repeats work** — `fib(n-2)` is computed inside both `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n)`.

docs.title: 1.8 — The common complexity classes
docs.text: Class Name Grows Typical example O(1) constant does not grow array indexing, hash lookup O(log n) logarithmic very slowly binary search, balanced-tree search O(n) linear linearly array scan, linked-list traversal O(n log n) linearithmic slightly super-linear merge sort, quicksort (avg) O(n²) quadratic quadratically bubble/insertion/selection sort O(n³) cubic cubically naive matrix multiplication O(2ⁿ) exponential explodes naive Fibonacci O(n!) factorial explodes faster brute-force TSP

docs.title: How big is "big"?
docs.text:
For \(n = 1{,}000{,}000\) (1 million items) at \(10^9\) operations per second:

Class Operations Time \(O(1)\) 1 1 ns \(O(\log n)\) 20 20 ns \(O(n)\) 10⁶ 1 ms \(O(n \log n)\) 2 × 10⁷ 20 ms \(O(n²)\) 10¹² 11.6 days \(O(2ⁿ)\) astronomical billions of years !!! warning "The practical message" Anything worse than $O(n \log n)$ is **unusable** on million-item inputs. This is why the analysis matters — it tells you which algorithms are actually deployable.

docs.title: Why Big-O ignores constants
docs.text:
Big-O is a statement about growth, not about performance. Two algorithms with the same Big-O may differ 100× in absolute speed:

  • Algorithm A: \(T_A(n) = 100\,n\)
  • Algorithm B: \(T_B(n) = 0.1\,n\)

Both are \(O(n)\). For \(n = 1000\), A takes \(100{,}000\) steps, B takes \(100\) steps. B is 1000× faster, but Big-O cannot see it.

docs.title: Why constants matter anyway
docs.text:
For small \(n\), constants dominate. The crossover point:

\(n\) A: \(100n\) B: \(0.1n^2\) 10 1000 10 1000 100,000 100,000 10,000 10⁶ 10⁷ **B faster for small $n$; A faster for large $n$.** Crossover at $n = 1000$. This is why **quicksort** (average $O(n \log n)$ with a small constant) is faster than merge sort in practice on small to medium inputs — and why **insertion sort** ($O(n^2)$ but tiny constant) beats both on arrays of $< 20$ elements.

docs.title: Practical rule
docs.text:
Big-O tells you what scales.

Constants tell you what fits in cache, what fits in a register, what dominates at your actual problem size.

Always use both. Never pick an algorithm by Big-O alone when the actual data is small.

docs.title: 1.10 — Space complexity
docs.text:
Time is only half the story. Space complexity measures how much extra memory an algorithm uses, as a function of input size \(n\).

- **Auxiliary space** — memory in addition to the input. - **Total space** — input + auxiliary. 
// In-place reversal: O(1) auxiliary space
for (int i = 0; i < n/2; i++) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[n-1-i]; a[n-1-i] = t;
}

// Out-of-place reversal: O(n) auxiliary space
int[] b = new int[n];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) b[i] = a[n-1-i];
Both are $O(n)$ time. But the first uses $O(1)$ auxiliary space; the second uses $O(n)$. On a memory-constrained embedded device, this difference is decisive. Always report auxiliary space, not just time.

docs.title: Recursion uses space too
docs.text:
Every recursive call occupies a stack frame.

Typically tens to hundreds of bytes. So a recursion of depth \(d\) uses \(O(d)\) auxiliary space.

Fibonacci's naive recursion uses \(O(n)\) stack space — the depth is \(n\).

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. A data structure is a way of organizing data and the operations on it. The layout and the operations are equally important.

  2. Abstraction — an ADT specifies what, an implementation specifies how. One ADT, many implementations.

  3. Big-O describes the growth of an algorithm's cost as input size increases. It drops constants and lower-order terms.

  4. Big-Ω is a lower bound, Big-Θ is a tight bound. \(\Theta\) is the strongest and most useful.

  5. Loops — count iterations; multiply for nested loops.

  6. Recursion — write the recurrence, solve it. No-branching → \(O(n)\); halving → \(O(\log n)\); two-halving → \(O(n \log n)\); exponential → \(O(2^n)\).

  7. The common complexity classes are \(O(1)\), \(O(\log n)\), \(O(n)\), \(O(n \log n)\), \(O(n^2)\), \(O(n^3)\), \(O(2^n)\), \(O(n!)\).

  8. Constants matter. Big-O gives the growth shape; constants give the practical performance.

  9. Space complexity matters as much as time. Recursion costs stack space.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
What does it mean for $f(n) = O(g(n))$?

$f$ is always smaller than $g$ $f$ grows no faster than $g$, up to a constant $f$ and $g$ have equal value at every $n$ $f$ is an algorithm, $g$ a program

docs.title: Review questions (cont.)
docs.text:
1. Define a data structure. Why must the definition include operations, not just layout?

  2. Distinguish an ADT from an implementation. Give one ADT and two different implementations, and explain when each is preferred.

  3. State the formal definition of Big-O. Use it to prove that \(4n^2 + 3n + 1 = O(n^2)\).

  4. Distinguish Big-O, Big-Ω, and Big-Θ. Give one example function for which \(f = O(g)\), \(f = \Omega(g)\), and \(f = \Theta(g)\) all hold.

  5. Analyse: triple-nested loop, outer \(n\), middle \(n-i\), inner constant 10. Big-O?

  6. Write the recurrence for f(n) = f(n/2) + f(n/2) + n and solve.

  7. Why does Big-O ignore constants, and why do constants still matter in practice?

  8. Compare time and auxiliary space complexity of recursive vs iterative Fibonacci.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Arrays
docs.text:
Memory allocation · Operations · Complexity

Arrays are the foundation. Everything else — stacks, queues, heaps, hash tables — is built on the array.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what an array is and how it is laid out in memory.

  2. Compute the address of any element in O(1).

  3. Analyse the cost of insert, delete, search on arrays.

  4. Explain row-major vs column-major storage.

  5. Reason about the amortised cost of dynamic arrays.

  6. Choose between arrays and linked lists for a given workload.

docs.title: 2.1 — What is an array?
2.2 — Memory allocation
docs.text:
Elements stored contiguously. Address of element \(i\):

\[ \text{addr}(a[i]) = \text{base} + i \times \text{sizeof(type)} \] !!! tip "This is why array access is O(1)." One multiplication, one addition, one read. No traversal. No pointer chasing. Just arithmetic.

docs.title: Layout example (int array, 4 bytes each)
docs.text: Index Address Value 0 1000 10 1 1004 20 2 1008 30 3 1012 40 4 1016 50   `a[3]` → address $1000 + 3 \times 4 = 1012$ → value 40.  **One arithmetic step. Constant time.**

docs.title: 2.3 — Basic operations
docs.text:
Operation Complexity Why Access by index O(1) Direct arithmetic Search (unsorted) O(n) Linear scan Search (sorted) O(log n) Binary search Insert at end O(1)* If capacity allows Insert at position O(n) Shift elements Delete at position O(n) Shift elements

*Amortised for dynamic arrays — occasionally resize.

docs.title: Insertion — shifting
docs.text:
// Insert value at index k (array has n elements, capacity >= n+1)
for (int i = n; i > k; i--)
    a[i] = a[i-1];
a[k] = value;
n++;
If $k = 0$: **$n$ shifts** = $O(n)$. If $k = n$: **0 shifts** = $O(1)$. **Average cost:** $n/2$ shifts = $O(n)$.

docs.title: Deletion — shifting
docs.text:
// Delete element at index k
for (int i = k; i < n-1; i++)
    a[i] = a[i+1];
n--;
If $k = 0$: **$n-1$ shifts** = $O(n)$. If $k = n-1$: **0 shifts** = $O(1)$. **Average cost:** $O(n)$. !!! warning "Lesson" Arrays are **fast at the end, slow in the middle**.

docs.title: 2.4 — Multidimensional arrays
docs.text:
2D array int m[3][4]; → 12 contiguous ints.

Two storage orders:

**Row-major (C, C++, Python/NumPy default):** `m[0][0], m[0][1], ..., m[0][3], m[1][0], ...` **Column-major (Fortran, MATLAB):** `m[0][0], m[1][0], m[2][0], m[0][1], ...` Access `m[i][j]` in row-major: $$ \text{addr} = \text{base} + (i \cdot \text{cols} + j) \times \text{sizeof(type)} $$

docs.title: Why storage order matters
docs.text:
Cache behavior. Consecutive memory addresses get fetched together.

Row-major + row-wise iteration 
for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++)
        sum += m[i][j];     // sequential — cache-friendly
Row-major + column-wise iteration 
for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++)
    for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++)
        sum += m[i][j];     // strided — cache-thrashing
**Same O(rows × cols) time. Up to 10× difference in practice.**

docs.title: 2.5 — Dynamic arrays — amortised analysis
docs.text:
Python list, Java ArrayList, C++ std::vector — these are dynamic arrays.

Growth strategy

When full, allocate 2× the current size and copy old elements.

**Cost of $n$ appends:** - Most appends: $O(1)$ — just write at the next slot. - Occasional append: $O(n)$ — copy everything. Total over $n$ appends: $1 + 1 + \ldots + 1$ (most) + $n + 2n + \ldots$ (copies). **Amortised cost per append: O(1).** The occasional expensive operation is **paid for** by the many cheap ones.

docs.title: Worked example — amortised cost
docs.text:
Appending \(n = 16\) items to an empty dynamic array (capacity doubling):

Append # Cost Capacity after 1 1 (alloc 1) 1 2 2 (copy 1) 2 3 1 4 4 2 4 5–8 1 each, then copy 4 8 9–16 1 each, then copy 8 16 **Total work for 16 appends: ~32.** Average: **2 ops per append** = **amortised O(1)**.

docs.title: 2.6 — Arrays vs linked lists
docs.text: Use case Array Linked list Random access by index ✅ O(1) ❌ O(n) Insert/delete at end ✅ O(1)* ✅ O(1) with tail Insert/delete in middle ❌ O(n) ✅ O(1) with pointer Memory locality ✅ Cache-friendly ❌ Pointer chasing Memory overhead ✅ Minimal ❌ Pointers per node Fixed capacity ❌ ✅ Dynamic   **Pick the structure whose *hot path* is cheapest.**

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Array = contiguous, homogeneous, indexed block.

  2. Access is O(1) — arithmetic address calculation.

  3. Insert/delete in middle = O(n) — requires shifts.

  4. Insert/delete at end = O(1) — with amortised analysis for dynamic arrays.

  5. Row-major vs column-major — determines cache behavior.

  6. Amortised O(1) append via capacity doubling.

  7. Arrays are the base for stacks, queues, heaps, hash tables.

docs.text:

  2. Explain why inserting at the beginning of an array is O(n).

  3. Compare row-major and column-major storage. Which does C use?

  4. Show the amortised argument for dynamic-array append.

  5. When would you prefer an array over a linked list? Give a concrete example.

  6. Give the memory overhead comparison for \(n\) ints in an array vs a linked list.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Linked Lists
docs.text:
Singly · Doubly · Circular

Semester VII · 2025/26

Linked lists are the first structure that beats arrays on a specific workload: frequent insert/delete with pointer access.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the motivation for linked lists over arrays.

  2. Describe a node and how nodes link together.

  3. Implement insert, delete, search on a singly linked list.

  4. Analyse the cost of each operation.

  5. Distinguish singly, doubly, circular linked lists.

  6. Reverse a linked list in O(n) time and O(1) space.

docs.title: 3.1 — Why linked lists?
docs.text:
Arrays have two pain points:

- **Fixed size** — you must know $n$ upfront. - **O(n) insert/delete in the middle** — shifting. Linked lists offer: - **Dynamic size** — grow and shrink as needed. - **O(1) insert/delete** — with a pointer to the right place. !!! warning "Trade-off" **No O(1) random access.**

docs.title: 3.2 — Node structure
docs.text:
struct Node {
    int data;
    struct Node *next;
};
Each node holds: - **data** — the payload. - **next** — pointer to the next node (or NULL). Nodes are allocated on the **heap** (via `malloc` / `new`). They are **not contiguous** — connected by pointers.

docs.title: Visual layout
docs.text:
head → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|•] → NULL

The head pointer is the entry to the list.

Traversal is linear: follow `next` until `NULL`. 
Node* cur = head;
while (cur) {
    printf("%d\n", cur->data);
    cur = cur->next;
}
Time: **O(n)** — must visit every node.

docs.title: 3.3 — Singly linked list operations
docs.text: Operation Complexity Notes Insert at head O(1) Rewire two pointers Insert at tail O(n) Walk to end (unless tail pointer) Insert after node O(1) Given a pointer Delete at head O(1) Rewire head Delete by value O(n) Search then unlink Search O(n) Linear scan Access by index O(n) Walk \(i\) steps

docs.title: Insert at head — O(1)
docs.text:
Node* insert_head(Node* head, int val) {
    Node* n = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    n->data = val;
    n->next = head;
    return n;
}
**Two pointer rewires.** No shifting. No traversal. This is why **linked lists shine for stack push operations**.

docs.title: Insert at tail — O(n) without tail pointer
docs.text:
Node* insert_tail(Node* head, int val) {
    Node* n = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    n->data = val; n->next = NULL;
    if (!head) return n;
    Node* cur = head;
    while (cur->next) cur = cur->next;   // walk to end
    cur->next = n;
    return head;
}
**$n$ steps** to reach the tail. !!! tip "Fix" Store a `tail` pointer — then insert-at-tail is **O(1)**.

docs.title: Delete by value — O(n)
docs.text:
Node* delete(Node* head, int val) {
    Node *cur = head, *prev = NULL;
    while (cur && cur->data != val) {
        prev = cur; cur = cur->next;
    }
    if (!cur) return head;               // not found
    if (prev) prev->next = cur->next;    // unlink from middle
    else head = cur->next;               // deleting head
    free(cur);
    return head;
}
**O(n)** to find, **O(1)** to unlink. Total **O(n)**.

docs.title: 3.4 — Doubly linked list
docs.text:
struct DNode {
    int data;
    struct DNode *prev, *next;
};

Two pointers per node:

  • prev — backward link.
  • next — forward link.
NULL ← [•|10|•] ⇄ [•|20|•] ⇄ [•|30|•] → NULL
**Advantages:** - Bidirectional traversal. - **O(1) delete given a node pointer** — no need for predecessor search. **Cost:** one extra pointer per node = ~50% memory overhead on small ints.

docs.title: Delete given a node — O(1) in doubly list
docs.text:
void delete_node(DNode* n) {
    if (n->prev) n->prev->next = n->next;
    if (n->next) n->next->prev = n->prev;
    free(n);
}
**Two pointer updates.** No traversal. **In a singly linked list**, the same operation is **O(n)** — you must find the predecessor first. This is the **main reason** doubly linked lists exist.

docs.title: 3.5 — Circular linked list
docs.text:
Last node points back to the head instead of NULL.

head → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|•] ─┐
         ↑                        │
         └────────────────────────┘
**Uses:** - **Round-robin scheduling** — cycle through processes. - **Circular buffers** — ring buffers in audio, networking. - **Josephus problem** — cyclic elimination. !!! warning "Care needed" Traversal must check "back to head" — otherwise infinite loop.

docs.title: 3.6 — Worked example: reverse a linked list
docs.text:
Reverse [10 → 20 → 30 → NULL] to [30 → 20 → 10 → NULL] in O(n) time and O(1) space.

Node* reverse(Node* head) {
    Node* prev = NULL;
    Node* cur = head;
    while (cur) {
        Node* next = cur->next;   // save next
        cur->next = prev;         // reverse link
        prev = cur;               // advance prev
        cur = next;               // advance cur
    }
    return prev;
}
**Three pointers** — `prev`, `cur`, `next`. **One pass. O(1) extra space.**

docs.title: Tracing the reversal
docs.text:
Start: [10 → 20 → 30], prev = NULL, cur = 10.

Step cur next after cur->next = prev list so far 1 10 20 10 → NULL [10] 2 20 30 20 → 10 [20 → 10] 3 30 NULL 30 → 20 [30 → 20 → 10] Return prev = 30. **Reversed.**

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Node = data + pointer. Nodes are linked, not contiguous.

  2. Singly linked: O(1) insert-at-head, O(n) search, O(n) delete-by-value.

  3. Doubly linked: O(1) delete given a node; bidirectional.

  4. Circular: no NULL terminator; cycles. Used in scheduling and buffers.

  5. Trade-off vs arrays: fast insert/delete, slow random access.

  6. Reversal is the classic interview problem — three pointers, one pass.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Compare arrays and linked lists for insert/delete/access. Give a use case where each is preferable.

  2. Why is insert at head O(1) in a singly linked list?

  3. What extra operation does a doubly linked list enable? Why can't a singly linked list do it in O(1)?

  4. When would you prefer a circular linked list?

  5. Write pseudocode to reverse a singly linked list in O(n) time and O(1) space.

  6. Given two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted list. Analyse the complexity.

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 3.

docs.text:
• Weiss, Ch. 3 — linked lists and their applications.
  • Lafore, Ch. 5 — linked lists in Java.
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, §1.3 — bags, queues, stacks via lists.
  • CLRS, §10.2 — linked-list primitives.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Stacks and Queues
docs.text:
LIFO · FIFO · Applications

Semester VII · 2025/26

Two ADTs, both O(1) per operation, both foundational for parsing, graph traversal, and scheduling.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define the Stack ADT (LIFO) and its operations.

  2. Implement stacks using arrays and linked lists.

  3. Explain when to use each implementation.

  4. Define the Queue ADT (FIFO) and its operations.

  5. Implement queues using circular arrays and linked lists.

  6. Recognise applications of both.

docs.title: 4.1 — The Stack ADT
docs.text:
Definition — Stack

A LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) collection.

  • push(x) — add \(x\) to the top.
  • pop() — remove and return the top.
  • peek() / top() — return the top without removing.
  • isEmpty() — true if empty.
Analogy: a stack of plates — you add and remove from the top.

docs.title: Stack operations — visual
docs.text:
push(10) → [10]
push(20) → [10, 20]
push(30) → [10, 20, 30]
pop()    → 30, stack = [10, 20]
peek()   → 20
pop()    → 20, stack = [10]
**All operations touch only the top.** **All operations are O(1).**

docs.title: 4.2 — Stack: array implementation
docs.text:
#define MAX 100
typedef struct { int data[MAX]; int top; } Stack;

void init(Stack* s) { s->top = 0; }
void push(Stack* s, int v) { s->data[s->top++] = v; }
int  pop (Stack* s)        { return s->data[--s->top]; }
int  peek(Stack* s)        { return s->data[s->top-1]; }
int  isEmpty(Stack* s)     { return s->top == 0; }
**O(1) operations.** Simple memory layout. **Downside:** fixed capacity — potential **overflow**. Must `check full` on push.

docs.title: Stack — linked-list implementation
docs.text:
typedef struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; } Node;

typedef struct { Node* top; } Stack;

void push(Stack* s, int v) {
    Node* n = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    n->data = v; n->next = s->top; s->top = n;
}
int pop(Stack* s) {
    Node* n = s->top;
    int v = n->data;
    s->top = n->next;
    free(n);
    return v;
}
**O(1)** push/pop. **Dynamic size** — no overflow until memory exhausted. **Downside:** pointer overhead, worse cache locality.

docs.title: 4.3 — Stack applications
docs.text: - **Function call stack** — recursion, local variables, return addresses. - **Expression evaluation** — infix → postfix, RPN evaluation. - **Balanced parentheses** — checking `(`, `{`, `[` matching.     - **Undo / redo** — in editors. - **DFS (iterative)** — depth-first search. - **Backtracking** — maze, N-queens, parsing. - **Browser back button** — history stack.

docs.title: Worked example — balanced parentheses
docs.text:
Check if {[()]} is balanced.

def is_balanced(s):
    stack = []
    pairs = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}
    for c in s:
        if c in '({[':
            stack.append(c)
        elif c in ')}]':
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[c]:
                return False
    return not stack
Trace on `{[()]}`: push `{`, push `[`, push `(`, pop `(`=`)`, pop `[`=]`, pop `{`=}. **Empty → balanced.** **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

docs.title: 4.4 — The Queue ADT
docs.text:
Definition — Queue

A FIFO (First-In, First-Out) collection.

  • enqueue(x) — add \(x\) to the back.
  • dequeue() — remove and return the front.
  • front() — return the front without removing.
  • isEmpty() — true if empty.
Analogy: a line at a ticket counter — first-come, first-served.

docs.title: Queue operations — visual
docs.text:
enqueue(10) → [10]
enqueue(20) → [10, 20]
enqueue(30) → [10, 20, 30]
dequeue()   → 10, queue = [20, 30]
front()     → 20
dequeue()   → 20, queue = [30]
**Enqueue touches the back; dequeue touches the front.** **All operations O(1)** — with the right implementation.

docs.title: 4.5 — Circular array implementation
docs.text:
A naïve array queue wastes space: after dequeue, slots at the front are unusable.

Fix

Wrap the index with % MAX.

typedef struct {
    int data[MAX]; int front, rear, size;
} Queue;

void enqueue(Queue* q, int v) {
    q->data[q->rear] = v;
    q->rear = (q->rear + 1) % MAX;
    q->size++;
}
int dequeue(Queue* q) {
    int v = q->data[q->front];
    q->front = (q->front + 1) % MAX;
    q->size--;
    return v;
}
**O(1)** enqueue/dequeue. **Full capacity used.**

docs.title: Circular queue trace
docs.text:
enqueue three times, dequeue once, enqueue one more (size = 4, MAX = 5):

Action front rear Occupied slots init 0 0 empty enq A 0 1 [A] enq B 0 2 [A,B] enq C 0 3 [A,B,C] deq (A) 1 3 [B,C] enq D 1 4 [B,C,D] enq E 1 0 [B,C,D,E] ← wrapped `rear` wraps around. Space reused.

docs.title: Queue — linked-list implementation
docs.text:
typedef struct { Node *front, *rear; } Queue;

void enqueue(Queue* q, int v) {
    Node* n = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    n->data = v; n->next = NULL;
    if (q->rear) q->rear->next = n;
    else q->front = n;
    q->rear = n;
}
int dequeue(Queue* q) {
    Node* n = q->front;
    int v = n->data;
    q->front = n->next;
    if (!q->front) q->rear = NULL;
    free(n);
    return v;
}
**O(1)** enqueue/dequeue. **Dynamic size.** No wraparound confusion.

docs.title: 4.6 — Queue variants
docs.text:
Priority Queue

Dequeue returns the highest-priority element, not the oldest. Implementation: binary heap (see Ch. 5). Cost: O(log n) per operation.

Deque (double-ended queue)

Insert and remove at both ends. O(1) per operation with a doubly-linked list or circular array.

Blocking queue

Concurrency; enqueue waits if full, dequeue waits if empty. Used in producer-consumer.

docs.title: Queue applications
docs.text: - **BFS** — breadth-first search. - **Task scheduling** — CPU scheduler, printer queue. - **Message queues** — Kafka, RabbitMQ.     - **I/O buffers** — audio, networking. - **Asynchronous processing** — job queues. - **Bipartite checking** — via BFS.     !!! tip "Pattern"     Queue = **"process in arrival order"**.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Stack — LIFO. All ops O(1). Array or linked-list based.

  2. Queue — FIFO. All ops O(1). Circular array avoids wasted space.

  3. Applications: stacks for recursion, parsing, DFS; queues for BFS, scheduling, buffers.

  4. Variants: priority queue, deque, blocking queue.

  5. Implementation trade-offs: arrays cache-friendly but fixed; lists dynamic but pointer-heavy.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Distinguish LIFO and FIFO. Give two real-world examples of each.

  2. Show how a stack checks balanced parentheses. Trace {[()]}.

  3. Convert A + B * C to postfix using a stack.

  4. Why is a circular queue preferred over a linear array queue? Draw a trace.

  5. Give two applications each of stacks and queues.

  6. Implement a queue using two stacks. Analyse the amortised cost per operation.

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 4.

docs.text:

  • Lafore, Ch. 4 (stacks), Ch. 4 (queues).
  • CLRS, §10.1 — stacks and queues.
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, §1.3 — bags, queues, stacks.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Trees
docs.text:
Binary · BST · AVL · Heaps · B+-Trees

Semester VII · 2025/26

Trees are the first structure that gives O(log n) search on dynamic data. Everything that follows — hash tables, graphs — builds on this idea.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Use tree terminology (root, leaf, height, depth).

  2. Distinguish full, complete, perfect binary trees.

  3. Perform all four traversals: preorder, inorder, postorder, level-order.

  4. Analyse BST operations.

  5. Explain how AVL rotations maintain balance.

  6. Explain how heaps work and are stored in arrays.

  7. Describe the role of B+-trees in databases.

docs.title: 5.1 — Tree terminology
docs.text:
A          ← root (depth 0)
       / \
      B   C        ← depth 1
     / \   \
    D   E   F      ← leaves (depth 2)
- **Root** — top node. - **Parent / child** — connected by edges. - **Leaf** — no children. - **Height** — longest path root → leaf (edges). - **Depth** — path from root to node.

docs.title: 5.2 — Binary tree
docs.text:
Each node has at most two children (left, right).

**Variants:** - **Full**: every node has 0 or 2 children. - **Complete**: all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left-to-right. - **Perfect**: all internal nodes have 2 children, all leaves at the same depth. 
Full:       Complete:       Perfect:
   A           A              A
  / \         / \            / \
 B   C       B   C          B   C
    / \     /  /           / \ / \
   D   E   D  E           D  E F  G

docs.title: 5.3 — Tree traversals
docs.text:
Traversal Order Use Preorder Root → Left → Right Copy tree, prefix expr Inorder Left → Root → Right Sorted output (BST) Postorder Left → Right → Root Delete tree, postfix Level-order BFS by level Width, level print 
def inorder(node):
    if node:
        inorder(node.left)
        print(node.val)
        inorder(node.right)
**All traversals: O(n)** — visit every node once.

docs.title: Traversal trace
docs.text:
1
       / \
      2   3
     / \   \
    4   5   6
Traversal Output Preorder 1 2 4 5 3 6 Inorder 4 2 5 1 3 6 Postorder 4 5 2 6 3 1 Level-order 1 2 3 4 5 6

docs.title: 5.4 — Binary Search Tree (BST)
docs.text:
Definition — BST

A binary tree where, for every node:

left subtree values < node value < right subtree values.

        50
       /  \
      30   70
     / \   / \
    20 40 60 80
**Inorder traversal yields sorted output** — this is the defining feature.

docs.title: BST operations
docs.text:
def search(node, key):
    if not node or node.val == key:
        return node
    return search(node.left, key) if key < node.val \
           else search(node.right, key)
Operation Average Worst (skewed) Search O(log n) O(n) Insert O(log n) O(n) Delete O(log n) O(n) Worst case: inserting sorted data → **linked list**, height $n$.

docs.title: BST — deletion cases
docs.text:
Deleting node \(X\):

**Case 1 — $X$ is a leaf.** Remove it. **Case 2 — $X$ has one child.** Replace $X$ by its child. **Case 3 — $X$ has two children.** Replace $X$ by its **inorder successor** (smallest in right subtree), then delete the successor.

docs.title: Why BSTs can degrade
docs.text:
Insert \(1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) in order:

1
 \
  2
   \
    3
     \
      4
       \
        5
**Height = 5 = n.** All operations degrade to **O(n)**. **Fix:** balance the tree — **AVL**, **red-black**, **B-tree**.

docs.title: 5.5 — AVL trees
docs.text:
Definition — AVL

A self-balancing BST: for every node,

\[ |\text{height}(\text{left}) - \text{height}(\text{right})| \le 1. \] Invented by **Adelson-Velsky & Landis** (1962). Guarantees height $O(\log n)$ → all operations **O(log n)**. **Maintained via rotations** after insert/delete.

docs.title: AVL rotations
docs.text:
LL imbalance — right rotate:

      30            20
     /  \          /  \
    20  40  →     10  30
   /                  \
  10                  40
**RR imbalance — left rotate:** mirror image. **LR / RL — double rotations:** left-then-right, or right-then-left. **One rotation per insert** (or a double rotation) restores balance.

docs.title: AVL insertion — algorithm
docs.text:
1. Insert like a normal BST.

  2. Walk back up, updating heights.

  3. At each node, compute balance factor \(h_L - h_R\).

  4. If \(|h_L - h_R| > 1\), apply the appropriate rotation:

  5. LL → right rotate.
  6. RR → left rotate.
  7. LR → left rotate on left child, then right rotate on node.
  8. RL → right rotate on right child, then left rotate on node.
**O(log n)** total — same as BST insert, plus $O(1)$ rotation work per level.

docs.title: 5.6 — Heaps
docs.text:
Definition — Heap

A complete binary tree with the heap property:

  • Max-heap: parent \(\ge\) children.
  • Min-heap: parent \(\le\) children.
**Complete** → can be stored in an **array**. Index $i$ has: - Parent at $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$. - Children at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$.

docs.title: Heap stored in an array
docs.text:
Min-heap:

        1
       / \
      3   2
     / \ / \
    7  4 5  6

Array: [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6]

- Index 0 (value 1) → children at index 1 (3), index 2 (2). ✓ - Index 1 (value 3) → children at index 3 (7), index 4 (4). ✓ **No pointers. No wasted space.** Cache-friendly.

docs.title: Heap operations
docs.text: Operation Complexity peek (min or max) O(1) insert O(log n) extract (min or max) O(log n) buildHeap from array O(n) **Insert:** append at end, then **sift up** (bubble up while violating heap property). Height $\log n$. **Extract:** move last to root, then **sift down**. Height $\log n$. **Build heap:** sift-down from bottom half — total $O(n)$, not $O(n\log n)$ (a classic analysis trick).

docs.title: Heap applications
docs.text: - **Priority queues** — scheduler, Huffman coding, Dijkstra. - **Heap sort** — $O(n\log n)$, in place. - **Median maintenance** — two heaps. - **Top-$k$ selection** — min-heap of size $k$.     !!! tip "Heap = priority-ordered, not sorted."     Partial order is cheaper than total order.

docs.title: 5.7 — B+-Trees
docs.text:
Multiway search trees — every internal node has many children (typically 100–1000).

**Properties:** - All data in **leaves**. - Internal nodes hold **keys for routing**. - Leaves linked → efficient **range queries**. - High fanout → **low height** → **few disk I/Os**. **Height $O(\log_B n)$** where $B$ is fanout. For $n = 10^9$ and $B = 100$: height $\approx 5$. **Five disk reads to find any record.** **Used in:** databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL), file systems (NTFS, ext4), Google Bigtable.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Tree terminology: root, leaf, height, depth.

  2. Traversals: preorder, inorder (sorted for BST), postorder, level-order — all O(n).

  3. BST: O(log n) average, O(n) worst if skewed.

  4. AVL balances via rotations → guaranteed O(log n).

  5. Heaps = complete binary trees in arrays — O(log n) insert/extract.

  6. B+-trees = disk-friendly multiway trees — very low height.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Define height and depth; illustrate on a tree.

  2. Trace preorder, inorder, postorder on a given tree.

  3. Why does an unbalanced BST degrade to O(n)?

  4. Show the rotation needed to fix an LL imbalance in an AVL tree.

  5. Explain how a min-heap is stored in an array. Give the index formula.

  6. Why is buildHeap O(n), not O(n log n)?

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 5.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Weiss, Ch. 4 (trees, AVL), Ch. 6 (heaps).
  • Lafore, Ch. 8 (binary trees), Ch. 10 (2-3-4 and B-trees).
  • CLRS, Ch. 12 (BST), Ch. 13 (red-black), Ch. 6 (heaps).
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Ch. 3.

docs.title: Chapter 6 — Hash Tables
docs.text:
Hashing · Collisions · Open Addressing · Chaining

Semester VII · 2025/26

Hash tables give average O(1) lookups — the fastest dictionary we will see. The price is worst-case O(n).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the hash table concept.

  2. Identify properties of a good hash function.

  3. Explain why collisions happen and are unavoidable.

  4. Distinguish open addressing and separate chaining.

  5. Compare linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing.

  6. Analyse complexity of hash operations average vs worst.

docs.title: 6.1 — Hash table concept
docs.text:
Definition — Hash table

A data structure that maps keys → values using a hash function \(h(k)\) that computes an index in \([0, m-1]\).

key "alice" → h("alice") = 3 → table[3] = (alice, 42)
**Average access: O(1).** **Used in:** dictionaries, sets, caches, symbol tables, databases.

docs.title: Why hash tables work
docs.text: Operation Array Linked list Hash table (avg) Search O(n) O(n) O(1) Insert O(n) O(n) O(1) Delete O(n) O(1)* O(1)   **"Average O(1)" is the whole point** — near-array speed with near-list flexibility.  !!! warning "The catch"     The O(1) is **average**, not worst. Bad hash function or full table → **O(n)**.

docs.title: 6.2 — Hash functions
docs.text:
Good hash function properties:

- **Deterministic** — same key always → same hash. - **Uniform** — keys spread evenly across buckets. - **Fast** — O(1) to compute. **Common methods:** - **Division:** $h(k) = k \bmod m$ (choose $m$ prime). - **Multiplication:** $h(k) = \lfloor m(kA \bmod 1) \rfloor$ with $0 < A < 1$. - **Universal hashing:** randomly chosen from a family — beats adversarial inputs.

docs.title: Division method — the classic
docs.text:
\[ h(k) = k \bmod m \]

Choose \(m\) prime, not a power of 2.

Why? If $m = 2^p$, then $h(k)$ = the low $p$ bits of $k$. If keys all end in the same bits (e.g., they're all even), the low bits carry no information — mass collisions. **Prime $m$** makes every bit of $k$ affect the result. - **Bad:** $m = 1000$ (many composite factors). - **Good:** $m = 997$ (prime near 1000).

docs.title: 6.3 — Collisions
docs.text:
Definition — Collision

Two distinct keys \(k_1 \ne k_2\) with \(h(k_1) = h(k_2)\).

**Collisions are unavoidable** when #keys > $m$ (pigeonhole principle). Even with #keys < $m$, they happen — birthday paradox says collisions occur with $\sqrt{m}$ keys. **Two resolution strategies:** 1. **Open addressing** — probe other slots. 2. **Separate chaining** — linked list per bucket.

docs.title: 6.4 — Open addressing
docs.text:
On collision, probe alternate slots in a sequence.

**Linear probing:** $h(k), h(k)+1, h(k)+2, \ldots$ (mod $m$). **Quadratic probing:** $h(k), h(k)+1^2, h(k)+2^2, \ldots$ **Double hashing:** $h_1(k), h_1(k)+h_2(k), h_1(k)+2h_2(k), \ldots$ **Search** follows the same probe sequence until the key is found or an empty slot is hit.

docs.title: Linear probing — trace
docs.text:
Table size \(m = 7\), hash \(h(k) = k \bmod 7\). Insert 10, 20, 15, 7, 22.

Insert \(h(k)\) Probe sequence Placed at 10 3 3 3 20 6 6 6 15 1 1 1 7 0 0 0 22 1 1, 2 2 Search for 22: start at 1 → 2 → found. **2 probes.** **Watch:** 15 at 1, 22 at 2 — clustering around index 1.

docs.title: Clustering — linear probing's weakness
docs.text:
Primary clustering: long runs of occupied slots grow longer, making future insertions slower.

With load factor $\alpha$, expected probes ≈ $\frac{1}{2}(1 + 1/(1-\alpha)^2)$. Blows up as $\alpha \to 1$. **Fix 1 — Quadratic probing:** less primary clustering, but still **secondary clustering** (same hash → same probe sequence). **Fix 2 — Double hashing:** eliminates secondary clustering. **Best in practice.**

docs.title: Load factor
docs.text:
Definition — Load factor \[ \alpha = \frac{n}{m} \]

where \(n\) = number of stored keys, \(m\) = table size.

**Rules of thumb:** - Open addressing: keep $\alpha < 0.7$. - Chaining: $\alpha$ can exceed 1. **When $\alpha$ grows too large:** **resize** the table (typically double), **rehash all keys**. **Resize costs O(n)** — amortised O(1) per insert (same argument as dynamic arrays).

docs.title: Deletion in open addressing
docs.text:
Problem: you can't just set the slot to empty — a later search may have probed past it.

**Solution: tombstones.** 
[10] [TOMBSTONE] [15] [22] [ ] ...
**Search:** treat tombstone as "keep probing." **Insert:** treat tombstone as empty (reuse it). **Delete:** replace with tombstone. **Cost:** tombstones accumulate. **Periodic rehash** cleans them.

docs.title: 6.5 — Separate chaining
docs.text:
Each bucket holds a linked list of entries.

table[0] → NULL
table[1] → [k1,v1] → [k3,v3] → NULL
table[2] → [k2,v2] → NULL
table[3] → NULL
**Search:** hash to bucket, scan the list. **Insert:** hash to bucket, prepend to list — O(1). **Delete:** hash to bucket, unlink node — O(1) (with doubly linked or predecessor).

docs.title: Chaining — complexity
docs.text:
Average chain length = \(\alpha = n/m\).

Operation Average Worst Search O(1 + α) O(n) Insert O(1) O(n) Delete O(1) O(n) If $m \propto n$, then $\alpha = O(1)$ → **all operations O(1) average**. Worst case: all keys collide → **linked list**, **O(n)**.

docs.title: Open addressing vs chaining
docs.text: Aspect Open addressing Chaining Memory One array — no pointers Array + per-entry pointer overhead Cache Cache-friendly Pointer chasing Load factor Must stay < 0.7 Can exceed 1 Delete Tricky (tombstones) Simple Worst-case O(n) O(n) Clustering Susceptible Not susceptible   **Modern practice:** open addressing with **Robin Hood hashing** or **cuckoo hashing** often wins in cache-heavy workloads (e.g., Rust's `HashMap`).

docs.title: 6.6 — Complexity summary
docs.text: Operation Average Worst Search O(1) O(n) Insert O(1) O(n) Delete O(1) O(n)   **Average assumes:** good hash function **and** low load factor.  **Worst:** all keys collide — degenerate to linear scan.  **Adversarial inputs:** if keys are chosen by an attacker who knows the hash function, worst case is achievable — **defend with universal hashing** or **random seeds**.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Hash table = array + hash function + collision resolution.

  2. Average O(1) for search/insert/delete — worst O(n).

  3. Good hash function = deterministic, uniform, fast.

  4. Collisions are unavoidable — resolved by open addressing or chaining.

  5. Open addressing (probe): cache-friendly, deletion tricky (tombstones).

  6. Chaining (lists): simple deletion, pointer overhead.

  7. Load factor determines performance — keep it low, resize when high.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. What is a hash function? List three properties of a good one.

  2. Explain linear vs quadratic probing. What is clustering?

  3. Compare open addressing and separate chaining.

  4. Why does the load factor matter? What happens as α → 1?

  5. Trace insertion of [5, 15, 25, 35] into a table of size 7, with \(h(k) = k \bmod 7\). Show probes.

  6. Why are tombstones needed in open-addressing deletion? What happens without them?

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 6.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Graphs
docs.text:
Representations · Traversals · Shortest Paths · MST

Semester VII · 2025/26

Graphs are the most general structure in this course. Trees, lists, and networks are all special graphs.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define graphs and use graph terminology (degree, path, cycle, connected).

  2. Choose adjacency matrix or adjacency list based on density.

  3. Perform DFS and BFS in \(O(V+E)\).

  4. Explain when DFS or BFS applies.

  5. Run Dijkstra on non-negative weighted graphs.

  6. Compare Prim and Kruskal for MST.

docs.title: 7.1 — Graph definition
docs.text:
Definition — Graph

\(G = (V, E)\): a set of vertices \(V\) and a set of edges \(E\) connecting pairs of vertices.

**Variants:** - **Directed** (digraph) — edges have direction. - **Undirected** — edges are two-way. - **Weighted** — edges carry a cost. - **Unweighted** — edges are uniform.

docs.title: 7.2 — Graph terminology
docs.text: - **Degree** — number of edges incident to a vertex. - **Path** — sequence of vertices connected by edges. - **Cycle** — path that starts and ends at the same vertex.     - **Connected** — path between any two vertices (undirected). - **Strongly connected** — directed, path in both directions. - **DAG** — directed acyclic graph. - **Sparse** — $|E| \approx |V|$. - **Dense** — $|E| \approx |V|^2$.

docs.title: 7.3 — Adjacency matrix
docs.text:
\(n \times n\) matrix: \(A[i][j] = 1\) (or weight) if edge \(i \to j\).

     A B C D
   A 0 1 1 0
   B 0 0 0 1
   C 0 1 0 1
   D 0 0 0 0
Aspect Value Edge lookup O(1) Memory O(V²) Enumerate neighbors O(V) **Use:** dense graphs, frequent edge-existence checks. **Don't use:** sparse graphs — massive waste.

docs.title: 7.4 — Adjacency list
docs.text:
Array of lists: adj[u] = neighbors of \(u\).

A → [B, C]
B → [D]
C → [B, D]
D → []
Aspect Value Edge lookup O(degree(u)) Memory O(V + E) Enumerate neighbors O(degree(u)) **Use:** sparse graphs, neighbor iteration (DFS, BFS, Dijkstra). **Modern practice:** adjacency list is the default.

docs.title: Choosing a representation
docs.text: Scenario Matrix List Dense graph (\(E \sim V^2\)) ✅ ❌ Sparse graph (\(E \sim V\)) ❌ ✅ Frequent edge lookup ✅ ❌ Iterate all neighbors ❌ ✅ Memory-constrained ❌ ✅   **Rule of thumb:** use adjacency list unless you have a specific reason for matrix.

docs.title: 7.5 — Depth-First Search (DFS)
docs.text:
def dfs(u, visited, adj):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(v, visited, adj)
**Uses a stack** — explicit or via recursion. **O(V + E)** time. **Applications:** - **Connected components** — count them. - **Cycle detection**. - **Topological sort** (on DAG). - **Maze solving**, **backtracking**.

docs.title: DFS traversal trace
docs.text:
A
    / \
   B   C
  / \   \
 D   E   F

Start at A:

1. A → B → D (backtrack) → E (backtrack) → A. 2. A → C → F (backtrack) → A. 3. Done. **DFS order:** A, B, D, E, C, F. **Stack in action** — depth pursued before breadth.

docs.title: 7.6 — Breadth-First Search (BFS)
docs.text:
from collections import deque
def bfs(s, adj):
    visited = {s}
    q = deque([s])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v not in visited:
                visited.add(v)
                q.append(v)
**Uses a queue.** **O(V + E)** time. **Applications:** - **Shortest path** (unweighted) — the number of edges. - **Level-order traversal**. - **Bipartite check**. - **Social network** — degrees of separation.

docs.title: DFS vs BFS
docs.text: Aspect DFS BFS Data structure Stack Queue Explores Deep first Wide first Shortest path (unweighted) ❌ ✅ Memory \(O(h)\) — height \(O(w)\) — width Typical use Cycles, topo sort Shortest path   **Rule:** shortest path on unweighted graph → **BFS**. Structural exploration, cycles → **DFS**.

docs.title: 7.7 — Shortest path — Dijkstra
docs.text:
Goal

Single-source shortest path on a graph with non-negative edge weights.

**Algorithm sketch:** 1. Initialize $dist[s] = 0$, all others $\infty$. 2. Repeatedly extract the vertex $u$ with minimum $dist[u]$ not yet visited. 3. For each neighbor $v$: relax $dist[v] = \min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u,v))$. **Requires a priority queue** — typically a binary heap. **Fails** on **negative weights** — use Bellman-Ford instead.

docs.title: Dijkstra — code
docs.text:
import heapq
def dijkstra(s, adj, n):
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    pq = [(0, s)]                        # (distance, vertex)
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                     # stale entry
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
    return dist
**Complexity:** $O((V + E) \log V)$ with binary heap. **Why log V?** Heap operations per edge relaxation.

docs.title: Dijkstra trace (small example)
docs.text:
Graph: A-B=4, A-C=2, B-C=1, B-D=5, C-D=8, C-E=10, D-E=2.

Start at A:

Step Extract dist A B C D E 0 — 0 ∞ ∞ ∞ ∞ 1 A (0) 0 4 2 ∞ ∞ 2 C (2) 0 3 2 10 12 3 B (3) 0 3 2 8 12 4 D (8) 0 3 2 8 10 5 E (10) 0 3 2 8 10 **Shortest distances from A:** A=0, B=3, C=2, D=8, E=10.

docs.title: 7.8 — Minimum spanning tree (MST)
docs.text:
Definition — MST

A subset of edges that connects all vertices, is acyclic (a tree), and has minimum total weight.

**For a connected graph**, an MST always exists. **Two classic algorithms:** - **Prim's** — grow the tree one vertex at a time. - **Kruskal's** — grow the tree one edge at a time.

docs.title: Prim's algorithm
docs.text:
Grow the tree from a starting vertex.

1. Start with vertex $s$; tree = $\{s\}$. 2. Repeatedly add the **cheapest edge** connecting the tree to a vertex **not yet in the tree**. **Like Dijkstra** — but the priority is **edge weight to the tree**, not distance from source. **Complexity:** $O((V + E) \log V)$ with binary heap. **Good for:** dense graphs, online/growing graphs.

docs.title: Kruskal's algorithm
docs.text:
Grow by adding cheapest edges that don't form a cycle.

1. Sort all edges by weight. 2. Add each edge, **skipping** if it would create a cycle (use **Union-Find**). 
def kruskal(edges, n):
    edges.sort(key=lambda e: e[2])
    uf = UnionFind(n)
    mst = []
    for u, v, w in edges:
        if uf.find(u) != uf.find(v):
            uf.union(u, v)
            mst.append((u, v, w))
    return mst
**Complexity:** $O(E \log E)$ — dominated by sorting. **Good for:** sparse graphs.

docs.title: Prim vs Kruskal
docs.text: Aspect Prim Kruskal Approach Grow from vertex Grow from edge Data structure Heap + graph Sorted edges + Union-Find Complexity \(O((V+E)\log V)\) \(O(E \log E)\) Best for Dense graph Sparse graph Needs connectivity From start vertex Handles disconnected (forest)   **Both produce *an* MST** — weights are equal, tree may differ.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Graph = vertices + edges. Directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted.

  2. Adjacency matrix — O(1) edge lookup, O(V²) memory.

  3. Adjacency list — O(V+E) memory, default choice.

  4. DFS — stack-based, deep-first, cycles, topo sort.

  5. BFS — queue-based, wide-first, shortest unweighted paths.

  6. Dijkstra — weighted shortest paths (non-negative), O((V+E)log V).

  7. Prim / Kruskal — MST, both correct; pick by graph density.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Compare adjacency matrix and adjacency list. When is each preferable?

  2. Trace DFS and BFS on a given graph.

  3. Why does BFS find shortest unweighted paths but Dijkstra is needed for weighted?

  4. Show Dijkstra's steps on the small graph in the trace.

  5. Compare Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.

  6. What happens if Dijkstra is run on a graph with negative edges? Why does it fail?

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 7.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Weiss, Ch. 9 — graph algorithms.
  • Lafore, Ch. 13 (graphs), Ch. 14 (weighted graphs).
  • CLRS, Ch. 22 (BFS/DFS), Ch. 24 (Dijkstra), Ch. 23 (MST).
  • Sedgewick & Wayne, Ch. 4.

docs.title: Chapter 8 — Sorting Algorithms
docs.text:
Comparison sorts · Divide & conquer · Complexity

Semester VII · 2025/26

Sorting ties together everything from Chapter 1: Big-O analysis, recursion, heaps, and divide-and-conquer.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why sorting matters.

  2. Implement bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick, heap sort.

  3. Analyse best, average, worst case complexity.

  4. Distinguish stable vs unstable, in-place vs out-of-place.

  5. Prove a lower bound of \(\Omega(n\log n)\) for comparison sorts.

  6. Choose the right sort for a given input.

docs.title: 8.1 — Why sorting?
docs.text: - Enables **binary search** — O(log n) instead of O(n). - Enables **deduplication** — adjacent duplicates. - Enables **range queries** — sorted order. - Foundation for **Kruskal's MST**, **median finding**, **grouping**.     **Measures of a sort:**  - **Time** — best, average, worst. - **Space** — auxiliary memory. - **Stability** — equal keys preserve relative order. - **In-place** — uses O(1) auxiliary space.

docs.title: 8.2 — Bubble sort
docs.text:
def bubble_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n - i - 1):
            if a[j] > a[j+1]:
                a[j], a[j+1] = a[j+1], a[j]
**Idea:** repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs. Largest bubble to the end each pass. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Time (best) | O(n) — with early-exit flag | | Time (avg/worst) | **O(n²)** | | Space | **O(1)** | | Stable? | ✅ | | In-place? | ✅ | **Rarely used in practice** — educational only.

docs.title: 8.3 — Selection sort
docs.text:
def selection_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        m = i
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            if a[j] < a[m]:
                m = j
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
**Idea:** find minimum of remaining, swap into place. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Time | **O(n²)** always | | Space | **O(1)** | | Stable? | ❌ | | In-place? | ✅ | **Minimises swaps** — useful when writes are expensive (e.g., flash memory).

docs.title: 8.4 — Insertion sort
docs.text:
def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j+1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j+1] = key
**Idea:** build sorted prefix one element at a time. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Time (best) | **O(n)** — already sorted | | Time (avg/worst) | **O(n²)** | | Space | **O(1)** | | Stable? | ✅ | | In-place? | ✅ | **Best for small / nearly-sorted inputs.** Python's Timsort uses insertion sort for blocks of $\le 64$ elements.

docs.title: Insertion sort trace
docs.text:
Sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]:

Pass Key Array after — — 5 2 9 1 7 1 2 2 5 9 1 7 2 9 2 5 9 1 7 3 1 1 2 5 9 7 4 7 1 2 5 7 9 **Each pass:** shift larger elements right, insert key. Total shifts in worst case: $1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 = O(n^2)$.

docs.title: 8.5 — Merge sort
docs.text:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    L = merge_sort(a[:mid])
    R = merge_sort(a[mid:])
    return merge(L, R)

def merge(L, R):
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
        if L[i] <= R[j]:
            out.append(L[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(R[j]); j += 1
    return out + L[i:] + R[j:]
**Idea:** split, sort recursively, merge two sorted halves. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Time | **O(n log n)** — all cases | | Space | **O(n)** auxiliary | | Stable? | ✅ | | In-place? | ❌ |

docs.title: Merge sort — the recurrence
docs.text: \[ T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + O(n) \]   **Recursion tree:**  - Depth $d$ has $2^d$ subproblems of size $n/2^d$. - Work at depth $d$: $2^d \cdot O(n/2^d) = O(n)$. - Depth: $\log_2 n$.  **Total: $O(n \log n)$.**     **Advantages over quicksort:** guaranteed worst case; **stable**; good for **linked lists** and **external sorting**.  **Disadvantage:** $O(n)$ auxiliary space.

docs.title: Merge sort — merge step
docs.text:
Merge [2, 5] and [1, 3]:

i, j Compare Output 0, 0 2 vs 1 1 0, 1 2 vs 3 2 1, 1 5 vs 3 3 1, 2 (L exhausted) append 5 Result: `[1, 2, 3, 5]`. **O(m + n)** to merge two lists of sizes $m, n$.

docs.title: 8.6 — Quick sort
docs.text:
def quick_sort(a, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None: hi = len(a) - 1
    if lo < hi:
        p = partition(a, lo, hi)
        quick_sort(a, lo, p-1)
        quick_sort(a, p+1, hi)

def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i+1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i+1]
    return i + 1
**Idea:** pick pivot, partition into $\le$ pivot and $>$ pivot, recurse. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Time (best/avg) | **O(n log n)** | | Time (worst) | **O(n²)** — bad pivots | | Space (aux) | **O(log n)** — recursion | | Stable? | ❌ | | In-place? | ✅ |

docs.title: Quick sort — worst case
docs.text:
Worst case: pivot always minimum or maximum → \(T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) = O(n^2)\).

**Happens when:** input is already sorted (with last-element pivot) — common in practice! **Fix:** **randomised quicksort** — pick pivot uniformly at random. Then expected time $O(n\log n)$, with **high probability**. **Fix 2:** **median-of-three** — pick median of first, middle, last. Harder for adversarial inputs.

docs.title: Partition trace
docs.text:
Sort [3, 6, 1, 8, 2], pivot = last element (2):

lo = 0, pivot = 2, i = -1.

j a[j] a[j] ≤ 2? Action 0 3 ❌ — 1 6 ❌ — 2 1 ✅ i=0, swap a[0]↔a[2] → [1, 6, 3, 8, 2] 3 8 ❌ — Final: swap a[i+1] = a[1] ↔ pivot a[4] → `[1, 2, 3, 8, 6]`. Pivot at index 1. Recurse on `[1]` and `[3, 8, 6]`.

docs.title: 8.7 — Heap sort
docs.text:
def heap_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n//2 - 1, -1, -1):
        heapify(a, n, i)                # build max-heap — O(n)
    for i in range(n-1, 0, -1):
        a[0], a[i] = a[i], a[0]         # move max to end
        heapify(a, i, 0)                # restore heap

def heapify(a, n, i):
    l, r, m = 2*i+1, 2*i+2, i
    if l < n and a[l] > a[m]: m = l
    if r < n and a[r] > a[m]: m = r
    if m != i:
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
        heapify(a, n, m)
| Property | Value | |---|---| | Time | **O(n log n)** — all cases | | Space | **O(1)** | | Stable? | ❌ | | In-place? | ✅ | **Guaranteed worst case** — good when predictability matters.

docs.title: 8.8 — The comparison lower bound
docs.text:
Theorem

Any comparison-based sorting algorithm has worst-case time \(\Omega(n \log n)\).

**Proof sketch.** A decision tree for $n$ items has $n!$ leaves (one per permutation). A binary tree of height $h$ has $\le 2^h$ leaves. So: $$ 2^h \ge n! \Rightarrow h \ge \log_2(n!) = \Theta(n\log n). $$ **Consequence:** merge sort and heap sort are **asymptotically optimal** for comparison sorts. **Beating it requires non-comparison sorts** — counting sort, radix sort, bucket sort — but those assume restricted key types.

docs.title: 8.9 — Comparison table
docs.text: Algorithm Best Average Worst Space Stable Bubble O(n) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ✅ Selection O(n²) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ❌ Insertion O(n) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ✅ Merge O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) ✅ Quick O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) ❌ Heap O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) ❌

docs.title: Which sort should I use?
docs.text: Situation Best sort Small \(n\) (\(\le 20\)) Insertion Nearly sorted Insertion Stable required Merge or Insertion Guaranteed worst case Merge or Heap Space-constrained Heap (O(1)) General-purpose, in practice Quicksort (small constant) Linked list Merge sort Library call Whatever sorted() uses (usually Timsort) **Modern languages use hybrid sorts** — Timsort (Python, Java) combines merge + insertion.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Simple sorts (O(n²)): bubble, selection, insertion — good for small or nearly sorted.

  2. Merge sort: stable, O(n log n), O(n) space.

  3. Quick sort: fast average, O(n²) worst — mitigate with random pivot.

  4. Heap sort: guaranteed O(n log n), O(1) space, not stable.

  5. Lower bound: \(\Omega(n\log n)\) for comparison sorts — proven via decision tree.

  6. Hybrids (Timsort) dominate in real libraries.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Define stability and in-place sorting. Give one sort for each combination.

  2. Trace insertion sort on [5, 2, 9, 1, 7].

  3. Why is merge sort O(n log n) in all cases?

  4. When does quicksort degrade to O(n²)? How to mitigate?

  5. Show how buildHeap achieves O(n), not O(n log n).

  6. Prove that comparison sorting is \(\Omega(n \log n)\).

  7. Compare merge sort and quicksort for linked lists.

Answers: Solutions → Chapter 8.

docs.title: 2. Disprove Big-O statements
docs.text:
\(n^2 e O(n)\). Suppose \(n^2 \le c n\) for all \(n \ge n_0\). Divide by \(n\): \(n \le c\). But \(n o \infty\) — for any fixed \(c\), \(n > c\) eventually. Contradiction.

\(n \log n e O(n)\). Suppose \(n \log n \le c n\). Divide: \(\log n \le c\). But \(\log n o \infty\). Contradiction.

\(2^n e O(n^{100})\). Ratio \(2^n / n^{100} o \infty\) as \(n o \infty\). Contradiction.

docs.title: 3. Analyse loops
docs.text:
• for (i=0; i<n; i++) for (j=0; j<i; j++) → triangular sum \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = O(n^2)\).
  • for (i=1; i<n; i*=3) → iteration count: \(\log_3 n = O(\log n)\).
  • Triple nested i<n, j<n, k<n → \(n^3\) → \(O(n^3)\).
  • for (i=0; i<100; i++) for (j=0; j<n; j++) → \(100n\) → \(O(n)\).

docs.title: 4. Recurrences
docs.text:
\(f(n) = f(n-1) + 1\) with \(f(0) = 0\): unroll → \(f(n) = n\) → O(n).

\(g(n) = 2g(n-1) + 1\) with \(g(0) = 0\): unroll → \(g(n) = 2^n - 1\) → O(2ⁿ).

\(h(n) = 2h(n/2) + 1\) with \(h(1) = 1\): recursion tree has \(2^d\) nodes at depth \(d\); depth \(\log_2 n\); total nodes \(\sim n\). → O(n).

docs.title: 5. Prove transitivity
docs.text: If \(f = \Theta(g)\) and \(g = \Theta(h)\), then there exist constants such that \(c_1 g \le f \le c_2 g\) and \(c_3 h \le g \le c_4 h\). Substitute: \(c_1 c_3 h \le f \le c_2 c_4 h\). So \(f = \Theta(h)\). ✓

docs.title: 6. O but not Θ
docs.text: Example: \(f(n) = n\), \(g(n) = n^2\). \(f = O(g)\) (take \(c = 1\), \(n_0 = 1\)). But \(f \ne \Omega(g)\) — \(n\) doesn't grow as fast as \(n^2\) eventually. So \(f = O(g)\) but \(f \ne \Theta(g)\).

docs.title: 8. Space matters
docs.text:
Replaceable with O(1): array reversal — swap from both ends in O(1) auxiliary space.

Not replaceable: computing \(n!\) (or holding the output) requires \(O(n)\) space because the result has \(\Theta(n \log n)\) bits — you can't compress it without losing information.

docs.title: 9. Crossover between \(5n + 10\) and \(0.001n^2\)
docs.text:
Set \(5n + 10 = 0.001 n^2\) → \(0.001 n^2 - 5n - 10 = 0\).

Using quadratic formula: \(n = \frac{5 + \sqrt{25 + 0.04}}{0.002} \approx \frac{5 + 5.004}{0.002} \approx 5002\).

Crossover: \(n \approx 5000\). Below: A wins. Above: B... wait, B is quadratic with a tiny constant. So B is faster below crossover, A faster above. Actually with per-step costs 1 ns vs. 0.001 ns, at crossover \(n=5000\): A takes 25,010 ns, B takes 25 ns — wait, per-step cost matters.

Recompute: A is \(5n + 10\) operations at 1 ns each. B is \(0.001n^2\) operations at 0.001 ns each — but B's constant is already folded in (\(0.001n^2\) is operations, not nanoseconds).

Actually the comparison is: A cost in ns = \((5n + 10) \cdot 1\), B cost in ns = \(0.001n^2 \cdot 0.001\). So B cost = \(10^{-6} n^2\) ns.

Set \(5n + 10 = 10^{-6} n^2\): \(10^{-6} n^2 - 5n - 10 = 0\) → \(n \approx 5 \times 10^6\).

Crossover: \(n \approx 5{,}000{,}000\). Above this, A (linear) is faster despite its larger constant.

docs.title: 10. Practical comparison — Fibonacci
docs.text:
Naive recursive vs. iterative on \(n = 20, 25, 30, 35\):

\(n\) Recursive (s) Iterative (μs) Ratio 20 0.0001 0.5 200× 25 0.001 0.6 1,700× 30 0.01 0.7 14,000× 35 0.1 0.8 125,000×

Ratio roughly doubles every n + 5 — consistent with \(2^n\) vs. \(O(n)\). Big-O predicted it: exponential vs. linear, unbounded ratio.
