docs.title: 1. Prove a[i] is O(1)
docs.text: Address = base + i*w. Computation: 1 multiply, 1 add, 1 load = 3 instructions. Independent of i, n. O(1). ✓

docs.title: 2. Insertion cost table for n = 100
docs.text:
Position Shifts 0 100 25 75 50 50 75 25 100 0

Cheapest: insert at the end (0 shifts) — O(1).

docs.title: 3. Amortised doubling, n = 32
docs.text: Resizes at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (copies: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16). Total copies = 31. Amortised per insert = 31/32 < 1. ✓

docs.title: 4. +1 growth, n = 32
docs.text: Resizes at every size 1..31, copying 1, 2, ..., 31. Total = \(31 \cdot 32 / 2 = 496\). Ratio to doubling: 496/31 = 16×. O(n²). ✓

docs.title: 5. Binary search on 1024
docs.text:
\(n = 1024\), iterations = \(\lceil \log_2 1024 \rceil = 10\).

  • First element: 10 iterations (or fewer — depends on midpoint landing).
  • Last element: ~10.
  • Missing element: 10.

docs.title: 6. reverse(a, i, j)
docs.text:
void reverse(int[] a, int i, int j) {
    while (i < j) { int t=a[i]; a[i]=a[j]; a[j]=t; i++; j--; }
}

Cost: O(j − i), in-place.

docs.title: 7. Rotate [1,2,3,4,5] by k = 2
docs.text:
Three reversals: 1. Reverse all → [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] 2. Reverse first k=2 → [4, 5, 3, 2, 1] 3. Reverse rest → [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]

Expected: rotate right by 2 → [4, 5, 1, 2, 3] ✓

docs.title: 8. Two-pointer sum in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], target 15
docs.text:
left=0, right=5: sum = 1+11=12 <15 → left=1. left=1, right=5: sum = 3+11=14 <15 → left=2. left=2, right=5: sum = 5+11=16 >15 → right=4. left=2, right=4: sum = 5+9=14 <15 → left=3. left=3, right=4: sum = 7+9=16 >15 → right=3. Exit.

No pair sums to 15 in this array. (Closest: 5+9=14, 7+9=16.)

docs.title: 9. Row-major vs column-major on int[1000][1000]
docs.text:
Expected wall-clock: row-major ~5 ms, column-major ~25 ms. Ratio ~5× due to cache misses in column-major traversal.

Same Big-O: O(n²) for both.

docs.title: 10. Shrink thrashing
docs.text:
With shrink at size < capacity / 2: after add-then-remove alternating near the boundary, each remove triggers a resize to capacity/2, then the next add triggers a resize to capacity (since size > capacity/2 after the add). Each pair of operations does O(n) work. Amortised: O(n) per operation.

With shrink at size < capacity / 4: after shrinking to capacity/2, the array needs to grow again only after capacity/4 more adds. Buffer prevents thrashing. Amortised: O(1).

docs.title: 11. Array vs. linked-list, n = 100,000 random lookups
docs.text:
• Array (binary search): 17 lookups × 17 iterations = ~289 comparisons.
  • Linked list (linear): 17 × 50,000 (average) = 850,000 comparisons.

Array wins by ~2900×. Plus better cache locality → actual wall-clock gap is even bigger (~10,000×).

docs.title: 12. Two-pointer on unsorted, with sort
docs.text: Sort O(n log n) + two-pointer O(n) = O(n log n) total. Better than brute force O(n²).

docs.title: 13. Sliding window max average
docs.text: Maintain a running sum. Add a[i], subtract a[i-k], update max. O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Naive recomputes the sum every window → O(n·k).

docs.title: 14. Duplicate detection
docs.text:
• O(n²): nested loops comparing every pair.
  • O(n log n): sort, then check adjacent duplicates.
  • O(n): hash set — insert each; check if present first. O(n) space.

docs.title: 15. Missing number
docs.text:
Sum formula: expected sum = \(n(n+1)/2\). Actual sum = array sum. Missing = expected − actual.

Or XOR: XOR all 1..n and all array elements → result is the missing number. O(n) time, O(1) space. ✓

docs.text: Back to Chapter 3

docs.title: 1. Insert at head — build 5→4→3→2→1 from 1,2,3,4,5
docs.text:
Insert 1: 1
Insert 2: 2 → 1
Insert 3: 3 → 2 → 1
Insert 4: 4 → 3 → 2 → 1
Insert 5: 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1

Order reversed relative to insertion. O(1) per insert.

docs.title: 2. Insert at tail — build 1→2→3→4→5
docs.text:
With tail pointer: each insert O(1). Final: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5.

Without tail pointer: each insert walks to end — O(n²) total.

docs.title: 3. Delete all occurrences of v
docs.text:
Node deleteAll(Node head, int v) {
    while (head != null && head.value == v) head = head.next;
    Node cur = head;
    while (cur != null && cur.next != null) {
        if (cur.next.value == v) cur.next = cur.next.next;
        else cur = cur.next;
    }
    return head;
}

Edge cases: v at head (loop at top), v is the only value (loop runs to null → return null). O(n).

docs.title: 4. Reverse — iterative vs. recursive
docs.text:
Iterative: three pointers (prev, cur, next). O(n) time, O(1) space.

Recursive: reverse(head.next), then head.next.next = head; head.next = null. O(n) time, O(n) stack space.

Iterative is preferred for large lists.

docs.title: 5. Merge [1,3,5] + [2,4,6]
docs.text: Using dummy node: dummy → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → null. O(m+n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: 6. Remove duplicates
docs.text:
Sorted list: single pass, skip equal neighbors. O(n).

Unsorted list: hash set to track seen values. O(n) time, O(n) space. Or sort first (O(n log n)) then use sorted approach.

docs.title: 7. Detect and remove cycle
docs.text: Floyd's algorithm detects the meeting point. Then find entry point: reset slow to head, advance both one step until they meet → entry point. Then set prev.next = null (or the predecessor of the entry point) to break the cycle.

docs.title: 8. Middle with two pointers — trace on 1→2→3→4→5
docs.text:
Step slow fast 0 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 5 exit 3 5 (fast.next = null)

Middle = 3 ✓

On 1→2→3→4:

Step slow fast 0 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 null exit 3 null

Middle = 3 (upper middle of 2,3).

docs.title: 9. Merge sort a linked list
docs.text:
Split by finding the middle (slow, fast), sort each half recursively, merge.

Cost. Same recurrence as array merge sort: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n).

Better than array merge sort for linked lists: split doesn't need O(n) auxiliary space (you just detach the next pointer at mid). Merge is O(1) space. So O(n log n) time, O(log n) space (only recursion stack).

docs.title: 10. Josephus
docs.text:
For J(7, 3): - Eliminations: 3, 6, 2, 7, 5, 1 - Survivor: 4 ✓

Circular list simulation: O(n·k) time (n eliminations, each k steps). Closed-form recursion: J(n,k) = (J(n-1,k) + k) % n, base J(1,k)=0 → O(n) time.

docs.title: 11. LRU cache
docs.text:
Hash map (key → node) + doubly-linked list (recency order). Head = most recent, tail = least recent.

  • get(k): O(1) lookup + O(1) move to head.
  • put(k,v): O(1) insert/update + O(1) evict tail if full.

Every operation O(1).

docs.title: 12. Palindrome check on a linked list
docs.text:
1. Find middle (two-pointer). O(n).
  2. Reverse second half. O(n).
  3. Compare first half with reversed second. O(n).
  4. (Optional) Reverse second half back. O(n).

Total O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: 13. Add two numbers
docs.text:
2→4→3 + 5→6→4 (reversed digits): - 342 + 465 = 807 - Result list: 7 → 0 → 8 ✓

Algorithm. Walk both lists simultaneously, sum digit + carry, create new node per digit.

docs.title: 14. Copy list with random pointers
docs.text:
Three-pass O(n) approach: 1. For each original node, insert a clone immediately after it: A → A' → B → B' → … 2. Set clone.random = original.random.next (uses cloned layout). 3. Split the interleaved list into original and clone.

O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

docs.title: 15. Intersection of two lists
docs.text:
1. Compute lengths lenA, lenB.
  2. Advance the head of the longer list by |lenA − lenB|.
  3. Walk both in lockstep — first common node is the intersection.

O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: 8. Palindrome with deque — "racecar"
docs.text:
• Remove first 'r', last 'r' → equal. Remaining: "aceca".
  • Remove 'a', 'a' → equal. "cec".
  • Remove 'c', 'c' → equal. "e".
  • Single element → done.

Palindrome ✓. O(n) time, O(n) space (deque holds up to n).

docs.title: 10. Recursion depth — count-down from n
docs.text:
At n = 100,000: crashes with StackOverflowError — call stack has a fixed size (~1 MB); each frame is ~100 bytes; 10⁵ frames × 100 bytes = 10 MB > 1 MB.

Iterative rewrite:

void countDown(int n) {
    while (n >= 0) { System.out.println(n); n--; }
}

Memory: O(1) — a single loop. Speed: microseconds vs. crash.

docs.title: 11. Round-robin scheduler
docs.text:
Processes P1 (5ms), P2 (3ms), P3 (8ms). Quantum 2ms.

Turn Process Remaining 1 P1 (2ms) P1=3 2 P2 (2ms) P2=1 3 P3 (2ms) P3=6 4 P1 (2ms) P1=1 5 P2 (1ms → done) P2=0 6 P3 (2ms) P3=4 7 P1 (1ms → done) P1=0 8 P3 (2ms) P3=2 9 P3 (2ms → done) P3=0

Completion order: P2, P1, P3.

docs.title: 12. Array stack vs. linked-list stack for 10⁶ push + 10⁶ pop
docs.text:
Array stack preferred — amortised O(1), excellent cache locality (all pushes touch the same cache line region), ~2-3 ns per operation.

Linked-list stack — O(1) worst case but each push is a heap allocation (~20-30 ns), each pop deallocates. Cache misses per operation.

Winner: array stack for typical workloads.

docs.title: 13. BFS on a tree
docs.text:
Root=1, children 2,3; grandchildren 4,5 (from 2), 6,7 (from 3).

BFS order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 — level by level. ✓

docs.title: 14. Queue from two stacks
docs.text:
Two stacks: in_stack (enqueue target) and out_stack (dequeue target).

  • enqueue(x): push onto in_stack. O(1).
  • dequeue(): if out_stack is empty, pop all from in_stack and push onto out_stack; then pop from out_stack.

Amortised cost: each element is pushed to in_stack once, transferred to out_stack once, popped from out_stack once. Total 3 pushes/pops per element = O(1) amortised.

docs.title: 15. Wildcard valid parentheses
docs.text:
( ) * (wildcard = (, ), or empty).

Greedy (two-pass) approach: 1. Left-to-right: treat * as ( and ). Track low (min unmatched opens) and high (max unmatched opens). If high < 0, return false. 2. After the pass, if low == 0, return true.

O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.text:
Insert Rotations 1 — 2 — 3 RR at 1 (1 left) 4 — 5 RR at 3 6 — 7 RR at 4 (after rebalance: 2 → 6 with children 4, 7; actually LR case at 2? Verify)

Let me re-trace:

  • After 1,2,3: rotate → 2 / 1 \ 3.
  • Insert 4: 2 / 1 \ 3 \ 4. bf(3)=+1, OK.
  • Insert 5: 2 / 1 \ 3 \ 4 \ 5. bf(3)=+2 → RR at 3. After: 2 / 1 \ 4 / 3 \ 5.
  • Insert 6: 2 / 1 \ 4 / 3 \ 5 \ 6. bf(5)=+1, OK.

Insert Array after sift-up 10 [10] 20 [10, 20] 5 [5, 20, 10] (sift 5 to root) 3 [3, 5, 10, 20] (sift 3 to root) 15 [3, 5, 10, 20, 15] (no sift) 8 [3, 5, 8, 20, 15, 10] (sift 8: parent(5)=index 2, swap 10↔8)

Final array: [3, 5, 8, 20, 15, 10].

docs.title: 10. Extract min from heap [3, 5, 8, 20, 15, 10]
docs.text:
Save min=3. Move last (10) to root: [10, 5, 8, 20, 15].

Sift-down: - Children 5, 8. Min=5. 10>5 → swap: [5, 10, 8, 20, 15]. - At index 1 (10): children 20, 15. Min=15. 10<15 → no swap.

Result: [5, 10, 8, 20, 15]. Extracted: 3.

docs.title: 11. Heapify [5, 8, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2] (min-heap)
docs.text:
n = 7. Last internal = index 7/2 - 1 = 2.

i=2 (value 3): children 7, 2. Min=2 (index 6). 3>2 → swap. [5, 8, 2, 9, 1, 7, 3].

i=1 (value 8): children 9, 1. Min=1 (index 4). 8>1 → swap. [5, 1, 2, 9, 8, 7, 3]. At index 4: no children.

i=0 (value 5): children 1, 2. Min=1 (index 1). 5>1 → swap. [1, 5, 2, 9, 8, 7, 3]. At index 1 (5): children 9, 8. Min=8 (index 4). 5<8 → no swap.

Final: [1, 5, 2, 9, 8, 7, 3].

docs.title: 13. Max in a min-heap
docs.text:
Min-heap: root = min. To find max, must check all leaves (nodes at indices n/2 to n-1).

O(n) time — can't do better because any leaf could be the max.

In a max-heap: root = max, O(1).

docs.title: 14. BST validity check
docs.text:
boolean isBST(TreeNode node, long min, long max) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (node.value <= min || node.value >= max) return false;
    return isBST(node.left, min, node.value) && isBST(node.right, node.value, max);
}
// call: isBST(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE)

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Common bug: only checking node.left.value < node.value < node.right.value — misses cases like:

    5
   / \
  3   8
     /
    4     ← 4 < 5 but in the right subtree — invalid

The min/max bound propagation is required.

docs.title: 15. Reconstruct from in-order + pre-order
docs.text:
in-order = [4, 2, 5, 1, 3], pre-order = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3].

Pre-order gives root = 1. Find 1 in in-order (index 3). Left subtree = in-order[0..2] = [4,2,5]; right = in-order[4..4] = [3].

Recurse on left: pre-order[1..3] = [2,4,5], in-order = [4,2,5]. Root = 2. Left = [4], right = [5].

Recurse on right of root: pre-order[4] = [3], in-order = [3]. Root = 3.

Tree: 

        1
       / \
      2   3
     / \
    4   5

docs.title: 16. Level-order reconstruction
docs.text:
No, not unique. Level-order [1, 2, 3] could be: - Root 1, left 2, right 3. - Root 1, left 3, right 2. - Root 1, only right child 2, whose left child is 3.

Without more information (like whether it's a BST, or null markers), level-order alone can't reconstruct the tree.

docs.title: 17. B+-tree motivation
docs.text:
Approach Disk reads Sorted array binary search ~20 (log₂ 10⁶) BST ~20 (log₂ 10⁶ in balanced case) B+-tree, branching 200 ~3 (log₂₀₀ 10⁶ = 3)

B+-tree reads 3 disk blocks per lookup; BST reads 20. The 7× speedup is why databases use B+-trees.

docs.title: 1. Division method — {3, 6, 9, 12, 15}
docs.text:
m = 4: h(k) = {3, 2, 1, 0, 3} — collision between 3 and 15 → 1 collision.

m = 5: h(k) = {3, 1, 4, 2, 0} — all distinct → 0 collisions.

m = 7: h(k) = {3, 6, 2, 5, 1} — all distinct → 0 collisions.

Best: m = 5 or 7 (prime, doesn't share factors with the common difference 3). Worst: m = 4 (has factor 2, doesn't divide 3 — so 3 and 15 collide).

Wait, m=4: 15 mod 4 = 3, 3 mod 4 = 3 — collide. Why? 15 - 3 = 12, and 12 is divisible by 4. Keys differing by multiples of m collide.

docs.title: 4. Chaining trace, m=5, keys {12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37}
docs.text:
h(k) = k mod 5: {2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2}. All collide at bucket 2!

Bucket 0 1 2 3 4 — — 37 → 32 → 27 → 22 → 17 → 12 — —

Max chain length: 6. This is a terrible hash function for these keys (all ≡ 2 mod 5). Fix: use a prime m that doesn't divide (17-12) = 5, (22-17) = 5, ... — wait, all differences are 5, so any m that divides 5 collides. Use m = 7 (prime, doesn't divide 5) → all distinct.

docs.title: 5. Linear probing, m=7, same keys
docs.text:
h(k) = k mod 7: {5, 3, 1, 6, 4, 2} — all distinct, no probing needed.

Hmm, that's different from problem 4 because m changed from 5 to 7. All distinct → 0 probes.

Let me redo with m=5 (same as problem 4): - Insert 12: h=2, empty → slot 2. - Insert 17: h=2, occupied by 12 → probe 3, empty → slot 3. - Insert 22: h=2, occupied by 12 → probe 3 (17) → probe 4 → slot 4. - Insert 27: h=2 → 3 → 4 → probe 0 → slot 0. - Insert 32: h=2 → 3 → 4 → 0 → 1 → slot 1. - Insert 37: h=2 → 3 → 4 → 0 → 1 → 2 → full — need resize.

Table: [27, 32, 12, 17, 22] (all 5 slots filled, then resize).

Max probes for insert 37: 6 (checked all 5 slots). Bad.

docs.title: 6. Quadratic probing, m=7, same keys {12,17,22,27,32,37}
docs.text:
h(k) = k mod 7 = {5, 3, 1, 6, 4, 2} — all distinct.

No probing needed. All slots filled directly.

docs.title: 7. Double hashing, m=11, keys {22,33,44,55,66}
docs.text:
h₁(k) = k mod 11, h₂(k) = 1 + (k mod 10).

Key h₁ h₂ Probe sequence 22 0 1+2=3 0, 3, 6, 9, 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8 33 0 1+3=4 0, 4, 8, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 10, 3, 7 44 0 1+4=5 0, 5, 10, 4, 9, 3, 8, 2, 7, 1, 6 55 0 1+5=6 0, 6, 1, 7, 2, 8, 3, 9, 4, 10, 5 66 0 1+6=7 0, 7, 3, 10, 6, 2, 9, 5, 1, 8, 4

All start at h₁=0 (collision) but follow different probe sequences thanks to h₂.

Insertion: - 22 → slot 0. - 33 → slot 0 occupied → probe 4 → slot 4. - 44 → 0 occupied, 4 occupied → probe 10 → slot 10. - 55 → 0, 4, 10 occupied → probe 1 → slot 1. - 66 → 0, 4, 10, 1 occupied → probe 7 → slot 7.

Final: slot 0=22, 1=55, 4=33, 7=66, 10=44.

No primary or secondary clustering — the probe sequences diverge. ✓

docs.title: 8. Tombstone trace
docs.text:
Insert {10, 20, 30} into m=5 with linear probing, h(k) = k mod 5.

  • 10 → slot 0.
  • 20 → slot 0 occupied → slot 1.
  • 30 → slot 0 occupied → slot 1 occupied → slot 2.

Table: [10, 20, 30, _, _].

Delete 20 → tombstone at slot 1: [10, X, 30, _, _].

Lookup 30: h(30)=0 → slot 0 (10, no match) → slot 1 (X, keep going) → slot 2 (30, match) ✓ — 3 probes.

Now delete 10 → tombstone at slot 0: [X, X, 30, _, _].

Lookup 30: slot 0 (X) → slot 1 (X) → slot 2 (30) ✓ — 3 probes.

Without tombstones (set deleted slots to EMPTY): after deleting 20, slot 1 is EMPTY. Lookup 30 starts at slot 0, sees 10 (no match), then slot 1 (EMPTY → stop), returns "not found" — WRONG.

This is why tombstones are required. ✓

docs.title: 9. Load factor α = 0.5, linear probing
docs.text:
Successful lookup: expected probes = ½(1 + 1/(1−0.5)) = ½(1 + 2) = 1.5.

Unsuccessful lookup: expected probes = ½(1 + 1/(1−0.5)²) = ½(1 + 4) = 2.5.

docs.title: 10. Amortised rehashing — 1000 inserts, doubling
docs.text:
Starting size 2, doubling at α > 0.75 → resize at sizes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024.

Rehash at sizes 2, 4, ..., 512: total work = 2 + 4 + 8 + ... + 512 = 1022 operations.

Plus 1000 inserts = 2022 operations total. Amortised per insert: 2.022 = O(1). ✓

docs.title: 13. Longest substring without repeating chars
docs.text:
Sliding window with hash map char → last index. Extend right pointer; if char repeats, jump left pointer to last index + 1. Track max window size.

O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

For "abcabcbb": - Window "abc" (max 3) → next 'a' repeats → new window "bca" → etc. - Answer: 3.

docs.title: 14. Group anagrams
docs.text:
For each string, sort characters → use as hash map key. Append original string to the value list.

O(n · k log k) time (k = max string length), O(n · k) space.

For ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]: - "eat" sorted = "aet" → ["eat"] - "tea" sorted = "aet" → ["eat", "tea"] - "tan" sorted = "ant" → ["tan"] - "ate" sorted = "aet" → ["eat", "tea", "ate"] - "nat" sorted = "ant" → ["tan", "nat"] - "bat" sorted = "abt" → ["bat"]

Groups: [["eat","tea","ate"], ["tan","nat"], ["bat"]].

docs.title: 15. Subarray sum = K
docs.text:
Track prefix sums in a hash map: prefix → count. For each index, target_prefix = current_prefix − K; if target_prefix is in the map, add its count to answer.

O(n) time, O(n) space.

For [1, 1, 1], K=2: - prefix = 1, map {0:1, 1:1} - prefix = 2, target=0 in map (count=1) → ans += 1. Map {0:1, 1:1, 2:1}. - prefix = 3, target=1 in map (count=1) → ans += 1. Map {0:1, 1:1, 2:1, 3:1}.

Answer: 2 (subarrays [1,1] at indices 0-1 and 1-2). ✓

docs.text: Back to Chapter 7

docs.title: 1. Adjacency matrix vs. list — graph from Example 7.1 (n=6, m=7)
docs.text:
Adjacency matrix: 6×6 = 36 ints × 4 bytes = 144 bytes.

Adjacency list: 6 header pointers × 8 bytes = 48 bytes, plus 14 entries (2 × 7 for undirected) × (int + pointer) = 14 × 12 = 168 bytes, total ≈ 216 bytes.

For sparse graphs (m ≈ n), memory is comparable, but list scales with m, matrix with n². For n=10,000, m=20,000: matrix = 400 MB, list ≈ 240 KB — 1600× difference.

docs.title: 3. DFS from 2 (recursive, sorted neighbors)
docs.text:
DFS(2) → visit 2 → neighbors [0, 4]. - DFS(0) → visit 0 → neighbors [1, 2]. - DFS(1) → visit 1 → neighbors [0, 3, 4]. - DFS(3) → visit 3 → neighbors [1, 5]. - DFS(5) → visit 5 → neighbors [3, 4]. - DFS(4) → visit 4 → neighbors [1, 2, 5] — all visited.

Visit order: 2, 0, 1, 3, 5, 4.

DFS tree edges: 2→0, 0→1, 1→3, 3→5, 5→4.

docs.title: 4. Connected components
docs.text:
int countComponents(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[adj.size()];
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < adj.size(); i++) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            bfsMark(adj, i, visited);
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

O(V + E) time.

docs.title: 5. Bipartite check
docs.text:
Color vertices with 2 colors such that every edge connects different colors. During BFS, alternate colors on each level. If an edge connects same-color vertices, graph is not bipartite.

O(V + E) time.

docs.title: 6. Cycle detection (undirected)
docs.text:
DFS: track parent. If a visited neighbor is not the parent, there's a cycle.

boolean hasCycle(int u, int parent, boolean[] visited, List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
        if (!visited[v]) {
            if (hasCycle(v, u, visited, adj)) return true;
        } else if (v != parent) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

O(V + E) time.

docs.title: 7. Cycle detection (directed)
docs.text:
3-color DFS: WHITE (unvisited), GRAY (in stack), BLACK (fully explored). Cycle if any back edge to a GRAY node.

The undirected approach (parent check) fails on directed graphs because u → v and u → w → v is not a cycle but a diamond — parent check flags v as seen which is wrong.

O(V + E) time.

docs.title: 8. Topological sort
docs.text:
DFS approach: reverse postorder.

void topoDFS(int u, boolean[] visited, Deque<Integer> stack, List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (!visited[v]) topoDFS(v, visited, stack, adj);
    stack.push(u);
}
// after all DFS starts, stack (bottom to top) is topological order

Kahn's algorithm (BFS): compute in-degrees; enqueue nodes with 0 in-degree; pop, decrement neighbors' in-degrees, enqueue new 0s.

Both O(V + E). Result may differ if multiple valid orderings exist.

docs.title: 10. Dijkstra fails with negative edges
docs.text:
Graph: s→u (1), s→v (4), u→v (-3).

Dijkstra from s: - Pop s (dist 0), relax: u←1, v←4. - Pop u (dist 1), relax u→v: 1 + (-3) = -2 < 4 → but wait, if v was already popped at dist 4, we'd have missed this. In this graph, u is popped before v (dist 1 < 4), so v gets updated to -2. Dijkstra actually works here.

Let me construct a failure case: s→u (1), s→v (2), u→v (-5). - Pop s (dist 0), relax: u←1, v←2. - Pop u (dist 1), relax u→v: 1 + (-5) = -4 < 2 → update v←-4. Still works because u is popped before v.

Construct: s→u (5), s→v (3), u→v (-10), u→w (1), v→w (1).

  • Pop s (0), relax: u←5, v←3.
  • Pop v (3), relax v→w: 3+1=4 → w←4. Also v→u? No edge.
  • Pop w (4), no outgoing. w finalized at 4.
  • Pop u (5), relax u→v: 5+(-10)=-5 < 3 → update v←-5. relax u→w: 5+1=6 > 4, no.
  • Pop v (-5). Done.

But w's dist was finalized at 4 — should have been 5 + (-10) + 1 = -4 via u→v→w. Dijkstra missed it because it finalized w before relaxing u.

Correct answer: w = -4. Dijkstra returns 4. Bellman–Ford gives -4. ✓

docs.title: 11. Bellman–Ford with negative cycle
docs.text:
Graph: edges (0,1,4), (0,2,5), (1,2,-3), (2,3,-1).

Pass dist [0..3] init [0, ∞, ∞, ∞] 1 [0, 4, 1, 0] 2 [0, 4, 1, 0] (stable) 3 [0, 4, 1, 0] (stable)

Converged in 2 passes. No negative cycle.

Add (3,1,-10) → cycle 1→2→3→1: -3 + (-1) + (-10) = -14, negative cycle.

Pass 3 would detect: relax (3,1) with dist[3] = 0: 0 + (-10) = -10 < 4 → update dist[1] = -10. Change on the V-th pass → negative cycle detected.

docs.title: 14. MST uniqueness
docs.text:
MST is unique iff all edge weights are distinct. If two edges have equal weight, there may be multiple MSTs (as in Example 7.5, where edges (1,3), (2,3), (1,3) all have weight 5 — choosing either (1,3) or a different weight-5 edge gives a valid MST).

Example: triangle with all weights 1. Any two edges form an MST — 3 possible MSTs, all weight 2.

docs.title: 15. Road network
docs.text:
Representation: adjacency list — road networks are sparse (average city has ~3-4 roads per intersection).

Shortest route: Dijkstra — road weights are non-negative (distance).

Cheapest construction: Kruskal or Prim for MST — connects all towns with minimum total road length.

docs.title: 16. Social network — 100M users, path from Alice to Bob
docs.text:
Adjacency matrix: 100M × 100M ints × 4 bytes = 40 quadrillion bytes = 40 petabytes. Impossible.

Adjacency list: 100M users × ~200 friends × 12 bytes ≈ 240 GB. Feasible on a large server.

Use adjacency list — sparse graph.

docs.title: 1. Bubble sort — [5, 3, 1, 4, 2]
docs.text:
Pass 1: - (5,3) swap → [3,5,1,4,2] - (5,1) swap → [3,1,5,4,2] - (5,4) swap → [3,1,4,5,2] - (5,2) swap → [3,1,4,2,5] (5 at end)

Pass 2: - (3,1) swap → [1,3,4,2,5] - (3,4) keep - (4,2) swap → [1,3,2,4,5]

Pass 3: - (1,3) keep - (3,2) swap → [1,2,3,4,5]

Pass 4: no swaps → done.

Total passes: 4. Total comparisons: 4+3+2+1 = 10. Swaps: 6.

docs.title: 3. Selection sort — [5, 3, 1, 4, 2]
docs.text:
i Min in suffix Swap 0 1 (idx 2) swap 5, 1 → [1, 3, 5, 4, 2] 1 2 (idx 4) swap 3, 2 → [1, 2, 5, 4, 3] 2 3 (idx 4) swap 5, 3 → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 3 4 (idx 3) no swap

Total swaps: 3. Comparisons: 4+3+2+1 = 10.

docs.title: 4. Merge sort — [5, 3, 1, 4, 2]
docs.text:
Divide: [5,3,1] | [4,2].

Recursively: [5] + [3,1] → [5] + [1,3] → [1,3,5].

[4] + [2] → [2,4].

Merge [1,3,5] + [2,4]: - 1 vs 2 → 1 - 3 vs 2 → 2 - 3 vs 4 → 3 - 5 vs 4 → 4 - 5 → 5

Result: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] ✓

Comparisons: level 1 (~2), level 2 (~2), merge (~4). Total ≈ 8. O(n log n).

docs.title: 5. Quicksort — [5, 3, 1, 4, 2], last-element pivot
docs.text:
Pivot = 2 (index 4).

Partition: i=-1. Scan j=0..3: - j=0, a[0]=5 > 2, no swap. - j=1, a[1]=3 > 2, no swap. - j=2, a[2]=1 < 2, i=0, swap a[0]↔a[2] → [1, 3, 5, 4, 2]. - j=3, a[3]=4 > 2, no swap.

Final: swap a[1]↔a[4] → [1, 2, 5, 4, 3]. Pivot at index 1.

Left [1] — sorted.

Right [5, 4, 3] (indices 2-4), pivot=3 (index 4): - Partition: j=2, a=5 > 3 no; j=3, a=4 > 3 no. Final swap a[2]↔a[4] → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Pivot at index 2.

Left [3] sorted. Right [4, 5], pivot=5: - Partition: j=3, a=4 < 5 → i=3, no swap (already at i). Final swap a[4]↔a[4] → no change. Pivot at index 4.

Left [4] sorted. Done.

Result: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Total comparisons ≈ 8.

docs.title: 6. Quicksort worst case — [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
docs.text:
Pivot = last element each time.

  • Partition 1 (pivot=6): 5 comparisons, splits off 6.
  • Partition 2 (pivot=5): 4 comparisons, splits off 5.
  • Partition 3 (pivot=4): 3 comparisons.
  • Partition 4 (pivot=3): 2 comparisons.
  • Partition 5 (pivot=2): 1 comparison.

Total comparisons: 15 = n(n−1)/2 = O(n²).

Compare with already-sorted vs random — for random, expected is O(n log n) ≈ 12–15 comparisons. Sorted input hits the worst case. Fix: random pivot or median-of-three.

docs.title: 7. Heapsort — [5, 3, 1, 4, 2]
docs.text:
Build max-heap:

  • i=1 (value 3): children indices 3, 4 (4, 2). Max child 4. 3 < 4 → swap. [5, 4, 1, 3, 2].
  • i=0 (value 5): children 4, 1. Max child 4. 5 > 4 → no swap.

Max-heap: [5, 4, 1, 3, 2].

Extract-max:

Step Array before After swap & sift 1 [5, 4, 1, 3, 2] [4, 3, 1, 2, 5] 2 [4, 3, 1, 2, 5] [3, 2, 1, 4, 5] 3 [3, 2, 1, 4, 5] [2, 1, 3, 4, 5] 4 [2, 1, 3, 4, 5] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] ✓

docs.title: 8. Stability test [(3,A), (1,B), (2,C), (3,D), (1,E)]
docs.text:
Merge sort (stable): → [(1,B), (1,E), (2,C), (3,A), (3,D)]. B before E, A before D. ✓

Quicksort (unstable): could produce [(1,E), (1,B), (2,C), (3,D), (3,A)] — E before B, D before A. ✗

Merge sort preserves relative order of equal keys.

docs.title: 9. Nearly-sorted (90% sorted) analysis
docs.text:
Insertion sort — its O(n) best case extends to nearly-sorted: if only k elements are out of place, insertion sort does at most O(n + k·inversions) work. For 90% sorted with ~10% out of place, inversions ≈ 0.1n × avg distance ≈ O(n).

Comparisons: ~1.1n. Best choice.

docs.text: Sort Best Average Worst Bubble 999 ~500k ~500k Insertion 999 ~250k ~500k Selection ~500k ~500k ~500k Merge ~10k ~10k ~10k Quicksort ~10k ~10k ~500k Heapsort ~10k ~10k ~10k

docs.title: 11. External sort — 10 GB on 1 GB RAM
docs.text:
External merge sort: 1. Read 1 GB chunks; sort each in memory; write back to disk as a run. → 10 sorted runs of 1 GB each. 2. K-way merge: open all 10 runs, keep one block from each in memory, merge using a heap. Write output sequentially.

Total disk I/O: 2 passes (read all, write all) + merge passes. O(n log(n/m)) where m = number of runs.

Feasible on any disk — the RAM constraint is respected throughout.

docs.title: 12. Counting sort for 10M integers in [0, 1000]
docs.text:
Counting sort: 1. Create a count array of size 1001. O(1001) space. 2. Count occurrences of each value. O(n). 3. Reconstruct sorted array. O(n + 1001).

Total O(n + k) = O(10M + 1001) ≈ 10M operations — 20× faster than O(n log n) ≈ 230M comparisons.

Requires: keys in a known bounded range (0..1000). ✓
